nodes.description: Amends HEA §458(a)(1) (20 U.S.C. 1087h(a)(1)) to read: 'There shall be available to the Secretary (in addition to any other amounts appropriated under any appropriations Act for administrative costs under this part and part B and out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated) $1,000,000,000 to be obligated for administrative costs under this part and part B, including the costs of servicing the direct student loan programs under this part, which shall remain available until expended.' Mandatory (non-appropriated) funding. Suggests administration anticipates substantial complexity in transitioning millions of borrowers off SAVE/ICR into RAP.

nodes.title: Icebreaker shipyard incumbent-protection qualification clause
nodes.description: SEC. 40001 item (8): '$816,000,000 is provided for procurement of light and medium icebreaking cutters...from shipyards that have demonstrated success in the cost-effective application of design standards and in delivering, on schedule and within budget, vessels of a size and tonnage that are not less than the size and tonnage of the cutters described in this paragraph.' This qualification requirement effectively restricts the eligible bidder pool to established large-vessel shipbuilders, creating a de facto incumbent-protection clause that disadvantages new entrants to icebreaker construction.

nodes.title: SEC. 50401 — Strategic Petroleum Reserve
nodes.description: 'there is appropriated to the Department of Energy for fiscal year 2025... to remain available until September 30, 2029 — (1) ,000,000 for maintenance of, including repairs to, storage facilities and related facilities of the Strategic Petroleum Reserve; and (2) ,000,000 to acquire, by purchase, petroleum products for storage in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve.' Total appropriation: ,000,000. Also repeals TCJA drawdown mandate: 'Section 20003 of Public Law 115–97 (42 U.S.C. 6241 note) is repealed.' The TCJA §20003 had required SPR drawdowns to fund federal budget operations — its repeal removes a scheduled future source of offsetting receipts that CBO had previously scored. Increases net deficit impact of broader legislation. Benefits national energy security and domestic petroleum producers (fewer government-driven SPR sales into market). Funds available through September 30, 2029.

nodes.title: SEC. 70511 — Termination of Clean Hydrogen Production Credit
nodes.description: Amends IRC § 45V(c)(3)(C) striking 'January 1, 2033' and inserting 'January 1, 2028'. Accelerates termination of clean hydrogen production credit (up to $3/kg for lowest-emission 'green' hydrogen) by 5 years. Credit enacted by IRA 2022 § 13204. Construction of hydrogen production facilities must begin before January 1, 2028. Facilities already under construction can still qualify. Only amends construction commencement cutoff — does NOT change 10-year credit period once facility qualifies (facility beginning construction Dec 31, 2027 could collect credits through 2037). CBO estimates exceeded $100 billion over the full original window. Loses: Plug Power, Air Products, Linde hydrogen projects, Bloom Energy, emerging electrolysis startups, hydrogen refueling, fuel cell vehicle developers, offshore wind projects paired with hydrogen production. Blue hydrogen (natural gas + CCS) and pink hydrogen (nuclear-powered electrolysis) remain available for shortened window.

nodes.title: Retroactive Reimbursement to January 20, 2021 — Political Targeting
nodes.description: Sec. 90005(b)(4): 'The Secretary of Homeland Security may provide grants from the fund established by paragraph (1) to State agencies and units of local governments for expenditures made for completed, ongoing, or new activities, in accordance with law, that occurred on or after January 20, 2021.' January 20, 2021 is the date of President Biden's inauguration — the effective date means the fund retroactively reimburses states for border enforcement activities conducted during the entire Biden administration. Texas alone spent $4B+ on Operation Lone Star during that period. Sec. 90005(b)(2)(D) also explicitly authorizes federal grants for 'Relocation of aliens who are unlawfully present in the United States from small population centers to other domestic locations' — legalizing and federally funding migrant busing programs operated by Republican governors (Texas Gov. Abbott, Florida Gov. DeSantis). This is a direct retroactive federal subsidy for actions taken in opposition to Biden-era federal immigration policy.

nodes.title: SEC. 10305 — Agriculture Risk Coverage
nodes.description: Amends 7 USC 9017. Extends ARC through 2031. Key changes: subsection (c)(1) inserts 'for each of the 2014 through 2024 crop years and 90 percent of the benchmark revenue for each of the 2025 through 2031 crop years' — raises guarantee trigger from 86% to 90% of benchmark revenue for 2025-2031. Subsection (d)(1) replaces subparagraph (B): '(i) for each of the 2014 through 2024 crop years, 10 percent of the benchmark revenue for the crop year applicable under subsection (c); and (ii) for each of the 2025 through 2031 crop years, 12 percent of the benchmark revenue for the crop year applicable under subsection (c).' — raises deductible from 10% to 12% for 2025-2031. Net effect: ARC payments trigger sooner (90% vs 86%) but each payment is slightly smaller (12% deductible vs 10%). Extended through 2031 in subsections (e), (g)(5), and (i)(5).

nodes.title: SEC. 71111 — Moratorium on Nursing Home Staffing Standards Rule (through Sept 30, 2034)
nodes.description: Prohibits HHS from implementing 89 Fed. Reg. 40876 (May 10, 2024), 'Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Minimum Staffing Standards for Long-Term Care Facilities and Medicaid Institutional Payment Transparency Reporting,' from enactment through September 30, 2034. Freezes 42 CFR §483.5 (definitions) and §483.35 (nursing services requirements as amended). The rule required: 3.48 total nurse staffing hours per resident per day; 0.55 hours from RN; 2.45 hours from nurse aide; RN on-site 24/7. No appropriation. Effective immediately. ~1.2 million long-term care residents live in facilities that do not currently meet staffing requirements. Compliance would have cost operators ~.4 billion annually. Research: higher staffing ratios reduce mortality, pressure ulcers, falls, infections, hospitalizations. Moratorium also freezes transparency reporting provisions — facilities not required to publicly disclose staffing levels.

nodes.title: SEC. 100008 — FORM I-94 FEE (8 U.S.C. 1807)
nodes.description: New $24 fee for any alien filing for a Form I-94 Arrival/Departure Record. Verbatim (lines 17175-17214): 'the Secretary of Homeland Security shall require the payment of a fee, equal to the amount specified in subsection (b), by any alien who submits an application for a Form I–94 Arrival/Departure Record.' INITIAL: greater of $24 or higher by rule. CPI-indexed rounded down to nearest dollar. DISPOSITION: '20 percent of the fees collected pursuant to this section— (A) shall be deposited into the Land Border Inspection Fee Account in accordance with section 286(q)(2) (8 U.S.C. 1356(q)(2)); and (B) shall be made available to U.S. Customs and Border Protection to retain and spend without further appropriation for the purpose of processing Form I–94; and (2) any amounts not deposited into the Land Border Inspection Fee Account... shall be deposited in the general fund of the Treasury.' So 20% to CBP; 80% to Treasury. NO FEE WAIVER. Currently I-94 is processed automatically for air/sea arrivals; land border travelers pay. This formalizes/expands fee to virtually all nonimmigrant arrivals. Cross-refs: INA § 286(q)(2) (8 U.S.C. 1356(q)(2)).

nodes.title: SEC. 60018 — Rescission of Funding for Environmental and Climate Data Collection
nodes.description: Verbatim bill text: 'The unobligated balances of amounts made available to carry out section 60401 of Public Law 117-169 (136 Stat. 2079) are rescinded.' Analysis: Cancels unspent IRA funds for collection and analysis of environmental and climate data, including monitoring infrastructure and scientific data systems. IRA appropriated $10 million under Sec. 60401. Effective on enactment. Losers: NOAA, EPA, and other agencies relying on this data; climate science community; emergency preparedness planners.

nodes.title: SEC. 71306 — Permanent Extension of Safe Harbor for Absence of Deductible for Telehealth Services
nodes.description: Subparagraph (E) of section 223(c)(2) is amended to read as follows: '(E) SAFE HARBOR FOR ABSENCE OF DEDUCTIBLE FOR TELEHEALTH.—A plan shall not fail to be treated as a high deductible health plan by reason of failing to have a deductible for telehealth and other remote care services.' Clause (ii) of section 223(c)(1)(B) is amended by striking '(in the case of months or plan years to which paragraph (2)(E) applies)' — removes temporal limitation, making the safe harbor permanent. EFFECTIVE DATE: plan years beginning after December 31, 2024. [Lines 14564–14576]

nodes.title: SEC. 20012 — Department of Defense Oversight
nodes.description: Appropriates $10,000,000 to the DoD Inspector General to monitor all programs funded under Title II. Bill text (lines 3096-3106), verbatim: 'there is appropriated to the Inspector General of the Department of Defense for fiscal year 2025, out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, $10,000,000, to remain available through September 30, 2029, to monitor Department of Defense activities for which funding is appropriated in this title, including— (1) programs with mutual technological dependencies; (2) programs with related data management and data ownership considerations; and (3) programs particularly vulnerable to supply chain disruptions and long lead time components.' The $10M IG appropriation is strikingly disproportionate: Title II contains approximately $150 billion in new appropriations, making this 0.006% oversight coverage. The IG mandate is also narrowed to three specific risk categories rather than general fraud/waste/abuse oversight. Appropriated directly to the IG (independent of SecDef), preserving some independence. Funds through September 30, 2029.

nodes.title: Presidential Private Residence Security — Mar-a-Lago Backdated to July 1, 2024
nodes.description: Sec. 90006: Appropriates $300,000,000 to FEMA available until September 30, 2029. Funds available only for costs 'incurred or incurs on or after July 1, 2024' — retroactive to before Trump's election win on November 5, 2024. The 'nongovernmental property' qualifier explicitly targets privately-owned presidential residences (Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach, FL and Bedminster, NJ) rather than Camp David or the White House. Palm Beach County has spent tens of millions on security perimeters. The retroactive date captures the period when Mar-a-Lago was a candidate's home, not yet a presidential residence. No cap on how many properties can qualify — if additional residences are designated by Secret Service, they become eligible. FEMA retains up to 3 percent (~$9M) for administration.

nodes.title: SEC. 70312 — Modifications to Determination of Deemed Paid Credit for Taxes Properly Attributable to Tested Income
nodes.description: Increases the deemed-paid FTC for CFC taxes on GILTI/tested income from 80% to 90%. §960(d)(1): '80 percent' to '90 percent'. §78 gross-up: '80 percent' to '90 percent'. New §960(d)(4): permanently disallows FTC for 10% of foreign income taxes paid or accrued on §959(a) exclusions (distributions of previously taxed net CFC tested income amounts). Rate increase effective: tax years beginning after December 31, 2025. New disallowance: applies to foreign income taxes paid/deemed paid on §959(a) exclusions after June 28, 2025. Benefits companies with high-tax CFCs operating in countries with foreign tax rates above ~18% — more of the foreign tax offsets U.S. GILTI liability.

nodes.title: Budget process waiver on $24.6B Coast Guard appropriation
nodes.description: SEC. 40001 waives 31 USC 1131, 1132, 1133, and 1156 — standard budget process controls — to allow 'expedited processes' for the $24.6 billion Coast Guard appropriation. Waived statutes govern budget justifications, apportionment, and allotment controls. Waiving these provisions reduces ordinary congressional and OMB oversight protections for the largest single-agency infusion in Coast Guard history.

nodes.title: SEC. 10306 — Equitable Treatment of Certain Entities
nodes.description: Amends 7 USC 1308 and related sections. Creates new definition: '(5) QUALIFIED PASS-THROUGH ENTITY.—The term qualified pass-through entity means— (A) a partnership (within the meaning of subchapter K of chapter 1 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986); (B) an S corporation (as defined in section 1361 of that Code); (C) a limited liability company that does not affirmatively elect to be treated as a corporation; and (D) a joint venture or general partnership.' Replaces prior 'except a joint venture or general partnership' language with 'except a qualified pass-through entity' throughout subsections (b) and (c). Also amends 7 USC 1308-1(b)(2), 1308-2(d), 1308-3a(d). Effect: S corporations and LLCs now receive same favorable payment attribution as joint ventures and general partnerships — each member counted separately for payment limit purposes, potentially multiplying total farm program payment limits for large operations.

nodes.title: SEC. 50402 — Repeals and Rescissions (IRA Energy Programs)
nodes.description: Full repeal: 'Section 50142 of Public Law 117–169... (commonly known as the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022) is repealed and the unobligated balance of amounts made available under that section... is rescinded.' §50142 = advanced industrial facilities decarbonization program. Rescissions (unobligated balances only): '(A) Section 50123 (42 U.S.C. 18795b)' — high-efficiency electric home rebate (HEEHRA) program; '(B) Section 50141' — clean energy technology accelerator; '(C) Section 50144' — industrial demonstration projects; '(D) Section 50145' — advanced manufacturing/clean energy loan guarantees; '(E) Section 50151 (42 U.S.C. 18715)' — ARPA-E; '(F) Section 50152 (42 U.S.C. 18715a)' — Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations; '(G) Section 50153 (42 U.S.C. 18715b)' — grid resilience and innovation; '(H) Section 50161 (42 U.S.C. 17113b)' — industrial decarbonization. Original IRA appropriations for these sections totaled several billion dollars. ARPA-E rescission notable — bipartisan program with broad congressional support. Only already-obligated funds unaffected. Effective immediately.

nodes.title: SEC. 60019 — Rescission of Neighborhood Access and Equity Grant Program
nodes.description: Verbatim bill text: 'The unobligated balances of amounts made available to carry out section 177 of title 23, United States Code, are rescinded.' Analysis: Cancels unspent funds for the Neighborhood Access and Equity Grant Program under 23 U.S.C. 177 — an IIJA/BIL (not IRA) program that funded removal or mitigation of highways and infrastructure barriers in low-income communities. IIJA appropriated $1 billion over five years. NOTE: This is a BIL/IIJA rescission, not an IRA rescission — one of only a few non-IRA rescissions in this title. BURIED PROVISION: A highway-program rescission embedded in an environmental title — effectively a transportation equity fund raid. Cross-ref IIJA Sec. 11509 (PL 117-58). Effective on enactment. Losers: cities and counties with pending applications to reconnect neighborhoods severed by urban freeways; environmental justice communities.

nodes.title: SEC. 71307 — Allowance of Bronze and Catastrophic Plans in Connection with Health Savings Accounts
nodes.description: Section 223(c)(2) is amended by adding at the end: '(H) BRONZE AND CATASTROPHIC PLANS TREATED AS HIGH DEDUCTIBLE HEALTH PLANS.—The term high deductible health plan shall include any plan which is—(i) available as individual coverage through an Exchange established under section 1311 or 1321 of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act, and (ii) described in subsection (d)(1)(A) or (e) of section 1302 of such Act.' Section 1302(d)(1)(A) = Bronze plan (60% actuarial value). Section 1302(e) = Catastrophic plan. EFFECTIVE DATE: months beginning after December 31, 2025. [Lines 14577–14590]

nodes.title: SEC. 100009 — ANNUAL ASYLUM FEE (8 U.S.C. 1808)
nodes.description: Annual recurring fee of $100 for every calendar year an asylum application remains pending. Verbatim (lines 17215-17246): 'for each calendar year that an alien's application for asylum remains pending, the Secretary of Homeland Security or the Attorney General, as applicable, shall require the payment of a fee, equal to the amount specified in subsection (b), by such alien.' INITIAL: greater of $100 or higher by rule. CPI-indexed rounded down to nearest dollar. DISPOSITION: 'All of the fees collected pursuant to this section shall be deposited into the general fund of the Treasury.' 100% to Treasury. NO FEE WAIVER. Current EOIR backlog exceeds 3 million cases; average wait is 4-7 years. Fee applies during periods of government-caused delay; no tolling. Fee accrues during BIA appeal and federal court petition periods. Cumulative cost for a 5-year pending case: $100 (initial filing, § 100002) + $500 (5 annual fees) + $550 (EAD, § 100003(a)) + $275+/yr (EAD renewals, § 100011) = $1,950+ before attorney fees. Cross-refs: INA § 208 (8 U.S.C. 1158).

nodes.title: SEC. 83001 / Subtitle D — Pell Grant Eligibility: Foreign Income Inclusion and High-SAI Cutoff
nodes.description: Two changes to Pell eligibility. (1) FOREIGN INCOME: Amends HEA §401(a)(2)(A) to redefine adjusted gross income for Pell purposes to include 'for Federal Pell Grant determinations made for academic years beginning on or after July 1, 2026, the foreign income (as described in section 480(b)(5)) of the student's parents' for dependent students; and equivalent for independent students. Previously, foreign income was excluded. Effective July 1, 2026. (2) HIGH-SAI CUTOFF: Adds §401(b)(1)(F): 'a student shall not be eligible for a Federal Pell Grant under this subsection for an academic year in which the student has a student aid index that equals or exceeds twice the amount of the total maximum Federal Pell Grant for such academic year.' At 2024-25 max Pell of $7,395, this creates a hard cutoff at SAI ≥ ~$14,790. Creates income cliff — students near the cutoff lose all Pell rather than receiving reduced amounts. Effective July 1, 2026.

nodes.title: SEC. 71112 — Reducing State Medicaid Costs (Retroactive Coverage Reduction)
nodes.description: Rewrites 42 U.S.C. 1396a(a)(34); amends 42 U.S.C. 1396d(a) and 42 U.S.C. 1397bb(b)(1)(B). Old rule: all Medicaid enrollees receive retroactive coverage for services in the 3 months before the month of application if eligible during that period. New rule — §1902(a)(34)(A): 'is enrolled under paragraph (10)(A)(i)(VIII) [ACA expansion adults], such assistance will be made available...in or after the month before the month in which the individual made application' (1 month retroactive). §1902(a)(34)(B): 'is not described in subparagraph (A), such assistance will be made available...in or after the second month before the month in which the individual made application' (2 months retroactive). §1905(a) amended: strikes 'in or after the third month before the month in which the recipient makes application for assistance' and substitutes differentiated periods per (a)(34)(A) and (B). CHIP: new clause (vi) — retroactivity capped at 2 months for CHIP (previously no explicit federal CHIP retroactivity limit). Effective: applications on or after first day of first quarter after December 31, 2026 (January 1, 2027). ,000,000 FY2026 implementation. Safety-net hospitals: unable to collect on 1–2 months of care already delivered for expansion adults. People with acute health events (accidents, sudden illness) who apply after hospitalization most harmed.

nodes.title: SEC. 70313 — Sourcing Certain Income from the Sale of Inventory Produced in the United States
nodes.description: New §904(b)(6): income from selling U.S.-produced inventory outside the U.S. through a foreign branch is treated as foreign-source income (up to 50% of such income). Applies to income from sale/exchange outside the U.S. of inventory property (§865(i)(1)) (i) produced in the U.S., (ii) for use outside the U.S., (iii) subject to §863(b) third sentence, and (iv) attributable to a foreign office or fixed place of business (§864(c)(5) rules). Amount treated as foreign-source capped at 50% of income from the sale. Effect: increases foreign-source income in FTC limitation basket, allowing more FTC utilization for U.S. manufacturers/exporters with foreign sales branches. Effective: tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.

nodes.title: FEHB Audit — Federal Workers Funding Their Own Eligibility Investigation
nodes.description: Sec. 90101 amends 5 U.S.C. 8909 to insert: 'In fiscal year 2026, $66,000,000, to be derived from all contributions, and to remain available until the end of fiscal year 2035.' The $66M is derived from FEHB fund contributions paid by federal employees and agencies — federal workers are funding their own eligibility audit. The amendment also inserts 'except that the amounts required to be set aside under subsection (b)(2) shall not be subject to the limitations that may be specified annually by Congress' — explicitly exempting the $66M from annual congressional spending caps on FEHB administrative spending, reducing Congress's future ability to limit OPM's FEHB administrative authority. No due process or appeals process is specified for disenrollment. OPM must develop disenrollment process within 180 days of enactment. Audit runs years 2–4 after enactment. Combined with DOGE-era mass firings context: the audit creates administrative burden on federal employees who may already face hostile workplace environment.

nodes.title: SEC. 60020 — Rescission of Funding for Federal Building Assistance
nodes.description: Verbatim bill text: 'The unobligated balances of amounts made available to carry out section 60502 of Public Law 117-169 (136 Stat. 2083) are rescinded.' Analysis: Cancels unspent IRA funds for federal building energy efficiency and electrification assistance programs administered by the General Services Administration (GSA). IRA appropriated $250 million under Sec. 60502. Effective on enactment. Losers: GSA capital improvement programs; federal building energy performance goals. Beneficiaries: Treasury; fossil fuel suppliers to federal buildings.

nodes.title: SEC. 20013 — Military Construction Projects Authorized
nodes.description: Authorizes appropriations for military construction, land acquisition, and military family housing across all military departments. Bill text (lines 3108-3118), verbatim: '(a) AUTHORIZATION OF APPROPRIATIONS.—Funds are hereby authorized to be appropriated for military construction, land acquisition, and military family housing functions of each military department (as defined in section 101(a) of title 10, United States Code) as specified in this title. (b) SPENDING PLAN.—Not later than 30 days after the date of the enactment of this title, the Secretary of each military department shall submit to the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and House of Representatives a detailed spending plan by project for all funds made available by this title to be expended on military construction projects.' This is an authorization of appropriations (not a direct appropriation) — funds must be separately appropriated. No specific dollar amounts listed; no project locations specified. Traditional MILCON authorizations in NDAAs list every project by installation, location, and cost — this section defers all specificity to an executive branch spending plan. Congress sees the plan but has no statutory approval mechanism to reject individual projects. The 30-day reporting deadline to Armed Services Committees is the only congressional check. Statutory basis: 10 U.S.C. § 101(a) for definition of military department.

nodes.title: SEC. 10307 — Payment Limitations
nodes.description: Amends 7 USC 1308(b) and (c). Raises per-person payment limit for both PLC and ARC from ,000 to ,000. Adds annual CPI-U inflation adjustment beginning with 2025 crop year. Exact text for new subsection (i): 'ADJUSTMENT.—For the 2025 crop year and each crop year thereafter, the Secretary shall annually adjust the amounts described in subsections (b) and (c) for inflation based on the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics of the Department of Labor.' ,000 increase (24%) per person. With S corp/LLC pass-through entity expansion from SEC. 10306, total farm operation could multiply this limit by number of members.

nodes.title: 3.1-3.45 GHz and 7.4-8.4 GHz spectrum permanently excluded from FCC auction authority
nodes.description: SEC. 40002 explicitly carves out two bands from FCC auction authority permanently: 3.1-3.45 GHz (critical mid-band 5G spectrum that had been subject of intense military-industry negotiation) and 7.4-8.4 GHz (government satellite and radar operations). Bill text: 'such authority shall not apply' to these bands. The 3.1-3.45 GHz exclusion permanently removes mid-band 5G spectrum from FCC regardless of future Pentagon assessments. The commercial-maximization standard for NTIA spectrum analysis ('maximize net proceeds of systems of competitive bidding for the Treasury') could override public safety, scientific, or research spectrum considerations.

nodes.title: SEC. 71308 — Treatment of Direct Primary Care Service Arrangements
nodes.description: Section 223(c)(1) is amended by adding new subparagraph (E): 'TREATMENT OF DIRECT PRIMARY CARE SERVICE ARRANGEMENTS: (i) A direct primary care service arrangement shall not be treated as a health plan for purposes of subparagraph (A)(ii). (ii) DIRECT PRIMARY CARE SERVICE ARRANGEMENT means an arrangement under which such individual is provided medical care consisting solely of primary care services provided by primary care practitioners (as defined in section 1833(x)(2)(A) of the Social Security Act), if the sole compensation for such care is a fixed periodic fee. LIMITATION: the term shall not include any arrangement if the aggregate fees exceed  (twice such dollar amount in the case of an arrangement that covers more than one individual). CERTAIN SERVICES EXCLUDED from primary care services: (I) procedures that require the use of general anesthesia, (II) prescription drugs (other than vaccines), and (III) laboratory services not typically administered in an ambulatory primary care setting.' Section 223(d)(2)(C) amended to add DPC fees as qualified medical expenses. Inflation adjustment applies for taxable years beginning after 2026. EFFECTIVE DATE: months beginning after December 31, 2025. [Lines 14591–14658]

nodes.title: SEC. 60021 — Rescission of Funding for Low-Carbon Materials for Federal Buildings
nodes.description: Verbatim bill text: 'The unobligated balances of amounts made available to carry out section 60503 of Public Law 117-169 (136 Stat. 2083) are rescinded.' Analysis: Cancels unspent IRA funds for procurement of low-carbon construction materials in federal building projects. IRA appropriated $2.15 billion under Sec. 60503 — one of the larger single rescissions in this title. Effective on enactment. Losers: domestic low-carbon materials industry; federal building projects pursuing sustainable construction. Beneficiaries: conventional construction materials suppliers.

nodes.title: DHS Slush Fund — Sec. 90007 $10B with No Oversight vs. DOD Oversight Provisions
nodes.description: Sec. 90007 appropriates $10,000,000,000 'to the Secretary of Homeland Security' for 'reimbursement of costs incurred in undertaking activities in support of the Department of Homeland Security's mission to safeguard the borders of the United States.' This is the least constrained appropriation in the bill: no enumerated uses, no reporting requirements, no spend plan, no component-agency designation. 'Reimbursement' framing could flow to DHS components or to DOD for military border support under 10 U.S.C. 284 or other military-civilian cooperation agreements. Cross-title tension: Title II (node 3) contains military border support provisions with more structured oversight and accountability requirements. This fund could effectively reimburse DOD for activities Title II authorizes — creating a parallel, less-overseen funding stream for the same activities. Compare to Sec. 90103 ($100M to OMB) which also has zero reporting requirements.

nodes.title: SEC. 50403 — Energy Dominance Financing
nodes.description: Amends 42 U.S.C. 16517 (Energy Policy Act of 2005 §1706). Prior qualifying purpose for DOE loan guarantees: avoided/reduced air pollutants or GHGs. New purposes added: '(2) increase capacity or output; or (3) support or enable the provision of known or forecastable electric supply at time intervals necessary to maintain or enhance grid reliability or other system adequacy needs.' Deletes subsection (c) which had required that guaranteed projects 'avoid, reduce, or sequester air pollutants or anthropogenic emissions of greenhouse gases' — transforms clean-energy financing tool into general energy/minerals loan program. New use-of-funds: 'for enabling the identification, leasing, development, production, processing, transportation, transmission, refining, and generation needed for energy and critical minerals.' Appropriation: ',000,000,000, to remain available through September 30, 2028, to carry out activities under this section.' Also extends IRA §50144(b) commitment authority from 2026 to 2028. Deletion of pollution-avoidance requirement enables federally-backed financing for new oil refineries, LNG facilities, and coal-to-liquids plants. 3% for admin.

nodes.title: SEC. 70321 — Modification of Deduction for Foreign-Derived Deduction Eligible Income and Net CFC Tested Income
nodes.description: Modifies §250 deduction rates and removes scheduled phasedown. FDII (renamed 'foreign-derived deduction eligible income'): §250(a)(1)(A) rate reduced from 37.5% to 33.34%. GILTI (renamed 'net CFC tested income'): §250(a)(1)(B) rate reduced from 50% to 40%. §250(a)(3) struck: removes the scheduled phasedown provision that would have reduced rates to 21.875% (FDII) and 37.5% (GILTI) after 2025. Net effective rates at 21% corporate rate: FDII ~13.125%, GILTI ~10.5% — rate-neutral vs. current law but prevents cliff risk from phasedown. Effective: tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.

nodes.title: SEC. 71113 — Federal Payments to Prohibited Entities (Defund Planned Parenthood)
nodes.description: For 1-year period beginning date of enactment (July 4, 2025 through ~July 4, 2026): no Federal funds that are direct spending under title XIX (Medicaid) shall be used to make payments to a 'prohibited entity,' including payments directly or under contract with a 'covered organization' (managed care entity, prepaid plan). 'Prohibited entity' means entity (including affiliates, subsidiaries, successors, clinics) that: (A)(i) is a 501(c)(3) organization; (ii) is an essential community provider under 45 CFR §156.235 primarily engaged in family planning services, reproductive health, and related medical care; AND (iii) provides abortions other than: rape/incest exceptions, or life-threatening physical condition certified by physician; AND (B) received more than ,000 in combined Federal and State Medicaid expenditures in FY2023, directly, by covered organization, or as part of nationwide health care provider network. Definition precisely matches Planned Parenthood Federation of America and affiliates. ,000,000 FY2026 for CMS implementation. ~1.6 million Medicaid patients receive care at Planned Parenthood annually (contraception, STI testing/treatment, cancer screening, reproductive health). State-level Planned Parenthood exclusions: increased chlamydia/gonorrhea rates, reduced contraception use, increased unintended pregnancies in research.

nodes.title: SEC. 60022 — Rescission of Funding for GSA Emerging and Sustainable Technologies
nodes.description: Verbatim bill text: 'The unobligated balances of amounts made available to carry out section 60504 of Public Law 117-169 (136 Stat. 2083) are rescinded.' Analysis: Cancels unspent IRA funds for the GSA program supporting emerging and sustainable technology adoption in federal facilities. IRA appropriated $975 million under Sec. 60504. Effective on enactment. Losers: clean technology companies seeking federal contracts; federal agencies' technology modernization goals.

nodes.title: SEC. 10308 — Adjusted Gross Income Limitation
nodes.description: Amends 7 USC 1308-3a(b). Adds new paragraph (4): 'EXCEPTION FOR CERTAIN OPERATIONS.— (A) DEFINITIONS.—...excepted payment or benefit means— (I) a payment or benefit under subtitle E of title I of the Agricultural Act of 2014 (7 U.S.C. 9081 et seq.); (II) a payment or benefit under section 196 of the Federal Agriculture Improvement and Reform Act of 1996 (7 U.S.C. 7333); and (III) a payment or benefit described in paragraph (2)(C) received on or after October 1, 2024. ...(ii) FARMING, RANCHING, OR SILVICULTURE ACTIVITIES.—The term farming, ranching, or silviculture activities includes agri-tourism, direct-to-consumer marketing of agricultural products, the sale of agricultural equipment owned by the person or legal entity, and other agriculture-related activities... (B) EXCEPTION.—In the case of an excepted payment or benefit, the limitation established by paragraph (1) shall not apply to a person or legal entity during a crop, fiscal, or program year, as appropriate, if greater than or equal to 75 percent of the average gross income of the person or legal entity derives from farming, ranching, or silviculture activities.' Removes ,000 AGI cap for high-income farming operations deriving 75%+ of income from farming. Retroactive: subparagraph (A)(i)(III) payments received on or after October 1, 2024 are retroactively eligible.

nodes.title: ARTCC closure mandates delegate painful restructuring to FAA without specifying facilities
nodes.description: SEC. 40003 pre-mandates ARTCC facility closures without identifying which ones. New ARTCC ($1.9B): 'at least 3 existing ARTCCs are divested and integrated into the newly constructed ARTCC.' Realignment ($100M): 'at least 10 existing ARTCCs are closed or consolidated.' Congress is directing a substantial restructuring of the national airspace system while delegating the specific closure determinations entirely to the FAA Administrator, creating uncertainty for affected states and workforce. Also: 2% planning/admin cap on new ARTCC could pressure rushed design decisions.

nodes.title: Title II total: ~$150B largest single-year defense supplemental in modern US history
nodes.description: Title II appropriates approximately $150 billion across 13 sections (SEC. 20001–20013), all available through September 30, 2029. Breakdown by pillar: quality of life ~$7.5B (SEC. 20001); naval shipbuilding ~$28.5B (SEC. 20002); missile defense and space ~$24.4B (SEC. 20003); munitions/supply chain ~$30.5B (SEC. 20004); low-cost/emerging tech ~$14.2B (SEC. 20005); readiness/nuclear ~$30B+ (SEC. 20008 + 20010). Total credit facility leverage: $1.5B in subsidy (SEC. 20004(d) + SEC. 20005(b)) supporting up to $200B in loan principal under 10 U.S.C. § 149(e) — CHIPS Act model without standalone legislation or equivalent transparency requirements. All 13 sections use the same appropriations formula: 'In addition to amounts otherwise available, there are appropriated to the Secretary of Defense for fiscal year 2025, out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, to remain available until September 30, 2029' — making these supplemental appropriations available for a 4-year obligation window.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: Border Wall Title IX (Sec. 90001) vs. Military Border Support Title II (node 3)
nodes.description: Title IX Sec. 90001 appropriates $46,550,000,000 to CBP for border wall construction, including 'waterborne' barriers and ground preparation. Title IX Sec. 90005(b) adds another $10B State Border Security Reinforcement Fund. Title IX Sec. 90007 adds $10B DHS Secretary catch-all potentially reimbursable to DOD. Title II (node 3) contains military border support provisions authorizing DOD deployment and operations at the border. Overlap risk: DOD border support authorized in Title II could be funded twice — once through DOD appropriations in Title II and again through Sec. 90007 'reimbursements' to agencies supporting DHS's border mission. The combined federal border spending across Title II and Title IX approaches $130B+, representing the largest single-purpose spending package in the bill. No coordination mechanism between DHS and DOD spending streams is specified.

nodes.title: SEC. 70512 — Termination and Restrictions on Clean Electricity Production Credit
nodes.description: Major multi-part section amending IRC § 45Y (Clean Electricity Production Credit, IRA 2022 § 13701). (a) TERMINATION FOR WIND AND SOLAR FACILITIES: Amends § 45Y(d), adding new paragraph (4): 'TERMINATION FOR WIND AND SOLAR FACILITIES. (A) IN GENERAL.—This section shall not apply with respect to any applicable facility placed in service after December 31, 2027. (B) APPLICABLE FACILITY.—means a qualified facility which (i) uses wind to produce electricity (within the meaning of such term as used in section 45(d)(1)...) or (ii) uses solar energy to produce electricity (within the meaning of such term as used in section 45(d)(4)...).' Non-wind/non-solar clean electricity (geothermal, hydro, nuclear, advanced nuclear, ocean energy, landfill gas) NOT terminated. (b) RESTRICTIONS — MATERIAL ASSISTANCE: New § 45Y(b)(1)(E): 'term qualified facility shall not include any facility for which construction begins after December 31, 2025, if the construction of such facility includes any material assistance from a prohibited foreign entity (as defined in section 7701(a)(52)).' New § 45Y(g)(13): Bars specified foreign entities and foreign-influenced entities from credit. (c) DEFINITIONS — new IRC § 7701(a)(51)-(52): Creates 'prohibited foreign entity' (specified + foreign-influenced), 'specified foreign entity' (references NDAA 2021 lists, Chinese military company lists), 'foreign-controlled entity' (covered-nation governments/agencies/citizens/entities), 'foreign-influenced entity' (25% single SFE ownership OR 40% aggregate SFE ownership OR 15% debt to SFEs OR effective control via licensing agreements). Effective control via licensing: royalties beyond year 10, service agreements > 2 years, restrictions on technical know-how transfer. 'Covered nation' per 10 U.S.C. 4872(f)(2). Existing-contract safe harbor: binding written contracts entered prior to June 16, 2025, placed in service before January 1, 2030. (d) WIND/SOLAR LEASING: New § 45Y(h): 'No credit shall be determined under this section with respect to any production of electricity during the taxable year with respect to property described in paragraph (1) or (4) of section 25D(d) (as applied by substituting lessee for taxpayer) if the taxpayer rents or leases such property to a third party.' Attacks community solar and third-party owned rooftop model. (h) CREDIT TRANSFER PROHIBITION: § 6418(g)(5): 'an eligible taxpayer may not elect to transfer any portion of such credit to a taxpayer that is a specified foreign entity (as defined in section 7701(a)(51)(B)).' (i) STATUTE OF LIMITATIONS: New § 6501(o): 6-year limitations period for deficiencies attributable to material assistance errors (double normal 3-year window). (j)-(k) PENALTIES: New § 6662(m): accuracy-related penalties for disallowance of applicable energy credits; new IRC § 6695B: penalty for substantial misstatements on supplier certifications (greater of 10% of underpayment or $5,000, 6-year limitations period). Effective dates: wind/solar termination applies to construction beginning after 12 months post-enactment (approx. Jul 4, 2026); material assistance bar applies to construction beginning after Dec 31, 2025; supplier penalty applies to certifications after Dec 31, 2025.

nodes.title: SEC. 100010 — FEE FOR RENEWAL AND EXTENSION OF EMPLOYMENT AUTHORIZATION FOR PAROLEES (8 U.S.C. 1809)
nodes.description: Each renewal/extension of parolee EAD: $275 minimum fee. Text (lines 17247-17293): 'the Secretary of Homeland Security shall require the payment of a fee, equal to the amount specified in subsection (b), for any parolee who seeks a renewal or extension of employment authorization based on a grant of parole. The employment authorization for each alien paroled into the United States, or any renewal or extension of such parole, shall be valid for a period of 1 year or for the duration of the alien's parole, whichever is shorter.' INITIAL: greater of $275 or higher by rule. CPI-indexed rounded to next lowest $10. DISPOSITION: 25% to USCIS (Immigration Examinations Fee Account § 286(m)); 75% to general Treasury. NO FEE WAIVER. 1-year validity cap forces annual $275 renewal regardless of parole duration. Cross-refs: INA § 212(d)(5); § 286(m) (8 U.S.C. 1356(m)).

nodes.title: SEC. 50404 — Transformational Artificial Intelligence Models
nodes.description: 'The Secretary of Energy shall — (1) mobilize National Laboratories to partner with industry sectors within the United States to curate the scientific data of the Department of Energy across the National Laboratory complex so that the data is structured, cleaned, and preprocessed in a way that makes it suitable for use in artificial intelligence and machine learning models; and (2) initiate seed efforts for self-improving artificial intelligence models for science and engineering powered by the data described in paragraph (1).' Microelectronics use: data 'may be used to rapidly develop next-generation microelectronics that have greater capabilities beyond Moore's law while requiring lower energy consumption.' AI models 'shall be provided to the scientific community through the American science cloud to accelerate innovation in discovery science and engineering for new energy technologies.' Appropriation: ',000,000, to remain available through September 30, 2026.' Anomalous provision: no organic connection to leasing, mining, or conventional energy policy. The 'self-improving artificial intelligence models' language (recursive/foundation model development at National Labs) is unusually far-reaching. 15-month funding window is extremely short for standing up a National Laboratory AI initiative.

nodes.title: SEC. 60023 — Rescission of Environmental Review Implementation Funds
nodes.description: Verbatim bill text: 'The unobligated balances of amounts made available to carry out section 178 of title 23, United States Code, are rescinded.' Analysis: Cancels unspent IIJA funds designated for states and agencies to implement environmental review processes under 23 U.S.C. 178 (IIJA) — meant to help states build capacity for conducting NEPA reviews for transportation projects. This is a BIL/IIJA rescission, not IRA. Cross-ref IIJA Sec. 11510 (PL 117-58). PATTERN (with Sec. 60014 and Sec. 60026): Defund public environmental review capacity, then monetize access to faster reviews. Rescinding review capacity funding while Sec. 60026 creates a pay-for-speed review option further shifts the burden onto project sponsors. Effective on enactment.

nodes.title: SEC. 70322 — Determination of Deduction Eligible Income
nodes.description: Expands types of income qualifying as 'deduction eligible income' for FDII/FDDEI calculation. New §250(b)(3)(A)(i)(VII): income and gain from sale or disposition (including deemed sales under §367(d)) of (aa) intangible property (§367(d)(4) definition) and (bb) any property subject to depreciation, amortization, or depletion by seller now qualifies as FDDEI — expands base eligible for §250 deduction when sold to foreign buyers. Effective for income inclusions: sales or dispositions after June 16, 2025. §250(b)(3)(A)(ii) amended: only 'expenses and deductions (including taxes), other than interest expense and research or experimental expenditures, properly allocable to such gross income' reduce the FDDEI base — prevents over-allocation shrinking the FDDEI base. Expense apportionment rule effective: tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.

nodes.title: SEC. 71114 — Sunsetting Increased FMAP Incentive for New Expansion States
nodes.description: Amends 42 U.S.C. 1396d(ii)(3) by adding new subparagraph (B). 5-percentage-point FMAP bonus for newly expanding states now requires the state to 'begin[] to expend amounts for all such individuals prior to January 1, 2026.' The 10 remaining non-expansion states as of 2025: Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Kansas, Mississippi, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Wisconsin, Wyoming. These states can no longer receive the 5-point FMAP sweetener for future expansion. ACA base 90% FMAP for expansion remains intact but marginal incentive eliminated. ~2.2 million people in non-expansion states currently in coverage gap (income above state Medicaid thresholds, below 100% FPL). Jan 1, 2026 cutoff effectively permanent for all current holdout states given legislative timelines. No appropriation.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: ICE Detention Title IX (Sec. 90003) vs. Enforcement Provisions Title X (node 15)
nodes.description: Title IX Sec. 90003 appropriates $45,000,000,000 to ICE for 'single adult alien detention capacity and family residential center capacity' through September 30, 2029. The Secretary sets detention standards 'in the discretion of the Secretary of Homeland Security.' Title X (node 15) likely contains immigration enforcement provisions that expand removal authorities, deportation procedures, or interior enforcement. The detention infrastructure funded by Sec. 90003 is the operational backend for enforcement actions authorized in Title X — meaning Title X's enforcement expansion would be functionally unimplementable without the $45B detention appropriation. Combined: Sec. 90003 provides the detention beds; Title X provides the enforcement authorities; Sec. 90002 provides the CBP agents to apprehend; Sec. 90001 provides the physical infrastructure to funnel encounters. The two titles should be read as integrated policy even though they appear in separate committee jurisdictions.

nodes.title: SEC. 71401 — Rural Health Transformation Program
nodes.description: Section 2105 of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 1397ee) is amended by adding: '(h) RURAL HEALTH TRANSFORMATION PROGRAM.—(1) APPROPRIATION: There are appropriated to the Administrator of CMS—,000,000,000 for each of fiscal years 2026, 2027, 2028, 2029, and 2030. Any amounts unexpended or unobligated as of October 1, 2032, shall be returned to the Treasury. (2) APPLICATION: States must submit by December 31, 2025 a detailed rural health transformation plan covering: (I) improve access to hospitals and health care items for rural residents; (II) improve health care outcomes; (III) prioritize new and emerging technologies emphasizing prevention and chronic disease management; (IV) initiate local and regional strategic partnerships between rural hospitals; (V) enhance economic opportunity for health care clinicians through enhanced recruitment and training; (VI) prioritize data and technology driven solutions; (VII) manage long-term financial solvency and operating models of rural hospitals; (VIII) identify specific causes driving the accelerating rate of stand-alone rural hospitals becoming at risk of closure, conversion, or service reduction. Certification required that none of the amounts shall be used for an intergovernmental transfer, certified public expenditure, or any other expenditure to finance the non-Federal share. (3) ALLOTMENTS: 50% split equally among participating states; 50% allocated by CMS based on rural population share, proportion of rural health facilities, and hospital situation. (4) NO MATCHING PAYMENT required. (5) TERMS AND CONDITIONS: States must use allotment for 3 or more of 10 specified activities; administrative cap 10%. (6) USE OF FUNDS: 3 or more of the following: (A) evidence-based chronic disease management; (B) payments to health care providers; (C) consumer-facing technology-driven solutions; (D) AI/robotics/remote monitoring adoption with training; (E) recruiting and retaining clinical workforce with 5-year rural service commitments; (F) IT advances for cybersecurity; (G) right-sizing health care delivery systems; (H) opioid/substance use disorder treatment; (I) value-based care models; (J) additional uses as determined by Administrator. (8) REVIEW: There shall be no administrative or judicial review under section 1116 or otherwise of amounts allotted or redistributed. IMPLEMENTATION FUNDING: ,000,000 for fiscal year 2025. [Lines 14663–14976]

nodes.title: SEC. 10309 — Marketing Loans
nodes.description: Extends nonrecourse marketing assistance loans through 2031 across multiple sections of Agricultural Act of 2014. New subsection (c) added to 7 USC 9032 for 2026-2031 crop years loan rates: wheat .72/bu, corn .42/bu, grain sorghum .42/bu, barley .75/bu, oats .20/bu, upland cotton /bin/zsh.55/lb, extra long staple cotton .00/lb, long grain rice .70/cwt, medium grain rice .70/cwt, soybeans .82/bu, other oilseeds .10/cwt, dry peas .87/cwt, lentils .30/cwt, small chickpeas .00/cwt, large chickpeas .40/cwt, graded wool .60/lb, nongraded wool /bin/zsh.55/lb, mohair .00/lb, honey .50/lb, peanuts /ton. Cotton storage payments (2026-2031): 'the payment rate shall be equal to the lesser of— (A) the submitted storage charge for the current marketing year; and (B) in the case of storage in— (i) California or Arizona, a payment rate of .90; and (ii) any other State, a payment rate of .00.' ELS cotton adjustment authority extended to July 31, 2032. Loan deficiency payments (LDPs) extended through 2031. Upland cotton price floor in subsection (e) raised from /bin/zsh.25 to /bin/zsh.30.

nodes.title: SEC. 83002 — Workforce Pell Grants: Short-Term Vocational Programs 150-600 Clock Hours
nodes.description: Adds §401(k) to HEA. Creates 'Workforce Pell Grants' for programs currently below minimum Pell length. Requirements under new §481(b)(3): 'at least 150 clock hours of instruction, but less than 600 clock hours...during a minimum of 8 weeks, but less than 15 weeks.' Not correspondence courses. Governor certifies program provides 'high-skill, high-wage...or in-demand' education and meets employer hiring requirements; leads to stackable/portable credential or occupation's sole recognized credential; prepares students to pursue further certificate/degree with transferable credits. Secretary determines: program offered for 'not less than 1 year'; 'verified completion rate of at least 70 percent, within 150 percent of the normal time'; 'verified job placement rate of at least 70 percent, measured 180 days after completion'; tuition/fees must not exceed 'the difference between the median earnings of such students, as adjusted by the State and metropolitan area regional price parities of the Bureau of Economic Analysis...and 150 percent of the poverty line applicable to a single individual.' Buried: Workforce Pell time 'shall be included in determining a student's duration limit under subsection (d)(5)' — counts against lifetime 6-year Pell cap. No concurrent standard Pell. Effective July 1, 2026.

nodes.title: SEC. 60024 — Rescission of Low-Carbon Transportation Materials Grants
nodes.description: Verbatim bill text: 'The unobligated balances of amounts made available to carry out section 179 of title 23, United States Code, are rescinded.' Analysis: Cancels unspent IIJA funds for grants to support use of low-carbon materials in transportation construction projects under 23 U.S.C. 179 (IIJA). Cross-ref IIJA Sec. 11511 (PL 117-58). This is a BIL/IIJA rescission, not IRA. Effective on enactment. Losers: transportation contractors and material suppliers using low-carbon alternatives; DOT's Buy Clean initiative. Beneficiaries: conventional construction materials industry.

nodes.title: Mars orbiter pre-screens bidder pool to FY2024-2025 design study recipients
nodes.description: SEC. 40005 Mars telecommunications orbiter must be 'selected from among the commercial proposals that — received funding from the Administration in fiscal year 2024 or 2025 for commercial design studies for Mars Sample Return.' This pre-qualifies only a narrow field of companies already in NASA's pipeline, while describing the procurement as 'a competitively bid, firm fixed-price contract.' The competition is technically open but the eligible field is pre-screened by prior NASA funding decisions. Contract 80JSC024CA002 ($325M, issued June 26, 2024) funded but not described in statutory text — blank-check fulfillment of an unnamed procurement.

nodes.title: SEC. 100011 — FEE FOR RENEWAL OR EXTENSION OF EMPLOYMENT AUTHORIZATION FOR ASYLUM APPLICANTS (8 U.S.C. 1810)
nodes.description: Asylum EAD renewal fee: $275 minimum PLUS critical EAD termination provisions. Text (lines 17294-17332): Fee 'of not less than $275 by any alien who has applied for asylum for each renewal or extension of employment authorization based on such application.' TERMINATION PROVISION (§ 100011(b)): 'Each initial employment authorization, or renewal or extension of such authorization, shall terminate— (1) immediately following the denial of an asylum application by an asylum officer, unless the case is referred to an immigration judge; (2) on the date that is 30 days after the date on which an immigration judge denies an asylum application, unless the alien makes a timely appeal to the Board of Immigration Appeals; or (3) immediately following the denial by the Board of Immigration Appeals of an appeal of a denial of an asylum application.' EAD terminates IMMEDIATELY on BIA denial — before federal circuit court petition for review can be filed (INA § 242, 8 U.S.C. 1252). This creates economic coercion to abandon judicial review. DISPOSITION: 25% to USCIS; 75% to Treasury. NO FEE WAIVER. Cross-refs: INA § 208(d)(2) (8 U.S.C. 1158(d)(2)); INA § 242 (8 U.S.C. 1252).

nodes.title: SEC. 50501 — Water Conveyance and Surface Water Storage Enhancement
nodes.description: 'there is appropriated to the Secretary of the Interior, acting through the Commissioner of Reclamation, for fiscal year 2025, out of any funds in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, ,000,000,000, to remain available through September 30, 2034, for construction and associated activities that restore or increase the capacity or use of existing conveyance facilities constructed by the Bureau of Reclamation or for construction and associated activities that increase the capacity of existing Bureau of Reclamation surface water storage facilities, in a manner as determined by the Secretary of the Interior, acting through the Commissioner of Reclamation.' Key carve-outs: 'for the purposes of section 203 of the Reclamation Reform Act of 1982 (43 U.S.C. 390cc) or section 3404(a) of the Reclamation Projects Authorization and Adjustment Act of 1992 (Public Law 102–575; 106 Stat. 4708), a contract or agreement entered into pursuant to this section shall not be treated as a new or amended contract.' Critical: 'none of the funds provided under this section shall be reimbursable or subject to matching or cost-sharing requirements.' The Reclamation Reform Act §203 carve-out bypasses acreage limits and full-cost pricing requirements that normally restrict large agricultural operations from receiving subsidized water. Secretary has near-complete discretion in project selection — no competitive process, geographic equity, or environmental criteria. Benefits western agricultural water users and irrigation districts.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: FEHB Audit Title IX (Sec. 90101) vs. Federal Workforce Impacts
nodes.description: Sec. 90101 (FEHB Protection Act of 2025) mandates a comprehensive 3-year audit of all federal employee FEHB dependents, requiring production of marriage and birth certificates. The $66M audit is funded from FEHB employee contributions. The audit runs years 2–4 after enactment (roughly FY 2027–2029). Context: DOGE-era mass firings and reductions-in-force have already reduced the federal workforce significantly. The FEHB audit creates additional administrative burden on remaining federal employees and could disenroll eligible dependents due to administrative errors in a high-stress environment. No due process specified for disenrollment. The $66M exemption from annual congressional caps sets a structural precedent for OPM to expand its authority over FEHB administration without appropriations approval. Sec. 90103 ($100M to OMB for 'efficiencies') is a parallel provision — together they represent the only explicit federal workforce/benefit reform provisions in Title IX, embedded in what is primarily a border security spending title.

nodes.title: SEC. 70323 — Rules Related to Deemed Intangible Income (GILTI Overhaul)
nodes.description: Fundamental restructuring of GILTI regime. §951A(a): 'global intangible low-taxed income' replaced with 'net CFC tested income' throughout the Code. §951A subsections (b) and (d) struck: removes the 10% 'deemed tangible income return' (DTIR) exclusion — previously 10% of QBAI (qualified business asset investment, i.e., tangible CFC assets) was excluded from GILTI. Remaining subsections redesignated: (c)→(b), (e)→(c), (f)→(d). All Code references updated: §250, §960(d), §172(d)(9), §904(d). Effect: ALL tested CFC income now subject to net CFC tested income inclusion (no QBAI carve-out). Slightly increases taxable income for companies with significant foreign tangible assets. Partially offset by higher deemed-paid credit (90% vs. 80%) in §70312. §951A(b)(1)(A) and (B): removes '(determined for each taxable year of such controlled foreign corporation which ends in or with such taxable year of such United States shareholder)' — now determined per §951(a)(3). Effective: tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.

nodes.title: SEC. 20011 border detention: immigration enforcement embedded in defense appropriations outside DHS oversight
nodes.description: SEC. 20011 explicitly funds 'the temporary detention of migrants on Department of Defense installations, in accordance with chapter 15 of title 10' — this is civilian immigration enforcement delegated to the military, funded through defense appropriations rather than DHS appropriations. The chapter 15 (Insurrection Act framework) citation signals that authority derives from the military's civil-enforcement powers, not traditional Title 10 military operations. By funding migrant detention through the Secretary of Defense rather than DHS, the provision removes it from: (1) the appropriations oversight structure that governs civilian immigration detention (ICE detention standards, congressional DHS oversight); (2) USCIS administrative processes applicable to DHS detention; (3) established legal frameworks for detainee rights in civilian custody. The section also funds 'the operation of national defense areas and construction in national defense areas' — converting border land to national defense areas removes civilian law enforcement primacy, a post-2025 militarization policy. No specified detainee legal framework, rights protections, or oversight mechanism appears in the text. Traditional counter-narcotics authority (10 U.S.C. § 284) is commingled with immigration detention in a single $1B lump sum, making disaggregation of spending impossible without SecDef reporting.

nodes.title: SEC. 10310 — Repayment of Marketing Loans
nodes.description: Amends 7 USC 9034. Revises repayment terms for upland cotton, long/medium grain rice, and ELS cotton. New paragraph (1)(B): '(i) in the case of long grain rice and medium grain rice, the prevailing world market price for the commodity, as determined and adjusted by the Secretary in accordance with this section; or (ii) in the case of upland cotton, the prevailing world market price for the commodity, as determined and adjusted by the Secretary in accordance with this section.' New 30-day refund provision for upland cotton: 'the Secretary shall provide to the producer a refund (if any) in an amount equal to the difference between the lowest prevailing world market price, as determined and adjusted by the Secretary in accordance with this section, during the 30-day period following the date on which the producer repays the marketing assistance loan and the repayment rate.' Upland cotton world market price calculation: 'the formula under paragraph (1)(A) shall be based on the average of the 3 lowest-priced growths that are quoted' — uses 3 lowest competing growths (lowering calculated world price, increasing loan gain for U.S. producers). ELS cotton adjustment authority through July 31, 2032.

nodes.title: SEC. 71115 — Provider Tax Hold Harmless Threshold Reduction (Expansion State Glide Path)
nodes.description: Amends 42 U.S.C. 1396b(w)(4) by adding new subparagraph (D). For fiscal years beginning on or after October 1, 2026, the applicable percent for the hold harmless provision is substituted for '6 percent.' Non-expansion states: frozen at current enacted rate (or 0% if no tax exists as of enactment). Cannot increase above rate in effect on date of enactment. Expansion states glide path (subparagraph D(i)(II)(aa)(BB) and D(ii)): FY2028: 5.5%; FY2029: 5.0%; FY2030: 4.5%; FY2031: 4.0%; FY2032 and each subsequent fiscal year: 3.5%. Carve-out (D(iv)): provider tax in expansion state in effect on enactment date for classes described in 42 CFR §433.56(a) paragraph (3) or (4) (managed care organizations, nursing facilities) that is already within hold harmless threshold retains current rate rather than following the glide path. Definitions added: 'expansion State' means state that beginning January 1, 2014 or thereafter elects to provide coverage to all §1902(a)(10)(A)(i)(VIII) individuals; 'non-expansion State' means not an expansion state. Applies only to 50 states + DC; not territories. ,000,000 FY2026 implementation. Background: provider taxes allow states to tax providers, use revenue to increase Medicaid payments, draw down federal matching funds. At or below threshold = presumptively not hold harmless = permissible. Current threshold: 6%. Multi-billion-dollar annual reduction in state Medicaid financing capacity in 39 expansion states + DC.

nodes.title: SEC. 83003 — Pell Shortfall: Mandatory Appropriation Increased from $2.17B to $12.67B
nodes.description: Amends HEA §401(b)(7)(A)(iii) (20 U.S.C. 1070a(b)(7)(A)(iii)) by striking '$2,170,000,000' and inserting '$12,670,000,000.' Net increase of $10.5 billion in mandatory shortfall appropriation. Covers the gap when Pell appropriations fall short of demand. The large jump likely reflects anticipated costs from new Workforce Pell Grant program and demographic enrollment shifts. No effective date specified; takes effect upon enactment (July 4, 2025).

nodes.title: SEC. 60025 — John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts
nodes.description: Verbatim bill text: '(a) IN GENERAL.—In addition to amounts otherwise available, there is appropriated for fiscal year 2025, out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, $256,657,000, to remain available until September 30, 2029, for necessary expenses for capital repair, restoration, maintenance backlog, and security structures of the building and site of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. (b) ADMINISTRATIVE COSTS.—Of the amounts made available under subsection (a), not more than 3 percent may be used for administrative costs necessary to carry out this section.' Analysis: DIRECT APPROPRIATION — NOT a rescission. The lone positive spending provision in a title otherwise composed entirely of rescissions. $256,657,000 for FY2025, available through September 30, 2029. Up to 3% for administrative costs. BURIED PROVISION: Placement of a cultural institution appropriation within an environmental rescissions title is unusual — may have been done to avoid scrutiny in a standalone bill or to garner votes. No thematic connection to rest of Title VI. Cross-ref Kennedy Center Act (20 U.S.C. 76h et seq.).

nodes.title: SEC. 100012 — FEE FOR RENEWAL AND EXTENSION OF EMPLOYMENT AUTHORIZATION FOR TPS (8 U.S.C. 1811)
nodes.description: TPS EAD renewal fee: $275 minimum. Text (lines 17333-17384): 'the Secretary of Homeland Security shall require the payment of a fee, equal to the amount specified in subsection (b), by any alien at the time such alien seeks a renewal or extension of employment authorization based on a grant of temporary protected status. Any employment authorization for an alien granted temporary protected status, or any renewal or extension of such employment authorization, shall be valid for a period of 1 year or for the duration of the designation of temporary protected status, whichever is shorter.' INITIAL: greater of $275 or higher by rule. CPI-indexed rounded to next lowest $10. DISPOSITION: 25% to USCIS (§ 286(m)); 75% to general Treasury. NO FEE WAIVER. 1-year EAD cap despite TPS designations running 18+ months. CUMULATIVE TPS ANNUAL COST: $500 TPS re-registration (§ 100006) + $275 EAD renewal = $775/year minimum; if new EAD required at each cycle: +$550 = $1,325. Cross-refs: INA § 244(a)(1)(B) (8 U.S.C. 1254a(a)(1)(B)); § 286(m).

nodes.title: Space vehicle transfer provision — likely Crew Dragon display near KSC
nodes.description: SEC. 40005(b) requires NASA to identify a previously flown crewed spacecraft 'transferred to a field center...involved in the administration of the Commercial Crew Program...placed on public exhibition at an entity within the Metropolitan Statistical Area where such center is located.' Widely understood as directing NASA to transfer a SpaceX Crew Dragon capsule to a museum in the KSC/Brevard County, FL area — without naming SpaceX directly. Administrator must identify vehicle within 30 days; transfer to exhibition entity within 18 months; $85M appropriated ($5M minimum for transport, remainder for facility construction).

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: OMB Efficiency Fund (Sec. 90103) — DOGE Appropriation with No Oversight
nodes.description: Sec. 90103: $100,000,000 to OMB 'for purposes of finding budget and accounting efficiencies in the executive branch.' No enumerated uses, no reporting requirements, available through FY 2029. 'Budget and accounting efficiencies' is undefined — could fund DOGE activities, cross-agency efficiency studies, reorganization plans, or IT modernization. OMB oversees all other agencies' budgets — OMB funding its own oversight of others creates a circular accountability gap. Compare to Sec. 90007 (DHS $10B with no oversight) and Sec. 90101 (FEHB $66M exempted from congressional caps): Title IX contains three distinct oversight-gap appropriations. No equivalent oversight exemptions appear in Title II (DOD provisions, node 3), which has statutory reporting requirements. The OMB fund represents the closest explicit DOGE appropriation in the entire bill — the language 'budget and accounting efficiencies' is the legislative vocabulary used by DOGE since 2025.

nodes.title: SEC. 71401: No judicial review clause gives CMS unchecked discretion over B program — allotment, withholding, and recovery decisions unreviewable
nodes.description: Paragraph (8) explicitly states: 'There shall be no administrative or judicial review under section 1116 or otherwise of amounts allotted or redistributed to States under this subsection, payments to States withheld or reduced under this subsection, or previous payments recovered from States under this subsection.' This is a  billion program with zero external accountability mechanism. Program is structured under CHIP title (Section 2105) rather than as standalone — likely to use existing CMS infrastructure and bypass certain procedural requirements. The 'right-sizing' activity (paragraph (6)(G)) explicitly contemplates helping communities transition hospitals to different service models, which could facilitate hospital closures dressed as 'transformation.'

nodes.title: SEC. 10311 — Economic Adjustment Assistance for Textile Mills
nodes.description: Amends 7 USC 9037(c). Raises textile mill user marketing certificate (Step 2) payment from 3 cents/lb to 5 cents/lb of upland cotton. New paragraph (2): 'VALUE OF ASSISTANCE.—The value of the assistance provided under paragraph (1) shall be— (A) for the period beginning on August 1, 2013, and ending on July 31, 2025, 3 cents per pound; and (B) beginning on August 1, 2025, 5 cents per pound.' 67% increase. Benefits domestic textile mills that use upland cotton — they receive larger marketing certificates.

nodes.title: SEC. 70331 — Extension and Modification of Base Erosion Minimum Tax Amount (BEAT)
nodes.description: Modifies §59A BEAT. §59A(b)(1): rate increased from 10% to 10.5%. §59A(b)(2) struck: removes the scheduled 12.5% rate increase that would have applied after 2025 — prevents larger planned increase. Paragraphs (3) and (4) redesignated as (2) and (3). Technical corrections: §59A(b)(2)(B)(ii): 'registered securities dealer' corrected to 'securities dealer registered'. §59A(h)(2)(B): cross-reference corrected from §6038B(b)(2) to §6038A(b)(2). §59A(i)(2): cross-references updated. Net effect vs. prior law: modest tax cut (prevents 12.5% rate); slight increase vs. original TCJA (10% to 10.5%). Applies to large corporations (M+ gross receipts) with related-party deductible payments to foreign affiliates. Effective: tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.

nodes.title: Coal three-part subsidy package: leasing + acreage + royalty cut
nodes.description: Sections 50201, 50202, and 50203 work together as an integrated coal industry subsidy: §50201 clears the leasing backlog in 90 days; §50202 cuts the royalty from 12.5% to 7% (~44% reduction) on ALL active leases retroactively through 2034 and issues retroactive credits to advance-royalty payers; §50203 opens 4,000,000 new acres 'notwithstanding FLPMA §202' in 90 days bypassing land-use planning. No comparable three-part subsidy package exists for any other energy sector in this title. Coal royalty cut also reduces state revenue shares (30 U.S.C. §191 distributes 50% of royalties to producing states).

nodes.title: SEC. 72001 — Modification of Limitation on the Public Debt
nodes.description: The limitation under section 3101(b) of title 31, United States Code, as most recently increased by section 401(b) of Public Law 118–5 (31 U.S.C. 3101 note), is increased by ,000,000,000,000. [Line 14979–14983]

nodes.title: SEC. 70513 — Termination and Restrictions on Clean Electricity Investment Credit
nodes.description: Mirrors § 70512 for the investment tax credit (ITC) side. Amends IRC § 48E (Clean Electricity Investment Credit, IRA 2022 § 13702). (a) TERMINATION: Adds § 48E(e)(4): 'TERMINATION FOR WIND AND SOLAR FACILITIES. (A) IN GENERAL.—This section shall not apply to any qualified property placed in service by the taxpayer after December 31, 2027, which is part of an applicable facility.' Exception: '(C) EXCEPTION.—This paragraph shall not apply with respect to any energy storage technology which is placed in service at any applicable facility.' (b) PROHIBITED FOREIGN ENTITIES: New § 48E(b)(6): 'qualified facility shall not include any facility or property the construction...of which begins after December 31, 2025, if the construction...includes any material assistance from a prohibited foreign entity (as defined in section 7701(a)(52)).' New § 48E(d)(6): bars specified foreign entities and foreign-influenced entities. (b)(3) RECAPTURE: New § 50(a)(4): '100 percent of the aggregate decrease in the credits allowed under section 38 for all prior taxable years' if taxpayer makes 'applicable payment' to PFE within 10-year period beginning on date property placed in service. Recapture applies to taxpayers allowed credit for any taxable year beginning after 2 years post-enactment. (c) LEASING: New § 48E(i): 'No credit shall be determined under this section for any qualified investment during the taxable year with respect to property described in paragraph (1) or (4) of section 25D(d)...if the taxpayer rents or leases such property to a third party.' (d) DOMESTIC CONTENT: Rewrites § 48E(a)(3)(B) — adjusted percentage: construction before Jun 16, 2025 = 40% (offshore wind 20%); Jun 16, 2025-Dec 31, 2025 = 45% (offshore wind 27.5%); calendar year 2026 = 50% (offshore wind 35%); after Dec 31, 2026 = 55%. (e) ENERGY CREDIT SET TO 0%: Amends § 48(a)(2)(A)(ii) from '2 percent' to '0 percent'; adds § 48(a)(2)(C) nonapplication of increases. (f) FUEL CELL EXTENSION: New § 48E(j) extends ITC to qualified fuel cell property at fixed 30% rate. Effective dates: wind/solar termination = construction beginning after 12 months post-enactment; domestic content rules apply from Jun 16, 2025; fuel cell property for construction beginning after Dec 31, 2025.

nodes.title: CAFE standards remain on paper but enforcement is zero — regulatory aspiration not mandate
nodes.description: SEC. 40006 zeros out CAFE civil penalties ($5/0.1 mpg passenger cars; $10/0.1 mpg light trucks) but does NOT repeal 49 USC 32902 CAFE standards themselves. Analysis: 'The provision does not repeal CAFE standards themselves — the fuel economy requirements in 49 U.S.C. § 32902 remain in force. The effect is to create a standard with no civil penalty for non-compliance, making CAFE a regulatory aspiration rather than an enforceable mandate.' Retroactivity eliminates pending NHTSA penalty assessments for luxury automakers. No reinstatement mechanism. Permanent unless Congress amends.

nodes.title: SEC. 83004 — Pell Grant Exclusion: Full Non-Federal Grant Coverage Disqualifies Federal Pell
nodes.description: Amends HEA §401(d) by adding paragraph (6): 'Beginning on July 1, 2026, and notwithstanding this subsection or subsection (b), a student shall not be eligible for a Federal Pell Grant under subsection (b) during any period for which the student receives grant aid from non-Federal sources, including States, institutions of higher education, or private sources, in an amount that equals or exceeds the student's cost of attendance for such period.' Applies to all non-federal grant sources including institutional grants and private scholarships. Students who receive full-ride scholarships or state grants covering 100%+ of cost of attendance lose all federal Pell eligibility. Risk: wealthy schools with large endowments providing full-ride packages may inadvertently make low-income students ineligible for federal Pell, potentially reducing institutional incentives for generosity. Effective July 1, 2026.

nodes.title: SEC. 20008 SLCM-N restoration and spent fuel reprocessing: major arms control policy reversals
nodes.description: SEC. 20008 contains two significant policy reversals embedded in a defense appropriations bill. First, $2,000,000,000 'to accelerate the development, procurement, and integration of the nuclear-armed sea-launched cruise missile' (DoD) plus $400,000,000 'to accelerate the development, procurement, and integration of the warhead for the nuclear-armed sea-launched cruise missile' (NNSA) — total $2.4B for the SLCM-N, which was canceled by the Obama administration. Restoration of this system may trigger responses under existing arms control frameworks (New START successor negotiations, nuclear posture reviews) but no treaty implications are addressed in the text. Second, $10,000,000 'for National Nuclear Security Administration evaluation of spent fuel reprocessing technology' — civilian spent fuel reprocessing has been banned as a matter of U.S. policy since 1977 (Carter administration) on nonproliferation grounds. Framing as 'defense purposes' under NNSA authority is a policy workaround that could undermine nonproliferation norms without explicit congressional authorization of the policy change. Neither reversal appears as a standalone policy amendment — both are buried as line items in appropriations tables. The $10M appears at first glance minor but opens the programmatic door to reprocessing infrastructure.

nodes.title: SEC. 71116 — State Directed Payments Cap at Medicare Rates
nodes.description: Directs HHS to revise 42 CFR §438.6(c)(2)(iii) (or successor regulation) to limit total payment rate for state directed payments (SDPs) under managed care. Caps: Expansion states (those providing coverage to all §1902(a)(10)(A)(i)(VIII) individuals equivalent to minimum essential coverage): 100% of the specified total published Medicare payment rate (or, in absence of published Medicare rate, the Medicaid State plan rate). Non-expansion states: 110% of the specified total published Medicare payment rate (or, in absence, Medicaid State plan rate). Applies to services furnished during rating periods beginning on or after enactment date. Grandfathering: payments with written prior approval (or good faith effort) made before May 1, 2025, or rural hospital payments with approval by enactment date, are grandfathered for 180 days post-enactment rating period; beginning January 1, 2028, grandfathered payments above cap reduced by 10 percentage points each year until reaching applicable cap. Rural hospitals (critical access, sole community, Medicare-dependent, low-volume, rural emergency hospitals) get longer transition. Treatment of new expansion states: 100% Medicare cap applies to services in rating periods beginning on or after enactment date. ,000,000/year for FY2026–FY2033 for CMS. Background: SDPs are CMS-approved supplemental payments through managed care used to supplement low Medicaid base rates. Many SDPs are 150–300%+ of Medicare. Safety-net hospitals, large urban teaching hospitals heavily reliant on SDPs will face drastic revenue cuts. Services without published Medicare rate default to Medicaid State plan rate — often even lower than Medicare.

nodes.title: SEC. 100013 — FEES RELATING TO APPLICATIONS FOR ADJUSTMENT OF STATUS (8 U.S.C. 1812)
nodes.description: Ten categories of immigration court fees. Text (lines 17385-17841): (a) Adjustment of status (IJ): $1,500; (b) Waiver of inadmissibility: $1,050; (c) TPS in immigration court: $500; (d) Appeal of IJ decision: $900 (exception: bond decisions exempt); (e) Appeal of DHS officer decision: $900; (f) Practitioner disciplinary appeal: $1,325; (g) Motion to reopen/reconsider IJ or BIA decision: $900 (exceptions: motion to reopen in absentia order per § 240(b)(5)(C)(ii) exempt; motion to reopen deportation order in absentia before April 1, 1997 exempt); (h) Suspension of deportation: $600; (i) Cancellation of removal for LPRs: $600; (j) Cancellation of removal for non-LPRs: $1,500. ALL FEES: CPI-indexed annually rounded to next lowest $10. DISPOSITION: 'not more than 25 percent of the fees collected pursuant to this subsection— (i) shall be derived by transfer from the Immigration Examinations Fee Account under section 286(n) (8 U.S.C. 1356(n)); and (ii) shall be credited to the Executive Office for Immigration Review to retain and spend without further appropriation; and (B) any amounts not derived by transfer and credited... shall be deposited into the general fund of the Treasury.' So 25% EOIR, 75% Treasury. NO FEE WAIVER on any. CRITICAL DEFUNDING PROVISION (§ 100013(k)): 'No fees collected pursuant to this section may be expended by the Executive Office for Immigration Review for the Legal Orientation Program, or for any successor program.'
