Cross-refs: INA §§ 240, 240A, 240B, 244, 245; § 286(n).

nodes.title: SEC. 70341 — Coordination of Business Interest Limitation with Interest Capitalization Provisions
nodes.description: Coordinates §163(j) business interest limitation with interest capitalization rules (§263(g) straddle transactions, §263A(f) UNICAP). New §163(j)(10): (i) §163(j) limit applies to business interest whether it would be deducted OR capitalized; (ii) any reference to deduction includes capitalization; (iii) when limited, capitalized interest has priority — allowed amount applied first to aggregate interest that would be capitalized, then remainder to deductible interest; (iv) disallowed interest carried forward under §163(j)(2) loses its capitalization character — NOT treated as interest subject to capitalization in future years. §163(j)(5) amended: adds exclusion — interest capitalized under §263(g) or §263A(f) is NOT 'business interest' for §163(j) purposes (UNICAP-capitalized interest excluded from limit). New §163(j)(11): regulatory authority for Secretary to coordinate with §59A BEAT. Effective: tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.

nodes.title: SEC. 10312 — Sugar Program Updates
nodes.description: Multiple amendments to FAIR Act and Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1938. Raw cane sugar loan rate: '24.00 cents per pound for raw cane sugar for each of the 2025 through 2031 crop years.' Refined beet sugar rate: 'a rate that is equal to 136.55 percent of the loan rate per pound of raw cane sugar under subsection (a)(6) for each of the 2025 through 2031 crop years' (~32.77 cents/lb). Sugar storage rates: refined sugar >= 34 cents/cwt/month; raw cane >= 27 cents/cwt/month. Sugar program extended through 2031. TRQ reallocation: new cessation clause — 'Paragraphs (1) and (2) shall cease to be in effect if— (A) the Agreement Suspending the Countervailing Duty Investigation on Sugar from Mexico, signed December 19, 2014, is terminated; and (B) no countervailing duty order under subtitle A of title VII of the Tariff Act of 1930...is in effect with respect to sugar from Mexico.' Study required: 'Not later than 180 days after the date of enactment of this subsection, the Secretary shall conduct a study on whether the establishment of additional terms and conditions with respect to refined sugar imports is necessary and appropriate.' Report to Agriculture Committees within 1 year. ,000,000 from implementation fund for the study. Beet sugar allocation: priority given to processors with available sugar when upward adjustments made.

nodes.title: SEC. 72001: T debt ceiling increase — largest single increase in U.S. history, calibrated to extend beyond 2026 midterms into next presidential term
nodes.description: Prior increases have typically been in the –2.5 trillion range (Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 = Public Law 118-5). Federal debt as of mid-2025 was approximately  trillion; this raises ceiling to approximately  trillion. Treasury analysts estimated this provides borrowing capacity through approximately 2028-2029. No sunset provision — effective immediately upon enactment. The size is calibrated to extend the limit beyond the 2026 midterm and likely into the next presidential term, reducing the need for another politically contentious debt limit vote.

nodes.title: SEC. 60026 — Project Sponsor Opt-In Fees for Environmental Reviews
nodes.description: Verbatim bill text: 'Title I of the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (42 U.S.C. 4331 et seq.) is amended by adding at the end the following: SEC. 112. PROJECT SPONSOR OPT-IN FEES FOR ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEWS. 42 USC 4336f. (a) PROCESS.— (1) PROJECT SPONSOR.—A project sponsor that intends to pay a fee under this section for the preparation, or supervision of the preparation, of an environmental assessment or environmental impact statement for a project shall submit to the Council— (A) a description of the project; and (B) a declaration of whether the project sponsor intends to prepare the environmental assessment or environmental impact statement under section 107(f). (2) COUNCIL ON ENVIRONMENTAL QUALITY.—Not later than 15 days after the date on which the Council receives information described in paragraph (1) from a project sponsor, the Council shall provide to the project sponsor notice of the amount of the fee to be paid under this section, as determined under subsection (b). (3) PAYMENT OF FEE.—A project sponsor may pay a fee under this section after receipt of the notice described in paragraph (2). (4) DEADLINE FOR ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEWS FOR WHICH A FEE IS PAID.—Notwithstanding section 107(g)(1)— (A) an environmental assessment for which a fee is paid under this section shall be completed not later than 180 days after the date on which the fee is paid; and (B) an environmental impact statement for which a fee is paid under this section shall be completed not later than 1 year after the date of publication of the notice of intent to prepare the environmental impact statement. (b) FEE AMOUNT.—The amount of a fee under this section shall be— (1) 125 percent of the anticipated costs to prepare the environmental assessment or environmental impact statement; and (2) in the case of an environmental assessment or environmental impact statement to be prepared in whole or in part by a project sponsor under section 107(f), 125 percent of the anticipated costs to supervise preparation of, and, as applicable, prepare, the environmental assessment or environmental impact statement.' Analysis: Adds new NEPA Sec. 112 (42 U.S.C. 4336f). Creates PAY-TO-PLAY NEPA fast-track. Fee = 125% of anticipated EA/EIS preparation costs. Hard deadlines: 180 days for EA; 1 year for EIS from notice of intent publication — overrides NEPA Sec. 107(g)(1) 'notwithstanding.' CEQ issues fee notice within 15 days. BURIED PROVISIONS: (1) 125% surcharge creates revenue incentive for CEQ — 25% above costs; (2) No limit on which project types qualify — fossil fuel, mining, industrial projects eligible equally with renewables; (3) Deadlines override 'notwithstanding section 107(g)(1)' — may supersede state-level rules for joint reviews; (4) If sponsor self-prepares under Sec. 107(f), fee is only 125% of CEQ's supervisory costs — potential loophole to reduce fee burden. PATTERN: Part of coherent three-part strategy with Sec. 60014 and 60023 — defund public review capacity, then monetize faster reviews.

nodes.title: Fossil fuel vs. renewable asymmetry in fee structures (Title V)
nodes.description: Title V imposes structurally different and more burdensome cost regimes on renewables than on fossil fuels: (1) §50302 imposes a 3.9% GROSS REVENUE capacity fee on wind/solar — applied to total electricity sales revenue. Fossil fuel royalties apply to extracted resource value net of depletion deductions. At equivalent energy output scales, the gross revenue fee is more aggressive. (2) §50302 allows right-of-way TERMINATION at 90 days non-payment; no equivalent termination-for-non-payment mechanism applies to oil/gas lease defaults in this title. (3) §§50101-50103 cut oil/gas royalties (12.5%, down from IRA's 16.67%) and repeal methane royalties entirely. §50202 cuts coal royalties to 7%. Meanwhile §50302 creates a new 3.9% gross revenue fee for renewables with NO equivalent for new fossil fuel development. (4) §50402 rescinds clean energy program funds (ARPA-E, industrial decarbonization, efficiency rebates); §50403 redirects loan guarantees toward fossil fuels/grid reliability by deleting the pollution-avoidance requirement. The title simultaneously subsidizes extraction and taxes renewable generation.

nodes.title: MWAA lease renegotiation is one-way ratchet — floor only, never decreases
nodes.description: SEC. 40007 renegotiation clause: 'The Secretary and the Airports Authority shall renegotiate the level of lease payments at least once every 10 years to ensure that in no year the amount specified in paragraph (1)(B) is less than $15,000,000 in 2027 dollars.' The 'ensure that in no year...is less than' language means renegotiation can only result in equal or higher payments — never lower. Disguised as periodic review; functions as a permanent one-way ratchet. May be passed through to airlines and passengers as higher fees at Reagan National (DCA) and Dulles.

nodes.title: SEC. 100014 — ELECTRONIC SYSTEM FOR TRAVEL AUTHORIZATION FEE (amendment to INA § 217(h)(3)(B))
nodes.description: Amends ESTA fee and extends program. Text (lines 17842-17871): Amendment to INA § 217(h)(3)(B) (8 U.S.C. 1187(h)(3)(B)): (1) inserts 'of not less than $10' after 'an amount' in existing travel authorization fee clause; (2) adds new subclause (III): 'not less than $13 per travel authorization'; (3) strikes 'October 31, 2028' and inserts 'October 31, 2034' (6-year extension); (4) adds CPI indexing clause for FY2026 onward. Combined minimum ESTA fee: $10 (existing component) + $13 (new per-authorization component) = $23 minimum per ESTA application, CPI-indexed from FY2026. ESTA applies to Visa Waiver Program travelers from UK, Germany, Japan, Australia, and ~40 other countries — millions of visitors annually. Program authorization extended through October 31, 2034. Cross-refs: INA § 217 (8 U.S.C. 1187) — Visa Waiver Program.

nodes.title: SEC. 70342 — Definition of Adjusted Taxable Income for Business Interest Limitation
nodes.description: Adds GILTI/Subpart F/§78 income to the ATI calculation for §163(j). New §163(j)(8)(A)(vi): adjusted taxable income now includes 'the amounts included in gross income under sections 951(a), 951A(a), and 78 (and the portion of the deductions allowed under sections 245A(a) (by reason of section 964(e)(4)) and 250(a)(1)(B) by reason of such inclusions).' Effect: U.S. multinationals with large Subpart F/GILTI inclusions have a higher ATI base, allowing more business interest to be deducted. Companion to §70303 EBITDA restoration for international income. Effective: tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.

nodes.title: SEC. 20012 oversight: $10M IG budget for $150B in spending = 0.006% coverage
nodes.description: SEC. 20012 appropriates $10,000,000 to the DoD Inspector General to monitor all Title II programs. This represents approximately 0.006% of the ~$150 billion in new appropriations being monitored — far below any reasonable oversight staffing ratio. The mandate is also narrowed to three specific categories: (1) 'programs with mutual technological dependencies'; (2) 'programs with related data management and data ownership considerations'; (3) 'programs particularly vulnerable to supply chain disruptions and long lead time components.' General fraud, waste, and abuse oversight is not specified. For comparison: the CHIPS Act ($52.7B) included $50M in IG funding = 0.09% coverage. Title II's 0.006% ratio is 15x lower coverage rate than CHIPS. The two massive credit facilities in SEC. 20004(d) and SEC. 20005(b) (aggregate $200B in loan authority from $1.5B subsidy) are particularly undermonitored — loan guarantee programs historically require substantial oversight infrastructure to prevent moral hazard. The IG's independence is preserved by appropriating directly to the IG rather than through SecDef.

nodes.title: SEC. 70514 — Phase-Out and Restrictions on Advanced Manufacturing Production Credit
nodes.description: Amends IRC § 45X (Advanced Manufacturing Production Credit, IRA 2022 § 13502). (a) INTEGRATED COMPONENTS: Rewrites § 45X(d)(4) — person treated as having sold primary eligible component when integrated into secondary component AND secondary component is sold to unrelated person, BUT only if 'not less than 65 percent of the total direct material costs...by the taxpayer to produce such secondary component are attributable to primary components which are mined, produced, or manufactured in the United States.' Effective taxable years beginning after Dec 31, 2026. (b) PHASE-OUT AND TERMINATION: Amends § 45X(b)(3) adding subparagraphs (C)-(E): '(C) PHASE OUT FOR APPLICABLE CRITICAL MINERALS OTHER THAN METALLURGICAL COAL: produced after December 31, 2030...phase out percentage: 2031 = 75 percent, 2032 = 50 percent, 2033 = 25 percent, after December 31, 2033 = 0 percent.' '(D) TERMINATION FOR WIND ENERGY COMPONENTS.—This section shall not apply to any wind energy component produced and sold after December 31, 2027.' '(E) TERMINATION FOR METALLURGICAL COAL.—This section shall not apply to any metallurgical coal produced after December 31, 2029.' (c) PFE RESTRICTIONS: Adds § 45X(c)(1)(C) — eligible component excludes property with material assistance from prohibited foreign entity (§ 7701(a)(52), applied with January 1, 2027 rather than January 1, 2030 for the existing-contract safe harbor). Adds § 45X(d)(4): bars specified foreign entities and foreign-influenced entities from credit. (d) BATTERY MODULE: Amends § 45X(c)(5)(B)(iii) adding subclause (III): 'which is comprised of all other essential equipment needed for battery functionality, such as current collector assemblies and voltage sense harnesses, or any other essential energy collection equipment.' (e) METALLURGICAL COAL: Adds new § 45X(c)(6)(R): 'METALLURGICAL COAL.—Metallurgical coal which is suitable for use in the production of steel (within the meaning of the notice published by the Department of Energy entitled Critical Material List; Addition of Metallurgical Coal Used for Steelmaking (90 Fed. Reg. 22711 (May 29, 2025))), regardless of whether such production occurs inside or outside of the United States.' Credit rate: § 45X(b)(1)(M) amended inserting '(2.5 percent in the case of metallurgical coal)' after '10 percent'. DOE critical material notice published May 29, 2025 — 36 days before enactment, clearly coordinated.

nodes.title: SEC. 71117 — Requirements Regarding Waiver of Uniform Tax Requirement for Medicaid Provider Tax
nodes.description: Amends 42 U.S.C. 1396b(w)(3)(E) by inserting new clause (iii); adds new definitions in paragraph (7) subparagraphs H, I, J. A tax is NOT generally redistributive if any of the following: '(I) Within a permissible class, the tax rate imposed on any taxpayer or tax rate group...explicitly defined by its relatively lower volume or percentage of Medicaid taxable units...is lower than the tax rate imposed on any other taxpayer or tax rate group explicitly defined by its relatively higher volume or percentage of Medicaid taxable units. (II) Within a permissible class, the tax rate imposed on any taxpayer or tax rate group...based upon its Medicaid taxable units...is higher than the tax rate imposed on any taxpayer or tax rate group based upon its non-Medicaid taxable unit...for any taxpayer or tax rate group. (III) The tax excludes or imposes a lower tax rate on a taxpayer or tax rate group...based on or defined by any description that results in the same effect as described in subclause (I) or (II) for a taxpayer or tax rate group. Characteristics that may indicate such type of exclusion include the use of terminology to establish a tax rate group — (aa) based on payments or expenditures made under the program under this title without mentioning the term Medicaid...; (bb) that closely approximates a taxpayer or tax rate group under the program under this title...' New definitions: 'Medicaid taxable unit' (H) = unit taxed within health care related tax applicable to Medicaid, includes Medicaid bed days, Medicaid revenue, Medicaid charges/claims/expenditures; 'non-Medicaid taxable unit' (I) = non-Medicaid payments/revenue/costs; 'tax rate group' (J) = group of entities within permissible class taxed at same rate. Effective on enactment; transition up to 3 fiscal years. Only applies to 50 states + DC.

nodes.title: SEC. 10313 — Dairy Policy Updates
nodes.description: Amends 7 USC 9051, 9055, 9056, 9057, 9059. Dairy Margin Coverage (DMC) production history: new text for 7 USC 9055(a): 'the production history of a dairy operation for dairy margin coverage is equal to the highest annual milk marketings of the participating dairy operation during any 1 of the 2021, 2022, or 2023 calendar years.' (Removes lock to first registration year.) New dairy operation provision: operations in existence less than one year may elect either extrapolated actual marketings or 'An estimate of the actual milk marketings of the participating dairy operation based on the herd size of the participating dairy operation relative to the national rolling herd average data published by the Secretary.' Tier I coverage threshold raised from 5,000,000 to 6,000,000 pounds (throughout 7 USC 9056, 9057). Premium discount schedule reset: '2026 through 2031' and 'January 2026' replace '2019 through 2023' and 'January 2019'. DMC extended through 2031 (strikes '2025' and inserts '2031' in 7 USC 9059). M from implementation fund for dairy production cost and product yield surveys.

nodes.title: SEC. 73001 — Ending Unemployment Payments to Jobless Millionaires
nodes.description: (a) PROHIBITION ON USE OF FEDERAL FUNDS: (1) IN GENERAL: No Federal funds may be used—(A) to make payments of unemployment compensation benefits under an unemployment compensation program of the United States in a year to an individual whose wages during the individual's base period are equal to or exceed ,000,000; or (B) for any administrative costs associated with making payments described in subparagraph (A). (2) COMPLIANCE: (A) SELF-CERTIFICATION: Any application for unemployment compensation under an unemployment compensation program of the United States shall include a form or procedure for an individual applicant to certify that such individual's wages during the individual's base period do not equal or exceed ,000,000. (B) VERIFICATION: Each State agency that is responsible for administering any unemployment compensation program of the United States shall utilize available systems to verify wage eligibility by assessing claimant income to the degree possible. (3) RECOVERY OF OVERPAYMENTS: Each State agency that is responsible for administering any unemployment compensation program of the United States shall require individuals who have received amounts of unemployment compensation under such a program to which they were not entitled to repay such amounts. (4) EFFECTIVE DATE: prohibition applies to weeks of unemployment beginning on or after the date of enactment. (b) UNEMPLOYMENT COMPENSATION PROGRAM OF THE UNITED STATES DEFINED: (1) unemployment compensation for Federal civilian employees under subchapter I of chapter 85 of title 5; (2) unemployment compensation for ex-servicemembers under subchapter II of chapter 85 of title 5; (3) extended benefits under the Federal-State Extended Unemployment Compensation Act of 1970 (26 U.S.C. 3304 note); (4) any Federal temporary extension of unemployment compensation; (5) any Federal program that increases the weekly amount of unemployment compensation payable to individuals; and (6) any other Federal program providing for the payment of unemployment compensation, as determined by the Secretary of Labor. [Lines 14986–15038]

nodes.title: SEC. 70351 — Permanent Extension of Look-Through Rule for Related Controlled Foreign Corporations
nodes.description: Makes permanent the §954(c)(6) CFC look-through rule. §954(c)(6)(C): strikes 'and before January 1, 2026' — removing the expiration date. Under this rule, dividends, interest, rents, and royalties paid between related CFCs are not treated as Subpart F passive income — they retain character of underlying active income. Simplifies cross-border cash management for U.S. multinationals with multiple CFC layers. Previously a temporary provision requiring periodic extension; now permanent. Effective: tax years of foreign corporations beginning after December 31, 2025.

nodes.title: IRA rescission pattern: Title IV sweeps NOAA, aviation fuel, and CHIPS wireless alongside Title III GRRP
nodes.description: SEC. 40008 (NOAA ~$3.655B IRA), SEC. 40010 (alternative aviation fuel ~$297M IRA), and SEC. 40011 (CHIPS Act wireless supply chain $850M) collectively represent a systematic rollback of Biden-era green and technology program unobligated balances. Combined with SEC. 30002 (Title III GRRP housing IRA rescission), this pattern appears across multiple Senate committees. Net Title IV: ~$35.6B new spending (Coast Guard $24.6B + FAA $12.5B + NASA $10B + NTIA $50M) vs. ~$1-4B in rescissions. Massive net spending increase with targeted rollback of prior-administration priorities.

nodes.title: NPR-A 2022 errata exclusion reopens ~13M ecologically sensitive acres
nodes.description: §50105 defines the governing NPR-A environmental document as including the 'errata sheet dated October 6, 2020' but EXPLICITLY EXCLUDING 'the errata sheet dated September 20, 2022.' The September 2022 errata sheet had added Special Areas protections for approximately 13 million acres of the most ecologically sensitive portions of the National Petroleum Reserve–Alaska. By naming this exclusion explicitly in the statutory definition, Congress strips those protections with surgical precision — it is not a general rollback but a targeted identification of the specific document that extended habitat protections, ensuring those 13 million acres are reopened to leasing. This is framed as a neutral definitional provision but is substantively one of the largest single wildlife habitat rollbacks in the bill.

nodes.title: SEC. 100015 — ELECTRONIC VISA UPDATE SYSTEM FEE (8 U.S.C. 1813)
nodes.description: New $30 fee for EVUS enrollment (primarily Chinese 10-year visa holders). Text (lines 17872-17929): 'the Secretary of Homeland Security shall require the payment of a fee, in the amount specified in subsection (b), by any alien subject to the Electronic Visa Update System at the time of such alien's enrollment in such system.' INITIAL: greater of $30 or higher by rule. CPI-indexed rounded to next lowest $0.25 (note: different rounding than other fees). DISPOSITION: Creates new 'CBP Electronic Visa Update System Account' within Treasury (amends INA § 286(w) — new subsection): 'There shall be deposited into the Account an amount equal to the difference between— (A) all of the fees received pursuant to section 100015... and (B) an amount equal to $5 multiplied by the number of payments collected.' Remaining: 'an amount equal to $5 multiplied by the number of payments collected pursuant to this section shall be deposited to the general fund of the Treasury.' So: $5/enrollment to Treasury; $25+ to CBP EVUS Account for system administration. NO FEE WAIVER. EVUS currently required for Chinese nationals with 10-year B-1/B-2 visas. Cross-refs: INA § 286 (8 U.S.C. 1356) new subsection (w).

nodes.title: SEC. 84001 / Subtitle E — Accountability: Federal Aid Cutoff for Low-Earning Degree Programs
nodes.description: Amends HEA §454 (20 U.S.C. 1087d). Adds §454(c): 'Notwithstanding section 481(b), an institution of higher education subject to this subsection shall not use funds under this part for student enrollment in an educational program offered by the institution that is described in paragraph (2).' A program is ineligible if: 'the median earnings...of the programmatic cohort of students who received funds under this title for enrollment in such program, who completed such program during the academic year that is 4 years before the year of the determination, who are not enrolled in any institution of higher education, and who are working, are, for not less than 2 of the 3 years immediately preceding the date of the determination, less than the median earnings of a working adult.' Comparison benchmark: undergraduate programs vs 'working adult who...is aged 25 to 34; is not enrolled in an institution of higher education; and has only a high school diploma or its recognized equivalent.' Graduate programs vs adults with 'only a baccalaureate degree.' Data source: Bureau of the Census for the state in which the institution is located (or national if fewer than 50% students are in-state). Graduate programs use THE LOWEST of: state adults, same-field adults in state (2-digit CIP code), same-field adults nationally. Small cohorts (<30): Secretary aggregates additional years, then aggregates similar-length programs at institution. Procedural protections: must fail 2 of 3 years; students notified after first failing year; appeal right; programs regain eligibility after 2+ years of ineligibility. Effective July 1, 2026. At risk: liberal arts, fine arts, humanities, education, social work, graduate programs at HBCUs in low-wage states.

nodes.title: SEC. 70515 — Restriction on the Extension of Advanced Energy Project Credit Program
nodes.description: Amends IRC § 48C(e)(3)(C) by striking 'shall be increased' and inserting 'shall not be increased'. Caps the § 48C Advanced Energy Project Credit program — the competitive grant-style credit program for advanced energy manufacturing facilities — at its current authorized level. Prevents any future supplemental appropriations from expanding the program. The existing $10 billion IRA appropriation (§ 13501 of P.L. 117-169) appears to remain intact; this section prevents a second or third tranche. Effective immediately upon enactment. One-sentence change with outsized effect — caps a competitive program that had already attracted thousands of applicants. Program included allocations for non-clean-energy advanced manufacturing including domestic critical mineral processing and industrial decarbonization.

nodes.title: Title VI IRA Rescissions: Systematic Dismantling of IRA Environmental Programs — Total ~$35B+
nodes.description: Analysis: Sections 60001-60018 and 60020-60022 constitute a nearly complete dismantling of the IRA's environmental and climate spending programs. Programs targeted: clean air (CAA Secs. 132-138), environmental justice (CAA Sec. 138), methane reduction (CAA Sec. 136), building efficiency (IRA Secs. 60502-60504), ESA recovery, and data collection. Dollar totals of IRA rescissions: Sec. 60001 $1B (clean vehicles); Sec. 60002 $27B (GGRF — largest); Sec. 60003 $60M (diesel); Sec. 60004 $117M (air pollution); Sec. 60005 $50M (schools); Sec. 60006 $100M (low emissions electricity); Sec. 60007 $20M (RFS); Sec. 60008 $60M (AIM Act HFC); Sec. 60009 $5M (enforcement tech); Sec. 60010 $5M (GHG reporting); Sec. 60011 $250M (EPD); Sec. 60012 $850M (methane fee); Sec. 60013 $5B (GHG plans); Sec. 60014 $100M (EPA NEPA reviews); Sec. 60015 $100M (low-carbon labeling); Sec. 60016 $3B (env justice); Sec. 60017 $125M (ESA); Sec. 60018 $10M (data); Sec. 60020 $250M (federal building); Sec. 60021 $2.15B (low-carbon federal materials); Sec. 60022 $975M (GSA tech). IRA-only subtotal: approximately $41.2B authorized, rescinding unobligated portions. IIJA/BIL rescissions (Secs. 60019, 60023, 60024) add additional billions in non-IRA clawbacks.

nodes.title: SEC. 10314 — Implementation
nodes.description: Amends 7 USC 9097(c). Appropriates ,000,000 from CCC for Subtitle C implementation. New paragraph (5): 'FURTHER FUNDING.—The Secretary shall make available to carry out subtitle C of title I...and the amendments made by that subtitle ,000,000, to remain available until expended, of which— (A) not less than ,000,000 shall be used to carry out paragraphs (3) and (4) of subsection (b); (B) ,000,000 shall be used for activities described in paragraph (3)(A); (C) ,000,000 shall be used for activities described in paragraph (3)(B); (D) ,000,000 shall be used— (i) to carry out mandatory surveys of dairy production cost and product yield information to be reported by manufacturers required to report under section 273 of the Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946 (7 U.S.C. 1637b), for all products processed in the same facility or facilities; and (ii) to publish the results of such surveys biennially; and (E) ,000,000 shall be used to conduct the study under subsection (d) of section 359k of the Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1938 (7 U.S.C. 1359kk).' Funds remain available until expended. The dairy survey mandate extends to 'all products processed in the same facility' — broader than just fluid milk.

nodes.title: Dual credit facility structure: $1.5B subsidy enables $200B in loan authority with minimal congressional oversight
nodes.description: SEC. 20004(d) and SEC. 20005(b) each create separate credit facilities under 10 U.S.C. § 149(e) with identical structure: a subsidy appropriation supports loan principal obligations at approximately 200:1 leverage. SEC. 20004(d): $500M subsidy, up to $100B principal for 'critical minerals and related industries and projects, including related Covered Technology Categories.' SEC. 20005(b): $1,000M subsidy, up to $100B principal for broader 'capital assistance program, including loans, loan guarantees, and technical assistance' for defense industrial base companies. Neither provision specifies: eligibility criteria for borrowers; interest rates or terms; Congressional notification requirements for individual loans; approval thresholds requiring Congressional consent; oversight framework beyond the SEC. 20012 $10M IG appropriation. Total aggregate: $1.5B in subsidy supporting up to $200B in loan obligations — this is a permanent expansion of DoD's balance sheet authority comparable in scale to the CHIPS Act ($52.7B in direct appropriations) but structured as a credit program with off-balance-sheet leverage and less transparency. The CHIPS Act had a standalone statute, public application process, and dedicated oversight. These provisions have none of that.

nodes.title: SEC. 71118 — Requiring Budget Neutrality for Medicaid Demonstration Projects Under Section 1115
nodes.description: Amends 42 U.S.C. 1315 by adding new subsection (g). Beginning January 1, 2027: Secretary may not approve application for (or renewal or amendment of) a Medicaid demonstration project unless the CMS Chief Actuary certifies that such project 'is not expected to result in an increase in the amount of Federal expenditures compared to the amount that such expenditures would otherwise be in the absence of such project.' Critical baseline definition: 'For purposes of this subsection, expenditures for the coverage of populations and services that the State could have otherwise provided through its Medicaid State plan or other authority under title XIX, including expenditures that could be made under such authority but for the provision of such services at a different site of service than authorized under such State plan or other authority, shall be considered expenditures in the absence of such a project.' Treatment of savings: if waiver generates savings during approval period, Secretary must specify methodology for how savings affect next approval period — prevents banking of hypothetical savings. ,000,000 each for FY2026 and FY2027. Old methodology: CMS constructed 'without waiver' baselines using hypothetical spending projections — counted coverage expansions as budget neutral because federal government would have paid for individuals anyway. New rule: states cannot credit hypothetical costs not actually incurred. Effect: most major current 1115 waivers (CalAIM, NY 1115, coverage expansion waivers) up for renewal will fail budget neutrality test. Ends use of 1115 waivers to expand Medicaid to populations not otherwise eligible.

nodes.title: NPS fund rescission vs. 250th anniversary appropriation — internal Title V contradiction
nodes.description: §50304 rescinds all unobligated IRA funds for NPS (§§50221-50223) — cutting NPS operational capacity, conservation programs, and deferred maintenance funding. Immediately following in §50305, ,000,000 is appropriated to NPS for '250th anniversary' events through FY2028. The same agency loses operating funds while gaining event/spectacle funds in consecutive sections of the same subtitle. This is not an inadvertent juxtaposition — both sections were enacted together. The operational cuts impair the agency's ability to manage the very parks and monuments where celebrations would occur.

nodes.title: SEC. 73001: Self-certification form required for ALL unemployment applicants — administrative burden extends well beyond the tiny millionaire population
nodes.description: The self-certification requirement creates new administrative forms for all unemployment applicants, not just millionaires. The 'recovery of overpayments' provision is standard but applies broadly to state agencies administering any of these programs — it reaffirms the duty to recover overpayments generally, which has broader application than just millionaires. The definition of 'unemployment compensation program of the United States' in subsection (b) is broad and includes 'any other Federal program providing for the payment of unemployment compensation, as determined by the Secretary of Labor' — an open-ended delegation that could be used to extend the framework to future programs. Fiscal savings: well under  million over 10 years (CBO would score as negligible). Federal funding restriction only — states may still use state funds to pay such benefits.

nodes.title: SEC. 85001 / Subtitle F — Delay Borrower Defense Rule: Biden 2022 Regs Suspended, 2020 Trump Rules Revived
nodes.description: Effective immediately upon enactment: 'for loans that first originate before July 1, 2035, the provisions of subpart D of part 685 of title 34, Code of Federal Regulations (relating to borrower defense to repayment), as added or amended by the final regulations published by the Department of Education on November 1, 2022...titled [87 Fed. Reg. 65904] shall not be in effect.' Effect: 'any regulations relating to borrower defense to repayment that took effect on July 1, 2020, are restored and revived as such regulations were in effect on such date.' 2022 Biden rules made it easier to prove fraud by schools; 2020 Trump rules required more specific evidence of misleading conduct and financial harm. Borrowers who attended predatory for-profit schools (ITT Tech, Corinthian Colleges) seeking loan discharges face harder evidentiary standard. For-profit college operators benefit. Suspension runs through June 30, 2035.

nodes.title: SEC. 70352 — Repeal of Election for 1-Month Deferral in Determination of Taxable Year of Specified Foreign Corporations
nodes.description: Repeals §898(c)(2) election allowing U.S. shareholders of specified foreign corporations to use a 1-month timing mismatch for tax year references. §898(c)(2) struck; paragraph (3) redesignated as (2). Transition: specified foreign corporations as of November 30, 2025 must align their first taxable year to the 'required year' (§898(c)(1)) ending after that date. Change treated as initiated by corporation with Secretary's consent. Secretary to issue regulations allocating foreign taxes between the short first year and succeeding year. Effective: taxable years of specified foreign corporations beginning after November 30, 2025.

nodes.title: Title VI NEPA Privatization Pattern: Defund Public Capacity, Monetize Speed (Secs. 60014, 60023, 60026)
nodes.description: Analysis: Three sections together form a coherent policy shift — NOT an accident of placement. (1) Sec. 60014 rescinds $100M IRA funding for EPA's NEPA review speed/accuracy capacity; (2) Sec. 60023 rescinds IIJA funding for state environmental review implementation capacity under 23 U.S.C. 178; (3) Sec. 60026 creates a new fee-based NEPA fast-track (42 U.S.C. 4336f) where project sponsors pay 125% of review costs to CEQ to lock in hard deadlines (180 days EA / 1 year EIS). NET EFFECT: The cost of faster reviews shifts from public budgets to project sponsors — effectively privatizing environmental review speed. Large developers (pipelines, LNG terminals, highways, data centers) who can afford fees gain speed advantage; smaller sponsors and community interveners lose the public review timeline as meaningful check. CEQ gains a 25% revenue stream above costs, creating perverse incentive to approve the fee mechanism. CROSS-TITLE RELEVANCE: Interacts with Title V (Energy/Natural Resources, node 6) NEPA changes affecting energy projects, and Title IV (Commerce/Transportation, node 5) infrastructure review impacts.

nodes.title: SEC. 10401 — Supplemental Agricultural Disaster Assistance
nodes.description: Amends 7 USC 9081. Multiple changes to livestock and farm disaster programs. Livestock predation indemnity: 'Indemnity payments to an eligible producer on a farm under paragraph (1)(A) shall be made at a rate of 100 percent of the market value of the affected livestock on the applicable date' (raised from 75%). Weather/disease losses remain at 75%. New unborn livestock provision: 'In the case of unborn livestock death losses incurred on or after January 1, 2024, the Secretary shall make an additional payment to eligible producers on farms that have incurred such losses in excess of the normal mortality due to a condition specified in paragraph (1).' Payment rate: 'less than or equal to 85 percent of the payment rate established with respect to the lowest weight class of the livestock.' Retroactive to January 1, 2024. Livestock Forage Disaster Program: drought trigger reduced from 8 consecutive weeks to 4 consecutive weeks (for 1 payment tier): 'county for not less than— (aa) 4 consecutive weeks during the normal grazing period for the county...shall be eligible to receive assistance under this paragraph in an amount equal to 1 monthly payment...or (bb) 7 of the previous 8 consecutive' (2-payment tier). Farm-raised fish bird depredation: minimum payment ' per acre of farm-raised fish'; 85% of total production acres eligible. Honeybee normal mortality: set at 15% by statute. Tree Assistance: loss threshold changed from '15 percent (adjusted for normal mortality)' to 'normal mortality'; reimbursement raised from '50' to '65' percent.

nodes.title: SEC. 70521 — Extension and Modification of Clean Fuel Production Credit
nodes.description: Amends IRC § 45Z (Clean Fuel Production Credit, IRA 2022 § 13704). Credit NOT terminated — extended and modified. (a) FOREIGN FEEDSTOCK PROHIBITION: Adds § 45Z(f)(1)(A)(iii): 'such fuel is exclusively derived from a feedstock which was produced or grown in the United States, Mexico, or Canada.' Effective for transportation fuel produced after December 31, 2025. (b) PROHIBITION ON NEGATIVE EMISSION RATES: Adds § 45Z(b)(1)(E): 'For purposes of this section, the emissions rate for a transportation fuel may not be less than zero.' BUT subsection (c) ANIMAL MANURE CARVE-OUT: adds § 45Z(b)(1)(B)(v) providing that for transportation fuel derived from animal manure, 'notwithstanding subparagraph (E), may provide an emissions rate that is less than zero' — preserving sub-zero benefit for dairy and hog farmers producing biogas. Also adds § 45Z(b)(1)(B)(iv) excluding indirect land use change emissions. (d) EXTENSION: Amends § 45Z(g) striking 'December 31, 2027' inserting 'December 31, 2029'. (e) DOUBLE CREDIT PREVENTION: Adds § 45Z(d)(5)(A)(iv): not produced from fuel for which § 45Z credit is allowable. (g) SAF COORDINATION: § 6426(k)(4) — § 6426(k) shall not apply to any gallon for which § 45Z credit is allowable. SAF definition at § 45Z(a)(3) rewritten: liquid fuel not kerosene, meeting ASTM D7566 or D1655 Annex A1, not derived from palm fatty acid distillates or petroleum. (h) SAF § 6426(k) TERMINATION: '(5) TERMINATION.—This subsection shall not apply to any sale or use for any period after September 30, 2025.' (j) SMALL AGRI-BIODIESEL: § 40A(b)(4)(A) per-gallon credit doubled from 10 cents to 20 cents; extended through December 31, 2026; credit is IN ADDITION to any § 45Z credit (§ 40A(b)(4)(D)). (k) PFE RESTRICTIONS: New § 45Z(f)(8): specified foreign entities barred immediately; foreign-influenced entities barred 2 years post-enactment.

nodes.title: SEC. 100016 — FEE FOR ALIENS ORDERED REMOVED IN ABSENTIA (8 U.S.C. 1814)
nodes.description: $5,000 fee imposed at arrest on aliens with in absentia removal orders. Text (lines 17931-17979): 'As partial reimbursement for the cost of arresting an alien described in this section, the Secretary of Homeland Security... shall require the payment of a fee... on any alien who— (1) is ordered removed in absentia pursuant to section 240(b)(5) (8 U.S.C. 1229a(b)(5)); and (2) is subsequently arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.' INITIAL: greater of $5,000 or higher by rule. CPI-indexed to next lowest $10. EXCEPTION: fee does not apply if order 'was rescinded pursuant to section 240(b)(5)(C) (8 U.S.C. 1229a(b)(5)(C)).' DISPOSITION: 50% to ICE Detention and Removal Office Fee Account (retained w/o appropriation); 50% to general Treasury. Fee imposed AT ARREST — before rescission motion can be filed; alien must pay, seek rescission, then seek refund. Many in absentia orders result from failure to receive notice. NO FEE WAIVER.

nodes.title: Title VI Sec. 60012 Buried Substantive Policy Change: Methane Fee 10-Year Delay (2024 to 2034)
nodes.description: Analysis: Section 60012(b) is the most consequential buried provision in Title VI. It amends CAA Sec. 136(g) (42 U.S.C. 7436(g)) by 'striking calendar year 2024 and inserting calendar year 2034.' This is a STATUTORY AMENDMENT — not a rescission — buried in a section otherwise labeled as a rescission. EFFECT: EPA cannot charge methane waste emission fees to oil and gas operators until after calendar year 2034 — a full decade delay from the original 2024 start. The methane waste emissions charge was the IRA's primary enforcement mechanism against oil and gas methane leaks. Value to industry: potentially billions in avoided fees over 10 years. Legislative structure: a five-word amendment ('2024' to '2034') with enormous practical consequence, easy to miss in a bill with hundreds of sections.

nodes.title: SEC. 70353 — Restoration of Limitation on Downward Attribution of Stock Ownership; New §951B
nodes.description: Partially reverses controversial TCJA §958(b)(4) repeal. Restores limitation on downward attribution: §958(b)(4) re-added: 'Subparagraphs (A), (B), and (C) of section 318(a)(3) shall not be applied so as to consider a United States person as owning stock which is owned by a person who is not a United States person.' Simultaneously creates new §951B for 'foreign controlled United States shareholders' and 'foreign controlled foreign corporations.' §951B definitions: 'foreign controlled United States shareholder' = U.S. person owning >50% of FCFC (using §951(b) with >50% substituted for 10%+ and §958(b) applied without paragraph (4)); 'foreign controlled foreign corporation' = foreign corporation that would be a CFC under §957(a) if foreign controlled U.S. shareholders were substituted. §951B applies Subpart F and GILTI rules separately to these entities. Prevents loophole where foreign-controlled groups avoided U.S. tax through intermediate foreign entities. Effective: tax years of foreign corporations beginning after December 31, 2025.

nodes.title: SEC. 85002 — Delay Closed School Discharge Rule: Biden 2022 Regs Suspended for Pre-2035 Loans
nodes.description: Effective immediately upon enactment: 'for loans that first originate before July 1, 2035, the provisions of sections 674.33(g), 682.402(d), and 685.214 of title 34, Code of Federal Regulations (relating to closed school discharges), as added or amended by the final regulations published by the Department of Education on November 1, 2022...titled [87 Fed. Reg. 65904], shall not be in effect.' Effect: 'the portions of the Code of Federal Regulations described in subsection (a)...shall be in effect as if the amendments made by such final regulations had not been made.' 2022 Biden rules created automatic discharge after 3 years of school closure. Pre-2022 rules require students to apply and demonstrate they could not complete their program elsewhere. Students at recently closed schools (particularly for-profit closures) who expected automatic discharge lose that protection. Suspension through June 30, 2035.

nodes.title: SEC. 10501 — Beginning Farmer and Rancher Benefit
nodes.description: Amends 7 USC 1502(b)(3) and 7 USC 1508(e). Extends definition of 'beginning farmer or rancher' from 5 to 10 years of farming experience: strikes '5' and inserts '10' in §502(b)(3). Deletes §522(c)(7)(F) (pilot program for beginning farmer crop insurance innovation — buried rollback). New premium assistance at §508(e)(9): 'ADDITIONAL SUPPORT.—In addition to any other provision of this subsection...a beginning farmer or rancher shall receive additional premium assistance that is the number of percentage points specified in subparagraph (B) greater than the premium assistance that would otherwise be available...' Percentage points: '(i) For each of the first and second reinsurance years...5 percentage points. (ii) For the third reinsurance year...3 percentage points. (iii) For the fourth reinsurance year...1 percentage point.' On top of standard premium assistance of 55-80% depending on coverage level.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: CAFE penalty zeroing (Title IV SEC. 40006) paired with EV credit terminations (Title VII SEC. 70501-70504) — double deregulatory relief for auto industry
nodes.description: Title IV SEC. 40006 eliminates all CAFE civil penalties (49 USC 32912 set to $0.00), removing financial consequences for building fuel-inefficient vehicles. Title VII simultaneously terminates all EV incentive credits: SEC. 70501 (Previously-Owned Clean Vehicle Credit), SEC. 70502 (Clean Vehicle Credit), SEC. 70503 (Qualified Commercial Clean Vehicles Credit), SEC. 70504 (Alternative Fuel Vehicle Refueling Property Credit). The combined effect: no penalty for not building EVs or efficient vehicles (CAFE), and no consumer incentive to buy EVs (credit termination). This is a comprehensive two-pronged rollback of auto decarbonization policy executed across two separate committees (Commerce/Science/Transportation in Title IV and Tax in Title VII). Automakers benefit twice: no enforcement liability and no market competition from federally-incentivized EV demand.

nodes.title: SEC. 100017 — INADMISSIBLE ALIEN APPREHENSION FEE (8 U.S.C. 1815)
nodes.description: $5,000 fee on every inadmissible alien apprehended between ports of entry. Text (lines 17980-18023): 'the Secretary of Homeland Security shall require the payment of a fee, equal to the amount specified in subsection (b), by any inadmissible alien at the time such alien is apprehended between ports of entry.' INITIAL: greater of $5,000 or higher by rule. CPI-indexed to next lowest $10. INTERNAL DRAFTING CONTRADICTION: Two subsections both titled 'DISPOSITION OF INADMISSIBLE ALIEN APPREHENSION FEES' give conflicting destinations: Subsection (c): '50 percent of the fees collected... (A) shall be credited to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement; (B) shall be deposited into the Detention and Removal Office Fee Account; and (C) may be retained and expended by... ICE without further appropriation; and (2) any amounts... not credited to ICE... shall be deposited into the general fund of the Treasury.' (50% ICE / 50% Treasury). Subsection (d) [conflicting]: 'All of the fees collected pursuant to this section shall be deposited into the general fund of the Treasury.' (100% Treasury). Verbatim bill text at line 18021-18023: 'SEC. 100017... (d) DISPOSITION OF INADMISSIBLE ALIEN APPREHENSION FEES.— All of the fees collected pursuant to this section shall be deposited into the general fund of the Treasury.' This internal contradiction requires regulatory or judicial resolution. NO FEE WAIVER. Most border crossers are indigent — fee creates permanent debt. Cross-refs: INA §§ 212, 235.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: Triple-layer immigration exclusion — Medicare (71201) + Medicaid (Title VII-B) + ACA/PTC (71301+71302) = complete federal health coverage exclusion for non-qualifying lawfully present non-citizens
nodes.description: Three provisions work in concert to create a complete exclusion from federal health coverage for non-citizens who do not fit the narrow four-category framework (LPRs, Cuban/Haitian entrants, COFA residents, U.S. citizens/nationals): (1) SEC. 71201 removes them from Medicare (effective 18 months post-enactment, ~Jan 4, 2027); (2) Title VII-B Medicaid provisions (node 11) impose or maintain the five-year bar and new work requirements that disenroll non-qualifying immigrants from Medicaid; (3) SEC. 71301 removes them from ACA premium tax credits; (4) SEC. 71302 closes the Medicaid-bridge PTC exception — the fallback pathway for those in the Medicaid five-year waiting period. The combined result: a lawfully present non-citizen who does not qualify under the four-category framework has no federal pathway to subsidized or publicly-funded health coverage — not Medicare, not Medicaid, not ACA marketplace subsidies. Affected groups include: DACA recipients (if any had qualifying access), TPS holders, H-1B/L-1/O-1 visa holders, certain asylees and refugees not covered by Cuban/Haitian entrant definition, and others with lawful but non-permanent status.

nodes.title: SEC. 70522 — Restrictions on Carbon Oxide Sequestration Credit
nodes.description: Amends IRC § 45Q (Carbon Oxide Sequestration Credit, IRA 2022 § 13104). Credit NOT terminated. (a) PFE RESTRICTIONS: Adds § 45Q(f)(10): 'No credit shall be determined under subsection (a) for any taxable year beginning after the date of enactment of this paragraph if the taxpayer is (A) a specified foreign entity (as defined in section 7701(a)(51)(B)), or (B) a foreign-influenced entity (as defined in section 7701(a)(51)(D), determined without regard to clause (i)(II) thereof).' (b) PARITY/RESTRUCTURING: Amends § 45Q(a) — strikes subparagraph (3)(B) and inserts three-category structure: '(i) disposed of by the taxpayer in secure geological storage and not used by the taxpayer as described in clause (ii) or (iii); (ii) used by the taxpayer as a tertiary injectant in a qualified enhanced oil or natural gas recovery project and disposed of by the taxpayer in secure geological storage; or (iii) utilized by the taxpayer in a manner described in subsection (f)(5).' Strikes paragraph (4) entirely. Dollar amounts: § 45Q(b)(1)(A) amended: 'for any taxable year beginning in a calendar year after 2024 and before 2027, $17, and for any taxable year beginning in a calendar year after 2026, an amount equal to the product of $17 and the inflation adjustment factor for such calendar year...determined by substituting 2025 for 1990.' Subparagraph (B) rate for EOR/geologic storage: 'shall be applied by substituting $36 for $17 each place it appears.' Effective dates: PFE restrictions for taxable years beginning after enactment; use/utilization parity changes for facilities placed in service after enactment. Benefits: Occidental Petroleum DAC, ExxonMobil CCS projects, Denbury Resources pipelines, blue hydrogen producers. Enhanced oil recovery operations injecting CO2 benefit from $36/ton rate retention.

nodes.title: SEC. 70354 — Modifications to Pro Rata Share Rules
nodes.description: Rewrites §951(a) with new daily-ownership based inclusion rules for Subpart F income. New §951(a)(1)(A): each U.S. shareholder owning stock on ANY DAY during the CFC year includes pro rata share of subpart F income for that year (vs. prior last-day-of-year rule). §951(a)(1)(B): §956 income inclusion for U.S. shareholders owning stock on last day the corporation is a CFC in the CFC year. §951(a)(2): pro rata share = portion attributable to stock owned during periods when all three conditions met (shareholder owned stock, was U.S. shareholder, corporation was CFC). §951(a)(3): inclusion year = year including the last day shareholder owns CFC stock in the CFC year. §951(a)(4): Secretary may require or permit year-closing on stock disposition. §951A(b)(1)(A) and (1)(B) conforming amendments. Transition rule: dividends paid on or before June 28, 2025, or paid between June 28, 2025 and CFC's first year after December 31, 2025, that don't increase U.S. taxable income are excluded from prior rules. Effective: tax years of foreign corporations beginning after December 31, 2025.

nodes.title: SEC. 10502 — Area-Based Crop Insurance Coverage and Affordability
nodes.description: Amends 7 USC 1508(c)(4). Raises maximum coverage levels: new clause (ii): 'may be purchased at any level not to exceed— (I) in the case of the individual yield or revenue coverage, 85 percent; (II) in the case of individual yield or revenue coverage aggregated across multiple commodities, 90 percent; and (III) in the case of area yield or revenue coverage (as determined by the Corporation), 95 percent.' SCO buy-up threshold: strikes '14' and inserts '10' in clause (ii) — reduces gap bridgeable by SCO from 14 to 10 percentage points above individual coverage. Area-based guarantee trigger: strikes '86' and inserts '90' in clause (iii)(I). Area-based premium subsidy: strikes '65' and inserts '80' in §508(e)(2)(H)(i) — raises area-based plan federal premium subsidy from 65% to 80%.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: Title II defense spending ($150B) vs. Title VII-B Medicaid cuts — fiscal asymmetry
nodes.description: Title II Armed Services appropriates approximately $150 billion in new defense spending (SEC. 20001-20013) while Title VII-B simultaneously cuts Medicaid by an estimated $700+ billion over 10 years (per CBO estimates for equivalent provisions). The fiscal asymmetry is stark: the bill substantially expands the defense budget while imposing the largest Medicaid cuts in the program's history. Key contrast: Title II creates new $200B in loan guarantee authority (SEC. 20004(d) + 20005(b)) with minimal oversight ($10M IG per SEC. 20012 = 0.006% coverage), while Title VII-B Medicaid cuts directly affect low-income health coverage for tens of millions of Americans. Both sets of provisions are permanent or long-term in effect. Cross-reference: Title II node 3; Title VII-B node 11; Title VII-B/C/D node 12. The SEC. 20012 oversight appropriation ($10M for $150B) contrasts with the scale of Medicaid integrity provisions in Title VII-B which impose new verification burdens on states and beneficiaries.

nodes.title: SEC. 86001 / Subtitle G — Garden of Heroes: $40M for Statues (UNRELATED RIDER)
nodes.description: BURIED PROVISION — outside HELP Committee jurisdiction. 'In addition to amounts otherwise available, there are appropriated to the National Endowment for the Humanities for fiscal year 2025, out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, to remain available through fiscal year 2028, $40,000,000 for the procurement of statues as described in Executive Order 13934 (85 Fed. Reg. 41165; relating to building and rebuilding monuments to American heroes), Executive Order 13978 (86 Fed. Reg. 6809; relating to building the National Garden of American Heroes), and Executive Order 14189 (90 Fed. Reg. 8849; relating to celebrating America's birthday).' Three Trump Executive Orders: EO 13934 (July 2020), EO 13978 (January 2021), EO 14189 (January 2025). Mandatory appropriation from general Treasury funds available through FY2028. No connection to higher education, student loans, or workforce development. Legislative rider using HELP Committee bill as vehicle for executive priority. Cross-reference: NEH (20 U.S.C. 951 et seq.).

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: IRA rescission cascade — Title V (§§50304, 50402) + Title VI + Title VII coordinate total IRA dismantling
nodes.description: The Big Beautiful Bill conducts a coordinated multi-title dismantling of the Inflation Reduction Act. Title V (node 6) alone rescinds/repeals: §50304 (NPS/BLM IRA funds §§50221-50223), §50402 (IRA §§50123, 50141-50145, 50151-50153, 50161, 50142 — industrial decarbonization, ARPA-E, home rebates, clean energy demos, grid resilience). Title VI (node 7) continues the cascade: SEC. 60001 (clean heavy-duty vehicles §132 CAA), SEC. 60002 (Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund — node 29), SEC. 60003 (diesel emissions), SEC. 60004-60005 (air pollution programs), SEC. 60006 (low emissions electricity), SEC. 60007 (§211(o) CAA), SEC. 60008 (American Innovation and Manufacturing Act), SEC. 60009 (enforcement technology), SEC. 60010 (GHG corporate reporting), SEC. 60011 (environmental product declarations), SEC. 60012 (Methane Emissions and Waste Reduction Incentive Program — node 111), SEC. 60013-60018 (GHG plans, ESA recovery, climate data collection), SEC. 60019-60025 (neighborhood equity, federal buildings, GSA, environmental review funds, transportation materials, JFK Center). Title VII (node 10) terminates IRA tax credits: §§70501-70513 terminate clean vehicle credits, residential clean energy credits, energy efficient home/commercial credits, zero-emission nuclear credit, clean hydrogen, clean electricity production/investment credits. The three titles together constitute a comprehensive legislative rollback of essentially the entire IRA energy and environment investment. Title V handles leasing/mining/lands; Title VI handles EPA programs; Title VII handles tax incentives.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: Spectrum expansion (Title IV SEC. 40002) vs. CHIPS wireless supply chain rescission (Title IV SEC. 40011) — internal strategic tension
nodes.description: Within Title IV itself: SEC. 40002 extends FCC spectrum auction authority through 2034 and mandates 800 MHz of new commercial spectrum for 5G/broadband deployment ($50M to NTIA). SEC. 40011 simultaneously rescinds $850M from the CHIPS Act Public Wireless Supply Chain Innovation Fund — which was specifically designed to fund Open RAN alternatives to Huawei/ZTE so U.S. carriers have trusted vendors to deploy on that newly auctioned spectrum. Analysis: 'SEC. 40011 cuts a CHIPS Act program designed to ensure the U.S. has trusted vendors to occupy that newly auctioned spectrum — raising a strategic tension within Title IV itself.' The bill expands the spectrum frontier while defunding domestic supply chain capacity to fill it securely. Beneficiaries of this tension: Huawei/ZTE (less government-backed competition) and established Western telecom equipment makers less threatened by Open RAN development.

nodes.title: SEC. 70401 — Enhancement of Employer-Provided Child Care Credit
nodes.description: Expands §45F employer child care credit. §45F(a)(1): credit rate increased from 25% to '40 percent (50 percent in the case of an eligible small business)' of qualified child care expenditures. §45F(b) rewritten: dollar cap raised to $500,000 ($600,000 for eligible small businesses), with CPI inflation adjustment annually from 2026 (base: 2025). §45F(c)(1)(A)(iii): adds intermediary contract pathway — expenses under a contract with an intermediate entity that contracts with one or more qualified child care facilities qualify. §45F(c)(2)(C): jointly owned or operated facilities qualify. New §45F(c)(4): 'eligible small business' = gross receipts test of §448(c) using 5-taxable-year (not 3-year) averaging period. §45F(g): regulations and guidance authority. Effective: amounts paid or incurred after December 31, 2025.

nodes.title: SEC. 70523 — Intangible Drilling and Development Costs for Adjusted Financial Statement Income
nodes.description: Amends IRC § 56A(c)(13) (Adjusted Financial Statement Income under 15% CAMT, enacted by IRA 2022 § 10101). Rewrites to allow oil and gas companies to deduct BOTH regular depreciation AND intangible drilling and development costs (IDCs) when computing adjusted financial statement income for CAMT purposes. New § 56A(c)(13)(A): 'reduced by (i) depreciation deductions allowed under section 167 with respect to property to which section 168 applies to the extent of the amount allowed as deductions in computing taxable income for the year, and (ii) any deduction allowed for expenses under section 263(c) (including any deduction for such expenses under section 59(e) or 291(b)(2)) with respect to property described therein to the extent of the amount allowed as deductions in computing taxable income for the year.' New § 56A(c)(13)(B)(i): 'to disregard any amount of (I) depreciation expense that is taken into account on the taxpayer's applicable financial statement with respect to such property, and (II) depletion expense that is taken into account on the taxpayer's applicable financial statement with respect to the intangible drilling and development costs of such property.' Effective: taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025. Reduces CAMT burden on oil and gas producers — targeted carve-out from a tax increase imposed 3 years earlier. CBO ~$2-5 billion over the budget window. Benefits: ExxonMobil, Chevron, ConocoPhillips, Devon, Pioneer successors.

nodes.title: SEC. 10503 — Administrative and Operating Expense Adjustments
nodes.description: Amends 7 USC 1508(k). Adds paragraphs (10)-(12). Paragraph (10) additional expenses for high-loss states: 'Beginning with the 2026 reinsurance year...the Corporation shall pay an additional administrative and operating expense subsidy to approved insurance providers for eligible contracts.' Amount: '6 percent of the net book premium.' Eligible contract defined: 'a crop insurance contract entered into by an approved insurance provider in an eligible State' (excludes catastrophic, area-based plans, and zero-loss-adjustment contracts). Eligible State: 'a State in which, with respect to an insurance year, the loss ratio for eligible contracts is greater than 120 percent of the total net book premium written by all approved insurance providers.' Paragraph (11) specialty crops minimum: 'the rate of reimbursement to approved insurance providers and agents for administrative and operating expenses with respect to crop insurance contracts covering agricultural commodities described in section 101 of the Specialty Crops Competitiveness Act of 2004...shall be equal to or greater than the percentage that is the greater of the following: (i) 17 percent of the premium used to define loss ratio. (ii) The percent of the premium used to define loss ratio that is otherwise applicable.' Paragraph (12) inflation adjustment: annual CPI-U increases beginning 2026, consistent with 2011-2015 RMA Bulletin MGR-10-007 methodology.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: ACA subsidy cuts (71301-71305) + Medicaid work requirement disenrollment (Title VII-B) = compounded coverage gap for low-income populations
nodes.description: Two parallel restriction stacks converge on the same vulnerable low-income population: (1) Title VII-B Medicaid provisions (node 11) impose community engagement/work requirements that will disenroll significant numbers of current Medicaid beneficiaries — CBO estimated millions of coverage losses. (2) SEC. 71301-71305 simultaneously restrict the ACA marketplace fallback: immigration restrictions (71301), Medicaid-bridge elimination (71302), new verification burdens (71303), elimination of income-based SEPs (71304), and unlimited APTC repayment (71305). People disenrolled from Medicaid due to work requirement failures who turn to ACA marketplace coverage will find: (a) income-based SEPs no longer provide subsidized access (71304); (b) they must pre-verify before credits count (71303); (c) any overpayment is fully collectable with no cap (71305). The 'coverage gap' created between Medicaid disenrollment and ACA marketplace access is not a design accident — it is the structural outcome of these two parallel restriction tracks.

nodes.title: SEC. 71119 — Medicaid Community Engagement Requirements (Work Requirements) for ACA Expansion Adults
nodes.description: Amends 42 U.S.C. 1396a by adding new subsection (xx). Conforming amendment to §1902(a)(10)(A)(i)(VIII) inserting 'subject to subsections (k) and (xx).' Beginning not later than the first day of the first quarter that begins after December 31, 2026 (January 1, 2027) — or earlier if state elects — state shall provide, as a CONDITION OF ELIGIBILITY, that applicable individuals must demonstrate community engagement under paragraph (2): FOR NEW APPLICANTS: 1–3 consecutive months immediately preceding month of application (state specifies how many months). FOR ENROLLED INDIVIDUALS: verified at each regularly scheduled redetermination of eligibility. COMPLIANCE STANDARDS — 80 hours/month: (A) works not less than 80 hours; (B) completes not less than 80 hours of community service; (C) participates in a work program not less than 80 hours; (D) enrolled in educational program at least half-time; (E) any combination of (A)-(D) totaling not less than 80 hours; (F) monthly income not less than federal minimum wage (FLSA §6, currently .25) × 80 hours = /month; (G) average monthly income over preceding 6 months not less than /month AND is a seasonal worker (IRC §45R(d)(5)(B)). MANDATORY EXEMPTIONS (state shall deem compliant; may elect not to require verification): (i) for part or all of month: was 'specified excluded individual' (see below), OR was under age 19, OR entitled to/enrolled in Medicare Part A or B, OR described in §1902(a)(10)(A)(i)(I)-(VII); (ii) was inmate of public institution at any point in 3-month period ending on first day of that month. SPECIFIED EXCLUDED INDIVIDUALS (not applicable individuals at all): (I) medically needy §1902(a)(10)(A)(i)(IX); (II) Indian, Urban Indian (Indian Health Care Improvement Act §4(13),(28)), California Indian §809(a), or determined eligible for IHS; (III) parent, guardian, caretaker relative, or family caregiver (RAISE Family Caregivers Act §2) of dependent child 13 years and under OR disabled individual; (IV) veteran with disability rated as total under 38 U.S.C. §1155; (V) medically frail or special medical needs (Secretary-defined), including: (aa) blind or disabled (§1614); (bb) substance use disorder; (cc) disabling mental disorder; (dd) physical/intellectual/developmental disability significantly impairing one or more ADLs; (ee) serious or complex medical condition; (VI)(aa) in compliance with TANF work requirements (§407); (VI)(bb) SNAP household member not exempt from SNAP work requirements; (VII) drug/alcohol treatment and rehabilitation program (Food and Nutrition Act §3(h)); (VIII) inmate of public institution; (IX) pregnant or postpartum up to 12 months (§1902(e)(5) or (16)). OPTIONAL SHORT-TERM HARDSHIP EXEMPTIONS (state may grant): (I) receiving inpatient hospital, nursing facility, ICF/IDD, inpatient psychiatric, or similar services; (II)(aa) Presidential disaster or emergency declaration in county; (II)(bb) county unemployment rate at or above the lesser of 8% or 1.5x national rate; (III) individual or dependent must travel outside community for extended period for medical services not available locally. NONCOMPLIANCE PROCEDURE: State cannot verify compliance → notice of noncompliance → 30 calendar days to make satisfactory showing → if no satisfactory showing: disenroll not later than end of month following month in which 30-day period ends. State must first determine other eligibility bases. Fair hearing rights preserved. APA BYPASS: implementing interim final rule due no later than June 1, 2026; exempt from 5 U.S.C. §553 notice-and-comment. COVERAGE GAP TRAP: §(xx)(7)(B): 'an individual shall be deemed to be eligible for minimum essential coverage described in section 5000A(f)(1)(A)(ii)...for a month if such individual would have been eligible for medical assistance...but for a failure to meet the requirement to demonstrate community engagement' — person disenrolled for work requirement noncompliance CANNOT receive ACA marketplace premium tax credit (§36B(c)(2)(B) IRC). ANTI-CONFLICT-OF-INTEREST: State shall not use managed care entity or specified entity to determine compliance if contractor has direct/indirect financial relationship with MCE covering that individual. TRANSITION: Secretary may exempt state demonstrating good faith effort. Exemptions expire not later than December 31, 2028 and CANNOT be renewed. WAIVER PROHIBITION: §(xx)(10): 'Notwithstanding section 1115(a), the provisions of this subsection may not be waived.' FUNDING: ,000,000 FY2026 CMS implementation; ,000,000 FY2026 state grants (population-based pro-rata on applicable individual count as of March 31, 2025); ,000,000 FY2026 equal distribution. Total: ,000,000. ~21 million ACA expansion enrollees subject. CBO prior estimates of similar proposals: 1.5–3 million lose coverage. ~60% already work; most non-workers are caregivers, students, recently unemployed, or have undiagnosed exempt conditions. Coverage loss driven primarily by paperwork failures, not substantive non-compliance.

nodes.title: SEC. 100018 — AMENDMENT TO AUTHORITY TO APPLY FOR ASYLUM (amendment to INA § 208(d)(3), 8 U.S.C. 1158(d)(3))
nodes.description: Changes asylum fee authority from discretionary to mandatory and removes cost cap. Text (lines 18024-18032): Amendment to § 208(d)(3): (1) 'in the first sentence, by striking "may" and inserting "shall"' — converts fee-charging from discretionary to MANDATORY; (2) 'by striking "Such fees shall not exceed" and all that follows and inserting the following: "Nothing in this paragraph may be construed to limit the authority of the Attorney General to set additional adjudication and naturalization fees in accordance with section 286(m)."' Prior law contained fee cap: fees could not exceed cost of adjudication. New law: cap removed entirely; AG authority to set fees above adjudication cost explicitly affirmed under § 286(m). AG now HAS NO DISCRETION to waive the duty to charge fees. Clears statutory path for fees in §§ 100002, 100009, 100011 to operate without challenge based on prior cost-cap language. Cross-refs: INA § 208(d)(3) (8 U.S.C. 1158(d)(3)); § 286(m) (8 U.S.C. 1356(m)).

nodes.title: SEC. 10504 — Premium Support
nodes.description: Amends 7 USC 1508(e)(2). Raises federal premium subsidies across all coverage levels by 5 percentage points at 65-80% levels and 3 points at 85%. Exact changes: subparagraph (C)(i) strikes '64' inserts '69' (65% coverage level); subparagraph (D)(i) strikes '59' inserts '64' (70% level); subparagraph (E)(i) strikes '55' inserts '60' (75% level); subparagraph (F)(i) strikes '48' inserts '51' (80% level); subparagraph (G)(i) strikes '38' inserts '41' (85% level). New subsidy table: 65% coverage = 69% federal subsidy; 70% = 64%; 75% = 60%; 80% = 51%; 85% = 41%. One of the largest cost items in the crop insurance subtitle — benefits all insured producers through lower out-of-pocket premiums.

nodes.title: SEC. 70402 — Enhancement of Adoption Credit
nodes.description: Makes $5,000 of the §23 adoption credit refundable. New §23(a)(4): 'So much of the credit allowed under paragraph (1) as does not exceed $5,000 shall be treated as a credit allowed under subpart C' — meaning families can receive up to $5,000 as refund even with zero tax liability. Remaining non-refundable portion continues with 5-year carryforward. §23(h) rewritten: inflation adjustments maintained from 2002 base (paragraph (3) and (4) amounts and subsection (b)(1) and (b)(2)(A)(i) amounts). Refundable $5,000 amount indexed from 2025 (calendar year 2024 as base). §23(c)(1): carryforward excludes refundable portion. Effective: tax years beginning after December 31, 2024.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: IRA Rescissions Total Across All Titles — Bill-Wide Environmental Rollback
nodes.description: Title VI (node 7) contains 21 IRA rescissions totaling ~$41B in authorized amounts. But IRA rescissions appear across multiple titles: Title III (node 4) Sec. 30002 rescinds GRRP housing retrofit funds (~$500M); Title IV (node 5) Sec. 40008 rescinds NOAA IRA funds (~$3.655B), Sec. 40010 rescinds alternative aviation fuel funds (~$297M); Title V (node 6) Sec. 50402 contains additional IRA energy program repeals and rescissions; Title VII (nodes 8-10) contains multiple IRA tax credit terminations (Secs. 70501-70515) eliminating EV credits, clean energy production/investment credits, clean hydrogen, advanced manufacturing. PATTERN noted at node 132: at least 12 IRA rescission provisions across Titles I, III, VI, and VII. Title VI is the largest single-title IRA rescission vehicle, but the bill-wide dismantling spans appropriations rescissions, statutory repeals (Sec. 60002 GGRF repeal), and tax credit terminations across every major title. Conservative total across all titles: $500B+ in present-value IRA climate investment eliminated or curtailed.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: Coast Guard recapitalization (Title IV SEC. 40001) overlaps with Title IX border enforcement missions (SEC. 90001-90007)
nodes.description: Title IV SEC. 40001 appropriates $24.6B to Coast Guard explicitly for 'interdiction of persons and controlled substances' and 'hardening of maritime approaches.' Offshore Patrol Cutters ($4.3B) and Fast Response Cutters ($1B) are described as providing 'operational presence and security of the maritime border and for interdiction of persons and controlled substances.' Title IX SEC. 90001-90007 funds border wall ($90001), CBP personnel/vehicles ($90002), detention capacity ($90003), border security technology ($90004), state/local assistance ($90005), presidential residence protection ($90006), and DHS border support ($90007). The Coast Guard's maritime interdiction mission (Title IV) and DHS/CBP land/air border enforcement (Title IX) address the same border security goals through different domains (sea vs. land/air), with overlapping jurisdictions at maritime approaches to ports and coastal borders. Combined effect: comprehensive multi-domain border enforcement investment.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: Methane policy — Title V §50103 (royalty repeal) vs. Title VI §60012 (waste reduction program rescission)
nodes.description: Methane — a greenhouse gas ~80x more potent than CO2 over 20 years — is targeted for deregulation by two separate titles working in tandem: (1) Title V §50103 (node 37) repeals IRA §50263 (30 U.S.C. 1727), eliminating royalty payments on methane vented or flared from federal oil and gas leases. This was the most direct federal GHG pricing mechanism ever enacted on federal land operations. (2) Title VI §60012 (node 111) rescinds unobligated balances from the IRA Methane Emissions and Waste Reduction Incentive Program, which had funded monitoring, reduction, and reporting of methane emissions at oil/gas facilities. Together: no financial penalty for venting/flaring methane (§50103), no federal program funding monitoring/reduction (§60012). The mandated expansion of O&G production under §§50101-50105 will increase total methane output. The triple effect — more production, no royalty penalty for venting, no waste reduction program — represents the most comprehensive reversal of federal methane policy ever enacted.

nodes.title: SEC. 10505 — Program Compliance and Integrity
nodes.description: Amends 7 USC 1515(l)(2). Raises mandatory funding cap for crop insurance program integrity from ,000,000 to ,000,000 beginning FY2026. New text: 'than— (A) ,000,000 for each of fiscal years 2009 through 2025; and (B) ,000,000 for fiscal year 2026 and each subsequent fiscal year.' Effective FY2026.

nodes.title: SEC. 70524 — Qualifying Income of Publicly Traded Partnerships: Hydrogen, Carbon Capture, Advanced Nuclear, Hydropower, Geothermal
nodes.description: Amends IRC § 7704(d)(1)(E) (Qualifying Income for PTPs — Mineral Resources). Rewrites to enumerate six new categories of qualifying income for publicly traded partnerships (MLPs). New text: 'income and gains derived from (i) the exploration [existing oil/gas language]; (ii) the transportation or storage of (I) any fuel described in subsection (b), (c), (d), (e), or (k) of section 6426, or any alcohol fuel defined in section 6426(b)(4)(A) or any biodiesel fuel as defined in section 40A(d)(1) or sustainable aviation fuel as defined in section 40B(d)(1), or (II) liquified hydrogen or compressed hydrogen; (iii) in the case of a qualified facility (as defined in section 45Q(d)...not less than 50 percent of the total carbon oxide production of which is qualified carbon oxide (as defined in section 45Q(c))) — (I) the generation, availability for such generation, or storage of electric power at such facility, or (II) the capture of carbon dioxide by such facility; (iv) the production of electricity from any advanced nuclear facility (as defined in section 45J(d)(2)); (v) the production of electricity or thermal energy exclusively using a qualified energy resource described in subparagraph (D) or (H) of section 45(c)(1) [hydropower and geothermal]; (vi) the operation of energy property described in clause (iii) or (vii) of section 48(a)(3)(A) [geothermal and fuel cell].' Effective: taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025. Revenue-negative — allows more income to flow through favorable pass-through structure. Wind and solar CONSPICUOUSLY ABSENT. Carbon capture inclusion effectively subsidizes EOR (enhanced oil recovery) via CO2 injection — indirect fossil fuel benefit.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: $5T debt ceiling (72001) vs. total new spending in Big Beautiful Bill — borrowing capacity calibrated to cover the bill's own costs
nodes.description: The $5 trillion debt ceiling increase in SEC. 72001 must be understood in the context of total new spending authorized by this bill. Key new spending in Title VII-B/C/D alone: Rural Health Transformation Program $50B (FY2026-2030) + Medicare physician fee bump ~$1-2B (CY2026) + HCBS implementation funding $150M + Rural hospital program implementation $200M. Across the full bill, massive new spending includes: defense enhancements, border infrastructure, tax cuts (reduced revenue), SNAP/agriculture changes, energy leasing. The CBO projected the full bill adds trillions to the deficit over 10 years. The $5 trillion ceiling is calibrated not just to avoid default but to provide runway through 2028-2029, funding both the bill's spending programs and ongoing government operations. This is structurally a self-funding debt authorization — Congress passed legislation that requires significant new borrowing and simultaneously authorized that borrowing.

nodes.title: SEC. 70403 — Recognizing Indian Tribal Governments for Purposes of Determining Whether a Child Has Special Needs for Purposes of the Adoption Credit
nodes.description: Amends §23(d)(3) to allow Indian tribal governments (not just states) to determine that a child has 'special needs' for purposes of the adoption credit. §23(d)(3)(A): inserts 'or Indian tribal government' after 'a State'. §23(d)(3)(B): inserts 'or Indian tribal government' after 'such State'. Effect: enables the maximum adoption credit for tribal children placed through tribal government processes — previously only state determinations qualified. Effective: tax years beginning after December 31, 2024.

nodes.title: SEC. 10506 — Reviews, Compliance, and Integrity
nodes.description: Amends 7 USC 1516(b)(2)(C)(i). Increases FCIC compliance reviews and data analysis appropriation to ,000,000/year beginning FY2026. Text: strikes 'for each fiscal year' and inserts 'for each of fiscal years 2014 through 2025 and ,000,000 for fiscal year 2026 and each fiscal year thereafter'. Effective FY2026.

nodes.title: SEC. 100051 — APPROPRIATION FOR THE DEPARTMENT OF HOMELAND SECURITY — $2,055,000,000
nodes.description: Mandatory appropriation to DHS for twelve enforcement purposes, available through September 30, 2029.
