Text (lines 18038-18147): 'there is appropriated to the Secretary of Homeland Security for fiscal year 2025, out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, $2,055,000,000, to remain available through September 30, 2029.' 12 purposes: (1) CBP agent hiring and training; (2) deportation transportation costs; (3) DHS employees and state officers for immigration enforcement per INA §§ 103(a) and 287(g); (4) background checks/vetting under INA §§ 212, 237; (5) fingerprint collection (INA § 262, § 235(a)(3),(b)) and DNA collection from aliens/children entering without valid visa (INA §§ 235(d) and 287(b)); (6) transport/return from contiguous territory (INA § 235(b)(2)(C)); (7) state/local participation in gang elimination, crime, trafficking, immigration enforcement including reimbursement; (8) REMOVAL OF SPECIFIED UNACCOMPANIED ALIEN CHILDREN — defined as UAC who: (I) found at land border/port AND is inadmissible; (II) 'has not been a victim of severe forms of trafficking in persons, and there is no credible evidence that such child is at risk of being trafficked upon return'; (III) 'does not have a fear of returning to the child's country... owing to a credible fear of persecution' — permitting withdrawal of application for admission per § 235(a)(4); (9) expedited removal of criminal aliens per § 235(b)(1); (10) removal of criminal aliens without hearings per § 235(c); (11) criminal/gang checks for UAC age 12+, 'including the examination of such unaccompanied alien children for gang-related tattoos and other gang-related markings'; (12) IT for immigration purposes. Cross-refs: INA §§ 103(a), 235, 237, 262, 287(g); TVPA § 103 (22 U.S.C. 7102).

nodes.title: SEC. 71120 — Cost Sharing Requirements for Expansion Individuals Above 100% FPL
nodes.description: Amends 42 U.S.C. 1396o by adding new subsection (k); amends §1902(a)(14) (mandatory imposition conforming amendment); amends §1916A(a)(1) (nonapplicability of alternative cost sharing). Beginning October 1, 2028. 'SPECIFIED INDIVIDUAL' = ACA expansion adult (§1902(a)(10)(A)(i)(VIII)) with family income (determined per §1902(e)(14)) exceeding the poverty line (§2110(c)(5)) applicable to family size AND enrolled under §1902(a)(10)(A)(i)(VIII) or equivalent MEC waiver. ~60–70% of expansion enrollees have income above 100% FPL. PREMIUMS: §(k)(1): no enrollment fee, premium, or similar charge may be imposed. REQUIRED COST SHARING: §(k)(2)(A): State plan SHALL, beginning October 1, 2028, provide for imposition of deductions, cost sharing, or similar charges determined appropriate by the State (in an amount GREATER THAN /bin/zsh) for certain care, items, or services. EXCLUDED FROM COST SHARING: (i) services under §1916(a)(2)(B)–(J) (categorically protected populations — children, pregnant women, etc.); primary care services; mental health care services; substance use disorder services; FQHC services (§1905(l)(2)); certified community behavioral health clinic (CCBHC, §1905(jj)(2)) services; rural health clinic (§1905(l)(1)) services. PER-SERVICE CAP:  per item or service (no exceptions under (ii)(I)). PRESCRIPTION DRUG CAP: amount that would apply under §1916A(c)(2)(A)(i) or (2)(B)(i). FAMILY AGGREGATE CAP: §(k)(2)(B)(iii): 'The total aggregate amount of deductions, cost sharing, or similar charges imposed under the State plan for all individuals in the family may not exceed 5 percent of the family income of the family involved, as applied on a quarterly or monthly basis (as specified by the State).' DENIAL OF CARE: §(k)(2)(C): 'Notwithstanding subsection (e), a State may permit a provider participating under the State plan to require, as a condition for the provision of care, items, or services to a specified individual...the payment of any deductions, cost sharing, or similar charges.' Provider may waive on case-by-case basis. ,000,000 FY2026 implementation. For people at 100–138% FPL (,580–,120 annual income),  co-pay for specialist visit or imaging is material. Provider-may-deny-care is explicit departure from prior Medicaid rules prohibiting denial for nonpayment. CCBHC exclusion protects behavioral health but CCBHCs not universally available.

nodes.title: SEC. 87001 / Subtitle H — ORR Unaccompanied Alien Children Vetting: $300M (UNRELATED RIDER)
nodes.description: BURIED PROVISION — immigration enforcement placed in education title. '$300,000,000, to remain available until September 30, 2028' appropriated to Office of Refugee Resettlement. Permitted uses: (1) Background checks on potential sponsors: name, SSN/TIN, DOB, residence, 'in-person or virtual interview with, and suitability study concerning, the potential sponsor and all adult residents of the potential sponsor's household'; 'national criminal history check based on fingerprints'; sex offender registry; public records background check. (2) Home studies. (3) GANG TATTOO EXAMINATION: 'conducting an examination of the unaccompanied alien child for gang-related tattoos and other gang-related markings and covering such tattoos or markings while the child is in the care of the Office of Refugee Resettlement.' (4) Data systems improvement supporting 'identification and investigation of child labor exploitation and child trafficking.' (5) Coordination with State child welfare agencies. Definition: 'unaccompanied alien child' per Homeland Security Act §462(g) (6 U.S.C. 279(g)). Mandatory appropriation, available through September 30, 2028. Cross-references: William Wilberforce Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008. ORR is within HHS (HELP Committee health jurisdiction), but immigration enforcement of unaccompanied minors policy is primarily Homeland Security Committee jurisdiction.

nodes.title: SEC. 70404 — Enhancement of the Dependent Care Assistance Program
nodes.description: Increases the §129 employer-provided dependent care FSA exclusion from $5,000 ($2,500 for married filing separately) to '$7,500 ($3,750' for MFS. §129(a)(2)(A) amended by striking '$5,000 ($2,500' and inserting '$7,500 ($3,750'. First increase to §129 limit in decades. Allows employees to set aside more pre-tax dollars for child/dependent care through employer FSA. No income limit — benefits mid-to-upper income workers most in absolute terms. Effective: tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.

nodes.title: SEC. 70525 — Allow for Payments to Certain Individuals Who Dye Fuel
nodes.description: Creates new IRC § 6435 'DYED FUEL' — refund mechanism for persons who remove indelibly dyed tax-exempt diesel fuel or kerosene from terminals where excise tax was previously paid. Text: '(a) IN GENERAL.—If a person establishes to the satisfaction of the Secretary that such person meets the requirements of subsection (b) with respect to diesel fuel or kerosene, then the Secretary shall pay to such person an amount (without interest) equal to the tax described in subsection (b)(2)(A) with respect to such diesel fuel or kerosene.' Eligibility: person removes from a terminal 'eligible indelibly dyed diesel fuel or kerosene' — defined as diesel/kerosene '(A) with respect to which a tax under section 4081 was previously paid (and not credited or refunded), and (B) which is exempt from taxation under section 4082(a).' Conforming amendments to §§ 6206, 6430, 6675. Effective: eligible indelibly dyed diesel/kerosene removed on or after 180 days after enactment (~January 1, 2026). Technical fix for double-taxation scenario — minor revenue item. Benefits: farmers, off-road equipment operators, distributors using dyed diesel/kerosene where excise taxes were erroneously collected upstream.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: Fossil fuel expansion (Title V) vs. clean energy termination (Title VII) — asymmetric energy transition reversal
nodes.description: Title V mandates massive expansion of fossil fuel extraction while Title VII terminates clean energy tax incentives, creating an asymmetric reversal of US energy transition policy: FOSSIL FUEL EXPANSION (Title V): §50101 mandates quarterly O&G lease sales in 9 states; §50102 mandates 30 Gulf + 6 Alaska offshore sales through 2040; §50103 repeals methane royalty; §50104 mandates 4 ANWR sales; §50105 mandates 5 NPR-A sales ≥4M acres; §50201-50204 accelerates coal leasing, cuts royalties to 7%, opens 4M new acres; §50403 redirects B loan guarantees away from clean energy toward 'energy and critical minerals.' CLEAN ENERGY TERMINATION (Title VII): §70501 terminates previously-owned clean vehicle credit; §70502 terminates clean vehicle credit; §70503 terminates commercial clean vehicles credit; §70504 terminates alternative fuel refueling credit; §70505 terminates energy efficient home improvement credit; §70506 terminates residential clean energy credit; §70507 terminates energy efficient commercial buildings deduction; §70508 terminates new energy efficient home credit; §70509 terminates cost recovery for energy property; §70510 modifies zero-emission nuclear credit; §70511 terminates clean hydrogen production credit; §70512-70513 terminates clean electricity production and investment credits. Title V simultaneously creates new barriers for renewables on federal land (§50302 gross revenue fee) while expanding fossil fuel access. No equivalent expansion mandates exist for renewable energy.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: Title VI Sec. 60026 NEPA Fee Mechanism vs. Title V Energy NEPA Changes (node 6)
nodes.description: Title VI Sec. 60026 creates a new NEPA opt-in fee mechanism (42 U.S.C. 4336f) that benefits any project type — including the energy extraction and fossil fuel projects that Title V (node 6) directly facilitates. Interaction: (1) Title V Sec. 50101 (Onshore Oil and Gas Leasing), 50102 (Offshore), 50103 (Royalties on Extracted Methane), 50104 (ANWR), 50105 (NPR-A) — all expand fossil fuel development that would require NEPA review; (2) Title VI Sec. 60026 enables those project sponsors to pay 125% of review costs to CEQ for hard deadlines of 180 days EA / 1 year EIS; (3) Title VI Sec. 60014 simultaneously rescinds the IRA funds that were meant to improve EPA's NEPA review capacity. NET EFFECT: Energy projects that Title V unleashes face a faster permitting pathway thanks to Title VI Sec. 60026, while the public capacity to conduct rigorous reviews (Secs. 60014, 60023) has been defunded. This is a coherent two-title regulatory acceleration strategy. ALSO: Title V Sec. 50402 IRA energy program rescissions (node 179) and Title VI rescissions are additive — together they strip both the regulatory capacity AND the competing clean energy investment.

nodes.title: SEC. 10507 — Poultry Insurance Pilot Program
nodes.description: Amends 7 USC 1523. Adds new subsection (j): 'POULTRY INSURANCE PILOT PROGRAM.— (1) IN GENERAL.—Notwithstanding subsection (a)(2), the Corporation shall establish a pilot program under which contract poultry growers, including growers of broilers and laying hens, may elect to receive index-based insurance from extreme weather-related risk resulting in increased utility costs (including costs of natural gas, propane, electricity, water, and other appropriate costs, as determined by the Corporation) associated with poultry production.' Location: 'conducted in a sufficient number of counties to provide a comprehensive evaluation of the feasibility, effectiveness, and demand among producers in the top poultry producing States.' Approval deadline: 'the Board shall approve a policy or plan of insurance based on the pilot program under paragraph (1)...not later than 2 years after the date of enactment of this subsection.' Specifically for CONTRACT growers — integrators who own the chickens are excluded. Covers utility cost increases, not livestock losses.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: Rural hospital $50B investment (71401) vs. ACA subsidy cuts + Medicaid disenrollment — internal tension: program funds hospitals whose patient base is being simultaneously uninsured
nodes.description: SEC. 71401 invests $50 billion in rural hospital infrastructure and transformation. However, the simultaneous coverage restriction provisions will reduce insurance rates in precisely the rural communities these hospitals serve: (1) ACA restrictions (71301-71305) will reduce marketplace enrollment — rural residents are disproportionately likely to use ACA marketplace coverage due to lower employer-sponsored insurance rates. (2) Medicaid work requirements (Title VII-B, node 11) will disenroll rural Medicaid beneficiaries — rural populations have higher Medicaid dependency rates. (3) Medicare immigration restrictions (71201) affect rural immigrant agricultural workers who may have had Medicare access. The rural hospital program funds infrastructure for hospitals whose patient base may become less insured, creating financial stress that the program is designed to alleviate but whose root cause is in the same legislation. Rural hospitals' financial viability is closely tied to payer mix — increasing uninsured rates while simultaneously funding hospital 'transformation' is internally contradictory. The 'right-sizing' provision (71401(6)(G)) may facilitate converting hospitals that become financially non-viable to ambulatory settings.

nodes.title: SEC. 70405 — Enhancement of Child and Dependent Care Tax Credit
nodes.description: Restructures §21 child and dependent care credit income-based reduction. New §21(a)(2): 'applicable percentage' means 50 percent — (A) reduced (but not below 35 percent) by 1 percentage point for each $2,000 or fraction by which AGI exceeds $15,000, AND (B) further reduced (but not below 20 percent) by 1 percentage point for each $2,000 ($4,000 for joint return) by which AGI exceeds $75,000 ($150,000 for joint). Prior law: phasedown began at $15,000 AGI all the way to 20% floor, making credit less generous for middle-income families. New law: maximum 50% rate applies broadly until AGI hits $75,000 single/$150,000 joint before second phasedown. Underlying expense limits ($3,000/$6,000) unchanged. Effective: tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.

nodes.title: SEC. 100052 — APPROPRIATION FOR U.S. IMMIGRATION AND CUSTOMS ENFORCEMENT — $29,850,000,000
nodes.description: Largest single immigration enforcement appropriation in U.S. history. Text (lines 18148-18250): 'there is appropriated to the Secretary of Homeland Security for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement for fiscal year 2025, out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, $29,850,000,000, to remain available through September 30, 2029.' 11 purposes: (1) Hiring/training ICE personnel 'prioritizing and streamlining the hiring of retired U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement personnel'; (2) Performance/retention/signing bonuses — RETENTION: 2-year commitment; SIGNING: 'hired on or after the date of the enactment of this Act' AND 'commits to 5 years of service' — written service agreement required with commencement/termination dates, bonus amount, conditions; (3) Recruitment, hiring, onboarding including IT, marketing, and staff therefor; (4) Transportation for deportation operations; (5) IT for enforcement/removal including fee collection improvements; (6) Facility upgrades; (7) Fleet modernization; (8) FAMILY UNITY: 'Promoting family unity by— (A) maintaining the care and custody, during the period in which a charge described in clause (i) is pending... of an alien who— (i) is charged only with a misdemeanor offense under section 275(a) of the INA (8 U.S.C. 1325(a)); and (ii) entered the United States with the alien's child who has not attained 18 years of age; and (B) detaining such an alien with the alien's child.' [NOTE: 'family unity' means family DETENTION together, not release]; (9) 287(g) agreement expansion; (10) VOICE Office hiring; (11) Additional OPLA attorneys for DHS representation in removal proceedings. Cross-refs: INA §§ 275(a), 287(g) (8 U.S.C. 1325(a), 1357(g)); 5 U.S.C. bonus authorities.

nodes.title: SEC. 70531 — Modifications to De Minimis Entry Privilege for Commercial Shipments
nodes.description: Amends Section 321 of the Tariff Act of 1930 (19 U.S.C. 1321) — de minimis entry provision. Unrelated to energy; placed in Chapter 5 ('Ending Green New Deal Spending'). (a) CIVIL PENALTY: Adds new § 321(c): 'Any person who enters, introduces, facilitates, or attempts to introduce an article into the United States using the privilege of this section, the importation of which violates any other provision of United States customs law, shall be assessed, in addition to any other penalty permitted by law, a civil penalty of up to $5,000 for the first violation and up to $10,000 for each subsequent violation.' Effective 30 days after enactment (~August 3, 2025). (b) REPEAL OF COMMERCIAL SHIPMENT EXCEPTION: Amends § 321(a)(2) — repeals the commercial shipment exception to de minimis entry (currently allowing packages valued at $800 or less to enter without customs inspection or duties). Effective July 1, 2027. Conforming repeal also removes the new civil penalty in § 321(c) when the commercial exception is repealed (meaning the civil penalty window is only 2 years). Benefits: U.S. retailers, domestic apparel/goods manufacturers competing with Shein, Temu, AliExpress. Loses: Chinese direct-to-consumer e-commerce platforms that rely on the $800 commercial de minimis exception. CBO estimates project billions in new duty collections annually. 2-year runway for business adjustment.

nodes.title: SEC. 10601 — Conservation
nodes.description: Amends multiple sections of Food Security Act of 1985 (16 USC 3841(a), 3871d, 3839bb-2(b), 3839bb-5(f)(1), 1012a) and Agriculture Improvement Act of 2018 (7 USC 8351 note). Sets new mandatory funding through FY2031: ACEP: M/M/M/M/M/M (FY2026-2031). EQIP: .655B/.855B/.255B/.255B/.255B/.255B (FY2026-2031). CSP: .3B/.325B/.35B/.375B/.375B/.375B (FY2026-2031). RCPP: M/M/M/M/M/M (FY2026-2031). Watershed Protection: ',000,000 for fiscal year 2026 and each fiscal year thereafter' (up from M). VPA-HIP: ',000,000 for the period of fiscal years 2025 through 2031'. Feral Swine: ',000,000 for the period of fiscal years 2025 through 2031'. Grassroots Water: ',000,000 beginning in fiscal year 2026'. RESCISSION — subsection (g): 'The unobligated balances of amounts appropriated by section 21001(a) of Public Law 117-169 (136 Stat. 2015) are rescinded.' This eliminates approximately .45B in IRA conservation funding. New authorized levels are lower than IRA-era levels. Cross-reference: SEC. 10201 (parallel IRA forestry rescission).

nodes.title: SEC. 71121 — HCBS Coverage Expansion and Worker Benefits Restriction
nodes.description: Amends 42 U.S.C. 1396n(c) by adding new paragraph (11). Beginning July 1, 2028: Secretary may approve a standalone waiver (separate from any other 1915(c) waiver) to provide HCBS to individuals who do NOT need institutional level-of-care (LOC) determination — gap population needing support but not nursing home-level care. Initial 3-year term; extended 5-year increments upon state request unless requirements not met. STATE REQUIREMENTS FOR WAIVER APPROVAL: (i) all existing 1915(c) waivers of state must be in compliance; (ii) state demonstrates approval will not result in material increase in average wait time for individuals with institutional LOC determinations; (iii) state establishes needs-based eligibility criteria (Secretary-approved) for new population; (iv) state establishes more stringent LOC criteria for institutional care than for HCBS eligibility; (v) state attests that average per capita HCBS expenditure for new population will not exceed average per capita expenditure for institutional care — for duration of waiver; (vi) state provides Secretary with data on number of individuals to be served; (vii) state reports annually (not less frequently): cost of services by type; length of time individuals received each service type; comparison data with institutional-LOC population and institutional care population; number served. WORKER BENEFITS RESTRICTION — paragraph (C): 'No payments made to carry out this paragraph shall be used by a State to make payments to a third party on behalf of an individual practitioner for benefits such as health insurance, skills training, and other benefits customary for employees, in the case of a class of practitioners for which the program established under this title is the primary source of revenue.' Targets personal care attendants and home health aides in consumer-directed programs. States had used HCBS funding to stabilize low-paid workforce via health insurance/training stipends. Funding: ,000,000 FY2026 (CMS implementation); ,000,000 FY2027 for state payments (proportional to state's share of all HCBS-eligible population under existing 1915(c) and 1115 authority). If Medicaid is not the primary revenue source for a class (e.g., licensed therapists with private patients), restriction does not apply.

nodes.title: SEC. 100053 — APPROPRIATION FOR FEDERAL LAW ENFORCEMENT TRAINING CENTERS — $750,000,000
nodes.description: FLETC training appropriation. Text (lines 18251-18269): 'there is appropriated to the Secretary of Homeland Security for the Federal Law Enforcement Training Centers for fiscal year 2025, out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, $750,000,000, to remain available until September 30, 2029.' TRAINING (subsection b): 'Not less than $285,000,000 of the amounts available under subsection (a) shall be for supporting the training of newly hired Federal law enforcement personnel employed by the Department of Homeland Security and State and local law enforcement agencies operating in support of the Department of Homeland Security.' FACILITIES (subsection c): 'Not more than $465,000,000 of the amounts available under subsection (a) shall be for procurement, construction and maintenance of, improvements to, training equipment for, and related expenses, of facilities of the Federal Law Enforcement Training Centers.' Hard floor/ceiling structure: at least $285M training; no more than $465M facilities. Enables rapid scaling of ICE/CBP agent corps funded under §§ 100051-100052.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: Environmental Review Impacts on Infrastructure — Title VI vs. Title IV (node 5)
nodes.description: Title IV (Commerce, Science, and Transportation, node 5) contains infrastructure provisions that are directly affected by Title VI environmental review changes. Interaction points: (1) Title IV Sec. 40003 (Air Traffic Control Improvements) and Sec. 40001 (Coast Guard) involve major infrastructure construction requiring NEPA review — these projects can use the Title VI Sec. 60026 pay-for-speed mechanism; (2) Title IV Sec. 40006 (CAFE civil penalties zeroed out) eliminates the vehicle emissions enforcement lever that complemented the clean vehicle programs Title VI rescinds (Sec. 60001); (3) Title VI Sec. 60023 rescinds IIJA environmental review implementation funds under 23 U.S.C. 178 — these were transportation funds, directly overlapping with Title IV infrastructure programs; (4) Title VI Sec. 60024 rescinds IIJA low-carbon transportation materials grants under 23 U.S.C. 179 — a transportation program placed in an environmental title. IIJA/BIL rescissions in Secs. 60019, 60023, 60024 are transportation equity/materials programs placed in Title VI but with direct Title IV implications — possible cross-committee coordination or deliberate obfuscation of which committee vehicle is being used.

nodes.title: SEC. 70411 — Tax Credit for Contributions of Individuals to Scholarship Granting Organizations
nodes.description: Creates new §25F: up to $1,700/year federal tax credit for individual contributions to 'scholarship granting organizations' (SGOs) in opt-in states. Credit reduced by state-level SGO credit for same contribution. 5-year carryforward. §170 charitable deduction denied for qualifying contributions. 'Covered states': states that voluntarily elect participation and submit SGO list to Treasury by January 1 each year (Governor or designee). 'Eligible student': household income ≤300% of area median gross income (§42) AND eligible to enroll in public K-12. 'Scholarship granting organization': §501(c)(3) public charity (not private foundation) that: maintains separate qualified contribution accounts; provides scholarships to 10+ students not all at same school; spends ≥90% of income on scholarships; no earmarking for specific students; income-verifies applicants; no self-dealing (§4946 rules); prioritizes continuing and sibling scholarship recipients. New §139K: scholarship amounts excluded from recipient's gross income. Effective: tax years ending after December 31, 2026. States submit SGO lists by January 1 each year.

nodes.title: IRA rescission buries ~.45B net cut as 'investment'
nodes.description: SEC. 10601(g) rescission of IRA §21001(a) conservation funds is the single largest fiscal provision in Title I but is buried in a subtitle titled 'Additional Investments in Rural America.' The IRA had tripled EQIP and doubled RCPP funding with climate-smart agriculture requirements. The new authorized levels in SEC. 10601 are lower than what was available under the IRA: EQIP under IRA was up to ~.5B/year vs new .255B/year ceiling. The section is framed as increasing conservation funding while the net effect relative to current law is a massive cut. Cross-reference: SEC. 10201 rescinds IRA forestry funds (.15B unobligated). Combined IRA rescissions in Title I could exceed B. This framing pattern — rescinding larger funding while announcing new lower funding — should be checked against other titles.

nodes.title: SEC. 70412 — Exclusion for Employer Payments of Student Loans
nodes.description: Makes permanent the §127 exclusion for employer payments of employee student loan principal and interest. §127(c)(1)(B): strikes 'in the case of payments made before January 1, 2026' — removing the expiration date. Previously created temporarily by CARES Act. $5,250 annual cap (same as other educational assistance under §127(a)(2)) remains unchanged but gains CPI inflation indexing: new §127(d) adds inflation adjustment starting 2027 using 2025 as base year, rounded to nearest $50. Effective: payments after December 31, 2025.

nodes.title: SEC. 70601 — Modification and Extension of Limitation on Excess Business Losses of Noncorporate Taxpayers
nodes.description: Amends IRC § 461(l) (Limitation on Excess Business Losses, enacted TCJA 2017 § 11012, extended by IRA 2022). (a) MADE PERMANENT: Amends § 461(l)(1) by striking 'and before January 1, 2029,' each place it appears — removes the expiration date, making the cap permanent. (b) BASE YEAR RESET: Amends § 461(l)(3)(C): (1) strikes 'December 31, 2018' inserting 'December 31, 2025'; (2) strikes '2017' inserting '2024'. Effective dates: rule made permanent for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2026; inflation adjustment update for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025. Cap: business losses above approximately $305,000 (single) / $610,000 (joint) annually disallowed and converted into net operating loss carryforwards. CBO estimated allowing this to expire would have cost $60-70 billion over 10 years — making permanent raises revenue by those amounts vs. prior law baseline. Note: 2025 base year reset for inflation adjustment actually reduces the effective cap relative to what it would have been had the old 2018 base year been retained. Loses: high-income noncorporate business owners (real estate investors, wealthy farmers, hedge fund managers with partnership interests) who had large business losses.

nodes.title: Coverage Gap Trap: Work Requirement Disenrollment Bars ACA Marketplace Subsidies
nodes.description: SEC. 71119(xx)(7)(B) deems individuals disenrolled for work requirement noncompliance to be 'eligible for minimum essential coverage described in section 5000A(f)(1)(A)(ii)' for IRC §36B(c)(2)(B) purposes. This means they CANNOT receive ACA marketplace premium tax credits. Result: lose Medicaid (work requirement noncompliance) + cannot get subsidized marketplace coverage + too poor for unsubsidized coverage = coverage gap with no safety net. This is an explicit structural coverage cliff created by the interaction of §(xx)(7)(B) with ACA subsidy rules. Compounds SEC. 71119 (work requirements) and SEC. 12 title (ACA subsidy restrictions in node 12). Estimated population in gap: millions of low-income adults annually.

nodes.title: SEC. 100054 — APPROPRIATION FOR THE DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE — $3,330,000,000
nodes.description: DOJ multi-purpose enforcement appropriation. Text (lines 18270-18391): 'there is appropriated to the Attorney General for the Department of Justice for fiscal year 2025, out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, $3,330,000,000, to remain available through September 30, 2029.' 7 purposes: (1) EOIR — 'Hiring immigration judges and necessary support staff for the Executive Office for Immigration Review to address the backlog of petitions, cases, and removals.' STAFFING CAP: 'Effective November 1, 2028, the Executive Office for Immigration Review shall be comprised of not more than 800 immigration judges, along with the necessary support staff.' [ceiling, not floor; backlog exceeds 3M cases]; (2) Drug trafficking including fentanyl/precursors; (3) Immigration prosecution: 'immigration matters, gang-related crimes involving aliens, child trafficking and smuggling involving aliens within the United States, unlawful voting by aliens, violations of the Alien Registration Act, 1940 (54 Stat., chapter 439), and violations of or fraud relating to title IV of the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Act of 1996'; (4) NONPARTY INJUNCTIVE RELIEF: 'Hiring additional attorneys... to conduct litigation and attend to the interests of the United States in suits pending in a court of the United States or in a court of a State in suits seeking nonparty or other injunctive relief against the Federal Government' [direct legislative funding to fight universal injunctions]; (5) BYRNE JAG/COPS: for violent crime, criminal enforcement, and 'immigration enforcement and removal efforts'; LIMITATION: 'No funds made available under this subsection shall be made available to community violence intervention and prevention initiative programs'; ELIGIBILITY: 'a State or local government shall be in full compliance, as determined by the Attorney General, with section 642 of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 (8 U.S.C. 1373)' [sanctuary city exclusion]; (6) Lawsuit settlements maximizing payments to Treasury rather than injured parties; (7) CRIMINAL ALIEN INCARCERATION COMPENSATION (SCAAP analogue): for states incarcerating aliens convicted of felony or 2+ misdemeanors who entered without inspection, in removal proceedings, or violated nonimmigrant status — SANCTUARY EXCLUSION at § 100054(7)(C): funds not available if state 'prohibits or in any way restricts a Federal, State, or local government entity, official, or other personnel from doing any of the following: (i) Complying with the immigration laws... (ii) Assisting or cooperating with Federal law enforcement entities regarding the enforcement of the immigration laws. (iii) Undertaking... law enforcement activities as such activities relate to information regarding the citizenship or immigration status... (I) Making inquiries... (II) Notifying the Federal Government regarding the presence of individuals encountered by law enforcement... (III) Complying with requests for such information.' Cross-refs: 8 U.S.C. § 1373; 28 U.S.C. §§ 516-518; Alien Registration Act 1940; PRWORA Title IV.

nodes.title: SEC. 70413 — Additional Expenses Treated as Qualified Higher Education Expenses for Purposes of 529 Accounts
nodes.description: Expands §529 qualified K-12 expenses and raises annual withdrawal limit. §529(c)(7) rewritten with expanded list: (A) tuition; (B) curriculum and curricular materials; (C) books or other instructional materials; (D) online educational materials; (E) tuition for tutoring or educational classes outside home (tutor must be licensed teacher in any state, or has taught at eligible educational institution, or is subject matter expert in relevant subject); (F) fees for nationally standardized norm-referenced achievement tests, AP exams, college/university admission exams; (G) dual enrollment fees; (H) educational therapies for students with disabilities by licensed/accredited practitioner (occupational, behavioral, physical, speech-language therapies). §529(e)(3) last sentence: annual K-12 withdrawal limit raised from $10,000 to $20,000. Expanded expense categories effective: distributions after date of enactment (July 4, 2025). $20,000 limit effective: tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.

nodes.title: SEC. 10602 — Supplemental Agricultural Trade Promotion Program
nodes.description: Creates new law at 7 USC 5623a. New permanent mandatory CCC appropriation for agricultural export promotion. Text: '(a) IN GENERAL.—The Secretary of Agriculture shall carry out a program to encourage the accessibility, development, maintenance, and expansion of commercial export markets for United States agricultural commodities. (b) FUNDING.—Of the funds of the Commodity Credit Corporation, the Secretary of Agriculture shall make available to carry out this section ,000,000 for fiscal year 2027 and each fiscal year thereafter.' No authorization ceiling on duration — permanent ongoing M/year. Over first decade: >.85B. Supplements existing MAP and FMD programs.

nodes.title: SEC. 70602 — Treatment of Payments from Partnerships to Partners for Property or Services
nodes.description: Amends IRC § 707(a)(2) (Disguised Payments — Partnerships). Changes '(a)(2) Under regulations prescribed by the Secretary...' to '(a)(2) Except as provided...' — removes the regulation-delegation qualifier, making the statutory rule self-executing rather than entirely dependent on Treasury regulations. Effective: services performed, and property transferred, after date of enactment. Rule of construction (subsection (c)): 'Nothing in this section, or the amendments made by this section, shall be construed to create any inference with respect to the proper treatment under section 707(a) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 with respect to payments from a partnership to a partner for services performed, or property transferred, on or before the date of the enactment of this Act.' Makes it harder for partnerships to avoid recharacterization of certain fee arrangements as disguised payments. Targets private equity funds, hedge funds, and large partnerships that structured management fee arrangements as partnership allocations to exploit favorable character treatment. Modest revenue raiser — primarily structural/enforcement change.

nodes.title: SEC. 10603 — Nutrition
nodes.description: Amends 7 USC 7507(d)(5). Extends The Emergency Food Assistance Program (TEFAP) commodity distribution authority through 2031. Strikes '2024' and inserts '2031' in Section 203D(d)(5) of Emergency Food Assistance Act of 1983. No new appropriation; extends existing TEFAP authority. Benefits food banks, food pantries, and low-income TEFAP recipients.

nodes.title: SEC. 70414 — Certain Postsecondary Credentialing Expenses Treated as Qualified Higher Education Expenses for Purposes of 529 Accounts
nodes.description: Allows 529 accounts to be used for 'qualified postsecondary credentialing expenses.' New §529(f): (1) qualified postsecondary credentialing expenses = tuition, fees, books, supplies, equipment for recognized credential programs; testing fees required to obtain/maintain credentials; continuing education required to maintain credentials. (2) Recognized credential programs = programs on WIOA state lists (29 U.S.C. §3152(d)), VA WEAMS directory, industry-recognized exam programs, or programs identified by Secretary with Secretary of Labor consultation. (3) Recognized postsecondary credentials = industry-recognized certifications (ICE/NCCA/ANSI accredited, DoD COOL directory, or Secretary-identified); apprenticeship completion certificates (registered under National Apprenticeship Act); occupational/professional licenses issued or recognized by state or federal government; WIOA §3(52) recognized postsecondary credentials from WIOA program. Effective: distributions after date of enactment (July 4, 2025).

nodes.title: SEC. 100055 — BRIDGING IMMIGRATION-RELATED DEFICITS EXPERIENCED NATIONWIDE (BIDEN) REIMBURSEMENT FUND — $3,500,000,000
nodes.description: New grant fund within DOJ, deliberately acronymed 'BIDEN'. Text (lines 18392-18440): 'There is established within the Department of Justice a fund, to be known as the "Bridging Immigration-related Deficits Experienced Nationwide (BIDEN) Reimbursement Fund"' (34 U.S.C. 61101). Verbatim appropriation: 'not to exceed $3,500,000,000, to remain available until September 30, 2028, for the Fund for qualified and documented expenses.' 7 eligible uses: (1) locating/apprehending aliens who committed crimes AND are unlawfully present; (2) counter-gang law enforcement intelligence; (3) investigating/prosecuting crimes by aliens and drug/human trafficking; (4) court operations for alien crime prosecution; (5) temporary criminal alien detention; (6) transporting criminal aliens for apprehension/detention/prosecution; (7) vehicle/logistics/transport support. RETROACTIVITY PROVISION (§ 100055(d)): 'The Attorney General may provide grants under this section to State agencies and units of local government for expenditures made by State agencies or units of local government for completed, ongoing, or new activities determined to be eligible for such grant funding that occurred on or after January 20, 2021.' Retroactive to first day of Biden administration. Must distribute to 'more than 1 State.' AG has discretionary determination of eligibility. $3.5B is ceiling ('not to exceed'). Cross-refs: INA §§ 101(a)(17), 1373; 34 U.S.C. § 61101.

nodes.title: Paperwork Burden Cascade: Compounding Administrative Barriers to Medicaid Coverage
nodes.description: Four SEC. 71101–71119 provisions compound to dramatically increase administrative burden, each creating independent disenrollment opportunities for eligible individuals: (1) SEC. 71101–71102: freeze streamlining rules → more documentation required for enrollment and renewal; ex parte renewals blocked; extended notice periods frozen. (2) SEC. 71104: quarterly Death Master File checks → 400,000–800,000 potential erroneous disenrollment events per cycle (0.5–1% error rate on 80M enrollees). (3) SEC. 71107: 6-month redeterminations → double the renewal events per year for 21M expansion enrollees; post-COVID unwinding shows 20–30% of disenrolled individuals later re-enrolled as eligible. (4) SEC. 71119: work requirement monthly documentation → continuous compliance burden; 30-day cure notice before disenrollment. Combined effect: a person who is genuinely eligible may face 4 independent administrative check points per year (two redeterminations + work requirement verification + address verification), each creating a disenrollment opportunity. Pre-COVID research: administrative barriers account for majority of Medicaid disenrollments among otherwise eligible individuals.

nodes.title: SEC. 70603 — Excessive Employee Remuneration from Controlled Group Members and Allocation of Deduction
nodes.description: Amends IRC § 162(m) ($1 Million Executive Compensation Deduction Cap, enacted TCJA 2017 § 13601; expanded ARP 2021). Adds new paragraph (7): '(7) REMUNERATION FROM CONTROLLED GROUP MEMBERS.— (A) IN GENERAL.—In the case of any publicly held corporation which is a member of a controlled group — (i) paragraph (1) shall be applied by substituting specified covered employee for covered employee, and (ii) if any person which is a member of such controlled group...provides applicable employee remuneration to an individual who is a specified covered employee of such controlled group and the aggregate amount...with respect to such specified covered employee exceeds $1,000,000 — (I) paragraph (1) shall apply to such person with respect to such remuneration, and (II) paragraph (1) shall apply to such publicly held corporation and to each such related person by substituting the allocable limitation amount for $1,000,000.' (B) ALLOCABLE LIMITATION AMOUNT: proportional share of $1,000,000 based on each member's share of aggregate compensation. (C) SPECIFIED COVERED EMPLOYEE: employees described in § 162(m)(3)(A), (B), or (D) with respect to the publicly held corporation; or any employee who would be described in (C) if applied by taking into account all members of the controlled group. (D) CONTROLLED GROUP: group treated as single employer under § 414(b), (c), (m), or (o). Effective: taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025. Closes structure where large companies spread executive pay among subsidiaries to stay under $1M per entity.

nodes.title: SEC. 70415 — Modification of Excise Tax on Investment Income of Certain Private Colleges and Universities
nodes.description: Completely rewrites §4968 excise tax on private university endowment investment income. New tiered rate structure based on 'student adjusted endowment' (aggregate FMV of assets / number of students): 1.4% for $500,000–$750,000/student; 4% for $750,000–$2,000,000/student; 8% for over $2,000,000/student. Applicable educational institution: ≥3,000 tuition-paying students; >50% U.S.-located students; student adjusted endowment ≥$500,000; not a state college or university. New income inclusions in net investment income: (A) student loan interest on institution-made loans (previously exempt under regulatory exception); (B) 'federally-subsidized royalty income' — royalties from IP where any federal grants or contracts were used in research/development/creation (overrides prior regulatory exception for student/faculty IP). Related organizations aggregated. Anti-avoidance regulations required. §6033: new reporting requirement — covered institutions must report number of tuition-paying students and student count on their Form 990 return. Effective: tax years beginning after December 31, 2025. Harvard-class schools (>>$2M/student) face 8% rate on investment income — hundreds of millions in additional annual taxes.

nodes.title: SEC. 100056 — APPROPRIATION FOR THE BUREAU OF PRISONS — $5,000,000,000
nodes.description: BOP staffing and facilities appropriation. Text (lines 18441-18459): 'there is appropriated to the Director of the Bureau of Prisons for fiscal year 2025, out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, $5,000,000,000, to remain available through September 30, 2029.' SALARIES/BENEFITS (b): 'Not less than $3,000,000,000 of the amounts made available under subsection (a) shall be for hiring and training of new employees, including correctional officers, medical professionals, and facilities and maintenance employees, the necessary support staff, and for additional funding for salaries and benefits for the current workforce of the Bureau of Prisons.' FACILITIES (c): 'Not more than $2,000,000,000 of the amounts made available under subsection (a) shall be for addressing maintenance and repairs to facilities maintained or operated by the Bureau of Prisons.' Hard floor ($3B salaries) and ceiling ($2B facilities). Driven by expected growth in federal criminal immigration enforcement: § 100054(3) funds prosecution of Alien Registration Act violations, unlawful alien voting, reentry, gang crimes. Cross-refs: 18 U.S.C. § 4042 et seq. (BOP authority).

nodes.title: Alien Eligibility Restrictions Appear in SNAP (node 2), Medicare (node 12), ACA (node 12), and Medicaid (node 11) — Coordinated Cross-Title Immigration Coverage Elimination
nodes.description: Three titles restrict federal benefits for non-citizen immigrants in a coordinated pattern: SNAP (SEC. 10101 area, node 2): SNAP work requirements and eligibility restrictions affect immigrant households. Medicare (SEC. 71201, node 12 scope): new 42 U.S.C. 1395mmm limits Medicare to citizens/nationals, LPRs, Cuban/Haitian entrants, COFA residents — same four-category structure as Medicaid SEC. 71109. Existing Medicare enrollees get 18-month transition; SSA must complete review within 1 year. Medicaid (SEC. 71109, node 11): beginning October 1, 2026, same four-category structure — citizens/nationals, LPRs, Cuban/Haitian entrants, COFA residents. Excludes DACA (~580K), TPS, parolees, asylum seekers, T-visas, work/student visa holders. ACA (node 12 scope): ACA subsidy restrictions compound immigrant coverage loss by blocking marketplace premium tax credits for many non-citizens. Cross-title coordination: a DACA recipient loses Medicaid (Oct 1, 2026), cannot get Medicare, and faces ACA subsidy restrictions — total federal coverage exclusion. The same four-category eligibility test appears identically across Medicaid (42 U.S.C. 1396b(v)(5)) and Medicare (42 U.S.C. 1395mmm). The structural alignment is deliberate and creates a uniform federal immigration-status test for all federal health coverage.

nodes.title: SEC. 10604 — Research
nodes.description: Multiple amendments extending and funding USDA research programs. (a) Urban agriculture research (7 USC 5925g): extended 'each of fiscal years 2024 through 2031'. (b) Foundation for Food and Agriculture Research (7 USC 5939): CCC transfer: 'Not later than 30 days after the date of enactment of this clause...the Secretary shall transfer to the Foundation to carry out this section ,000,000, to remain available until expended.' (c) 1890 HBCU Scholarships (7 USC 3222a): ',000,000 for fiscal year 2026, to remain available until expended.' (d) Assistive Technology for Farmers with Disabilities (7 USC 5933): ',000,000 for fiscal year 2026, to remain available until expended.' (e) Specialty Crop Research Initiative (7 USC 7632): ',000,000 for each of fiscal years 2014 through 2025; and (ii) ,000,000 for fiscal year 2026.' (f) Research Facilities Act (7 USC 390d) — new mandatory CCC: 'the Secretary shall make available to carry out the competitive grant program under section 4 ,000,000 for fiscal year 2026 and each fiscal year thereafter' — permanent M/year ongoing commitment buried in research section.

nodes.title: SEC. 70416 — Expanding Application of Tax on Excess Compensation Within Tax-Exempt Organizations
nodes.description: Expands §4960 21% excise tax on excess compensation (>>$1M) paid by tax-exempt organizations by broadening 'covered employee' definition. §4960(c)(2) rewritten: 'covered employee' means 'any employee of an applicable tax-exempt organization (or any predecessor of such an organization) and any former employee of such an organization (or predecessor) who was such an employee during any taxable year beginning after December 31, 2016.' Previously limited to top 5 highest-paid current or former employees. Now applies to ANY current or former employee ever employed after 2016 — no cap on number of covered employees, no dollar floor below $1M threshold. Impact: nonprofits paying above $1M to any former employee (consulting fees, settlement payments, deferred compensation) now trigger 21% excise. Creates complex exit arrangement planning issues. Effective: tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.

nodes.title: SEC. 100057 — APPROPRIATION FOR THE UNITED STATES SECRET SERVICE — $1,170,000,000
nodes.description: Secret Service personnel and bonus appropriation. Text (lines 18460-18508): 'there is appropriated to the Director of the United States Secret Service... for fiscal year 2025, out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, $1,170,000,000, to remain available through September 30, 2029.' USE: (1) 'additional United States Secret Service resources, including personnel, training facilities, programming, and technology'; (2) performance/retention/signing bonuses. BONUS STRUCTURE mirrors ICE (§ 100052(2)): PERFORMANCE: Director's discretion for 'exemplary service'; RETENTION: 2-year additional service commitment; SIGNING: agent/officer/analyst 'hired on or after the date of the enactment of this Act' AND 'commits to 5 years of service with the United States Secret Service.' Written service agreement required: commencement/termination dates, bonus amount, conditions, termination provisions. Cross-refs: 18 U.S.C. § 3056 (Secret Service authority); 5 U.S.C. (Federal bonus authority). TOTAL TITLE X APPROPRIATIONS: $2.055B (DHS) + $29.85B (ICE) + $750M (FLETC) + $3.33B (DOJ) + $3.5B (BIDEN Fund) + $5B (BOP) + $1.17B (USSS) = $45,655,000,000.

nodes.title: SEC. 10605 — Energy
nodes.description: Amends 7 USC 8105(g)(1)(F). Extends Bioenergy Program for Advanced Biofuels (Section 9005 of FSRIA 2002) through FY2031. Strikes '2024' and inserts '2031'. No new appropriation specified; extends authorization for existing program. Benefits advanced biofuel producers.

nodes.title: SEC. 70604 — Excise Tax on Certain Remittance Transfers
nodes.description: Creates new IRC § 4475 (new Subchapter C of Chapter 36 — 'Remittance Transfers'). '(a) IN GENERAL.—There is hereby imposed on any remittance transfer a tax equal to 1 percent of the amount of such transfer.' '(b)(1) IN GENERAL.—The tax...shall be paid by the sender.' '(b)(2) COLLECTION.—The remittance transfer provider shall collect the amount...from the sender and remit such tax quarterly to the Secretary.' '(b)(3) SECONDARY LIABILITY.—Where any tax imposed by subsection (a) is not paid at the time the transfer is made, then to the extent that such tax is not collected, such tax shall be paid by the remittance transfer provider.' '(c) TAX LIMITED TO CASH AND SIMILAR INSTRUMENTS.—The tax imposed under subsection (a) shall apply only to any remittance transfer for which the sender provides cash, a money order, a cashier's check, or any other similar physical instrument (as determined by the Secretary) to the remittance transfer provider.' '(d) NONAPPLICATION TO CERTAIN NONCASH REMITTANCE TRANSFERS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to any remittance transfer for which the funds being transferred are (1) withdrawn from an account held in or by a financial institution (A) which is described in subparagraphs (A) through (H) of section 5312(a)(2) of title 31, United States Code, and (B) that is subject to the requirements under subchapter II of chapter 53 of such title, or (2) funded with a debit card or a credit card which is issued in the United States.' '(f) APPLICATION OF ANTI-CONDUIT RULES.—For purposes of section 7701(l), with respect to any multiple-party arrangements involving the sender, a remittance transfer shall be treated as a financing transaction.' Definitions imported from Electronic Fund Transfer Act § 919(g) (15 U.S.C. 1693o-1(g)). Effective: transfers made after December 31, 2025. Regressive by design: banked/card-using remitters pay zero; unbanked cash senders pay 1%. Affects primarily unbanked/underbanked immigrants (disproportionately Hispanic, Central/South American). U.S. remittances ~$60-80B/year; cash-based subset ~$10-20B; annual yield ~$100-200M. CBO estimates $8-10B over 10 years. Countries dependent: Mexico, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Dominican Republic, Philippines, India. Western Union cash services, MoneyGram, Ria Financial face secondary liability compliance burden.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: Title VIII student loan caps vs. Title VII-A Trump Accounts / child savings provisions
nodes.description: Title VIII (Subtitle B, Sec. 81001) imposes hard lifetime loan caps: $100,000 for graduate students, $200,000 for professional students, $257,500 total lifetime, $65,000 lifetime Parent PLUS per child. Title VII-A (Chapter 1-2 area, node 8) includes 529 account expansions (SEC. 70413, 70414) and employer student loan payment exclusion (SEC. 70412). Interaction: (1) The loan cap regime assumes students will borrow less — but the tax-advantaged savings vehicles in Title VII benefit primarily upper-middle-income families who can afford to save. Lower-income families who rely on loans face hard caps without equivalent savings accumulation capacity. (2) SEC. 70412 exclusion for employer student loan payments may partially offset the elimination of SAVE plan benefits for employed borrowers, but only for those with generous employers. (3) The RAP's 30-year forgiveness timeline vs. the 529 expansion covering postsecondary credentialing (SEC. 70414) creates divergent tracks: wealthy families use tax-advantaged savings to avoid loan system entirely; low-income families are locked into a more stringent loan system. Net distributional effect: loan caps and RAP changes are regressive for those who cannot accumulate 529 savings.

nodes.title: SEC. 10606 — Horticulture
nodes.description: Multiple amendments to horticulture and organic programs. (a) Plant Pest/Disease Management (7 USC 7721): ',000,000 for each of fiscal years 2018 through 2025; and....,000,000 for fiscal year 2026.' (b) Specialty Crop Block Grants (Specialty Crops Competitiveness Act §101): ',000,000 for each of fiscal years 2018 through 2025; and....,000,000 for fiscal year 2026.' (c) Organic Production/Market Data (7 USC 5925c): ',000,000 for the period of fiscal years 2026 through 2031.' (d) International Trade Technology (7 USC 6522): ',000,000 for fiscal years 2024 and 2025, and ,000,000 for fiscal year 2026.' (e) Organic Certification Cost-Share (7 USC 6523): extended through 2031 (strikes '2024' inserts '2031'). (f) Multiple Crop and Pesticide Use Survey (Public Law 115-334 §10109): 'FURTHER MANDATORY FUNDING.—Of the funds of the Commodity Credit Corporation, the Secretary shall use to carry out this section ,000,000 for fiscal year 2026, to remain available until expended.' Benefits specialty crop producers, organic farmers, state departments of agriculture.

nodes.title: Work Requirements Compound: Medicaid SEC. 71119 + SNAP SEC. 10102 Create Dual Administrative Burden for Low-Income Adults
nodes.description: SNAP work requirements (SEC. 10102, node 2): expands able-bodied adult SNAP work requirements, reduces categorical exemptions, requires 20+ hours/week (80+ hours/month) for ABAWDs. Medicaid work requirements (SEC. 71119): requires 80 hours/month work/community service/education for ACA expansion adults 19–64. Overlap population: individuals who are both SNAP recipients and Medicaid expansion enrollees — estimated 5–8 million adults nationally. These individuals now face DUAL monthly administrative compliance requirements: SNAP work compliance AND Medicaid community engagement compliance, each verified separately by different agencies using different systems, each subject to independent disenrollment. SNAP exemption creates Medicaid exemption: SEC. 71119(xx)(9)(A)(ii)(VI)(bb) — SNAP household member 'not exempt from a work requirement under [SNAP]' is a specified excluded individual for Medicaid (exempt from work requirement). But this exemption only applies to SNAP households not exempt from SNAP work requirements — meaning the two systems interact in an asymmetric way. If SNAP is successfully meeting work requirements, the person is exempt from Medicaid work requirements. If the person is exempt from SNAP work requirements, they may still need to demonstrate Medicaid community engagement. The administrative interaction creates unpredictable coverage outcomes for the millions in both programs.

nodes.description: Funds analysis and reporting on universal/nationwide injunctions. Text (lines 18511-18528): 'there is appropriated to the Director of the Administrative Office of the United States Courts, out of amounts in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, $1,250,000 for each of fiscal years 2025 through 2028, for the purpose of continuing analyses and reporting pursuant to section 604(a)(2) of title 28, United States Code, to examine the state of the dockets of the courts and to prepare and transmit statistical data and reports as to the business of the courts, including an assessment of the number, frequency, and related metrics of judicial orders issuing non-party relief against the Federal Government and their aggregate cost impact on the taxpayers of the United States, as determined by each court when imposing securities for the issuance of preliminary injunctions or temporary restraining orders against the Federal Government pursuant to rule 65(c) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.' $5,000,000 total over 4 years. PURPOSE: Build evidentiary record quantifying how often and at what cost courts issue universal injunctions against federal immigration/other enforcement actions. This data will be used in future litigation or legislation to curtail universal injunction authority. Part of 3-pronged anti-injunction strategy (§§ 100054(4), 100101, 100102). Subtitle B — Judiciary Matters. Cross-refs: 28 U.S.C. § 604(a)(2); FRCP Rule 65(c).

SEC. 70421 — Permanent Renewal and Enhancement of Opportunity Zones
nodes.description: Transforms OZ program from temporary to permanent with decennial renewal. Decennial designations: §1400Z-1(c)(2)(B): 'applicable start date' = January 1 after certification; 'decennial determination date' = July 1, 2026 and each July 1 ten years thereafter. Each designation lasts 10 years. Old Puerto Rico special rule struck (effective December 31, 2026). Low-income community definitions updated: ≤70% area/statewide median family income, OR ≥20% poverty rate AND ≤125% area/statewide MFI. Contiguous tract rule repealed. Capital gains changes: §1400Z-2(b) rewritten — deferral period reduced from 7 to 5 years (gain recognized at earlier of sale of OZ investment or 5 years after investment). Basis step-up: 10% for 5-year holds (30% for Rural Opportunity Fund investments). 10-year hold: basis stepped to FMV (capped at FMV at 30-year anniversary). Rural Opportunity Fund (new): 90% assets in rural zones (outside cities >50,000 and adjacent urbanized areas); 30% basis step-up; substantial improvement threshold reduced to 25% of adjusted basis (vs. 50% urban). New reporting: §6039K (annual fund returns — assets, property, investments, employment, dispositions); §6039L (business statements to funds); §6726 (penalties: $500/day max $10,000/$50,000 for large funds; intentional disregard: $2,500/day max $250,000); mandatory electronic filing. $15M IRS appropriation through September 30, 2028 for reporting/analysis. Annual public reports by Secretary including economic impact analysis. Effective: new capital gains rules for investments after December 31, 2026; reporting for years after enactment.

FY2026-2030: ',000,000 for each of fiscal years 2026 through 2030, of which— (i) not less than ,000,000 shall be made available for each such fiscal year to carry out subsection (a); (ii) not less than ,000,000 shall be made available for each such fiscal year to carry out subsection (b); and (iii) not less than ,000,000 shall be made available for each such fiscal year to carry out subsection (c).' CLIFF: drops from M to M in FY2031 — a 68% cut in animal disease preparedness funding. (b) Sheep Production and Marketing Grant: ',000,000 for fiscal year 2026.' (c) Pima Cotton Trust Fund (7 USC 2101 note): extended through 2031. (d) Agriculture Wool Apparel Manufacturers Trust Fund (7 USC 7101 note): extended through 2031. (e) Wool Research and Promotion: extended through 2031. (f) Emergency Citrus Disease Research Trust Fund (7 USC 7632 note): extended through 2031 (strikes '2024' inserts '2031').

nodes.title: SEC. 100102 — APPROPRIATION TO THE FEDERAL JUDICIAL CENTER — $1,000,000/year FY2025-2028
nodes.description: Funds judicial training on anti-injunction doctrine. Text (lines 18529-18544): 'there is appropriated to the Director of the Federal Judicial Center, out of amounts in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, $1,000,000 for each of fiscal years 2025 through 2028.' USE: 'The Federal Judicial Center shall use the amounts appropriated under subsection (a) for the continued implementation of programs pursuant to section 620(b)(3) of title 28, United States Code, to stimulate, create, develop, and conduct programs of continuing education and training for personnel of the judicial branch, including training on the absence of constitutional and statutory authority supporting legal claims that seek non-party relief against the Federal Government, and strategic approaches for mitigating the aggregate cost impact of such legal claims on the taxpayers of the United States.' $4,000,000 total over 4 years. EXTRAORDINARY PROVISION: Congress appropriating funds to train judges that universal injunctions lack 'constitutional and statutory authority' — directing specific doctrinal content of judicial education unprecedented in American legislative history. The phrase 'absence of constitutional and statutory authority' presupposes the legal conclusion in the training mandate itself. Part of 3-pronged anti-injunction strategy with §§ 100054(4) and 100101. Cross-refs: 28 U.S.C. § 620(b)(3).

nodes.title: SEC. 70605 — Enforcement Provisions with Respect to COVID-Related Employee Retention Credits
nodes.description: Standalone provisions (not fully codified in IRC). (a) ASSESSABLE PENALTY: '$1,000 per failure' for COVID-ERTC promoters who fail to comply with due diligence requirements. Due diligence requirements 'shall be similar to the due diligence requirements imposed under section 6695(g).' (b) COVID-ERTC PROMOTER definition: person that provides aid/assistance/advice for a COVID-ERTC document AND (A) charges fee based on refund/credit amount AND gross receipts from ERTC work exceed 20 percent of gross receipts for taxable year, OR (B) aggregate gross receipts from ERTC documents exceed 50 percent of gross receipts, OR both aggregate ERTC receipts exceed 20 percent and exceed $500,000. Exception for certified professional employer organizations (§ 7705). Aggregation rule applies (§ 52(a)/(b), § 414(m)/(o)). (c) COVID-ERTC DOCUMENT: any return, affidavit, claim, or other document related to any credit under § 3134. (d) LIMITATION ON CREDITS AND REFUNDS: 'Notwithstanding section 6511...no credit under section 3134...shall be allowed, and no refund...shall be made, after the date of the enactment of this Act, unless a claim for such credit or refund was filed by the taxpayer on or before January 31, 2024.' Hard cutoff — bars claims filed in 2024 (after Jan 31, 2024) and all 2025 claims. (e) EXTENSION OF LIMITATION ON ASSESSMENT: Rewrites § 3134(l): 'EXTENSION OF LIMITATION ON ASSESSMENT.—(1) IN GENERAL.—Notwithstanding section 6501, the limitation on the time period for the assessment of any amount attributable to a credit claimed under this section shall not expire before the date that is 6 years after the latest of (A) the date on which the original return...is filed, (B) the date on which such return is treated as filed under section 6501(b)(2), or (C) the date on which the claim for credit or refund...is made.' Also: improperly claimed ERTC wages deduction claim window matches the 6-year assessment window. (f) ERRONEOUS CLAIM PENALTY: Amends § 6676(a) striking 'income tax' inserting 'income or employment tax'. IRS estimated over $100 billion in potentially fraudulent/erroneous ERC claims. Jan 31, 2024 cutoff likely subject to constitutional challenges re: due process for taxpayers who filed relying on IRS statements.

nodes.title: Provider Tax Restrictions (SEC. 71115-71117) and State Directed Payment Cap (SEC. 71116) Hit Expansion States Already Harmed by SALT Cap (node 8)
nodes.description: Expansion state fiscal triple squeeze: (1) SEC. 71115 provider tax glide path reduces hold harmless threshold from 6% to 3.5% by FY2032 for expansion states ONLY. Non-expansion states frozen at current rate. This directly reduces state Medicaid revenue generation capacity by billions. (2) SEC. 71116 SDP cap at 100% Medicare for expansion states (110% for non-expansion). Safety-net hospitals in expansion states face massive revenue cuts as SDPs above Medicare rates phase down 10 points/year from Jan 1, 2028. (3) SALT cap (node 8, VII-A Tax): limits state/local tax deductibility, reducing effective federal subsidy for high-tax expansion states (CA, NY, NJ, IL). High-tax states that expanded Medicaid get hit by SALT cap on their tax base AND by provider tax restrictions on their Medicaid financing simultaneously. Compound effect: expansion states (39 + DC) face lower state revenue (SALT cap reduces tax collections indirectly through economic effects), lower Medicaid financing capacity (provider tax), and lower hospital payments (SDP cap) — all at once. Non-expansion states face none of these restrictions. This represents a structural fiscal penalty on the political coalition that expanded Medicaid under the ACA.

nodes.title: Animal disease funding cliff FY2031: M drops to M
nodes.description: SEC. 10607(a)(D) creates a sharp funding cliff for animal disease preparedness: after FY2030, mandatory funding drops from M/year to M/year (68% reduction). This is buried in a section that appears to increase animal disease funding (compared to prior authorization). The cliff affects National Animal Health Monitoring (subsection a), National Animal Disease Preparedness (subsection b, which retains M of the M), and Animal Disease Prevention and Management (subsection c, drops entirely from M to /bin/zsh as a separate line). Given the risk of avian flu and other agricultural biosecurity threats, this cliff represents a significant long-term vulnerability. The section does not explain the rationale for the FY2031 cut.

nodes.title: SEC. 70422 — Permanent Enhancement of Low-Income Housing Tax Credit
nodes.description: Two major LIHTC changes. (1) §42(h)(3)(I): permanently increases state housing credit ceiling by 12% (multiplier 1.12) for calendar years beginning after December 31, 2025 — slight decrease from prior temporary 12.5% boost (2018-2021). (2) §42(h)(4)(B) rewritten — reduces tax-exempt bond financing threshold from 50% to 25% under new dual-path test: path (i): ≥50% of aggregate basis financed by PABs (existing rule); path (ii): ≥25% of aggregate basis financed by PABs, AND at least one obligation in a new issue dated after December 31, 2025 provides financing for ≥5% of aggregate basis. The 25%/5% dual requirement prevents rolling old bonds into new threshold. Dramatically expands number of affordable housing projects that can access 4% LIHTC and tax-exempt bonds without consuming as much limited bond volume cap. Rehabilitation expenditures treated as separate new buildings: effective date determined by §42(e)(4) placed-in-service date. Effective: credit ceiling for calendar years after 2025; bond threshold for buildings placed in service in tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.

nodes.title: Military Construction (SEC. 20013) may include border infrastructure overlapping with border wall (SEC. 90001)
CROSS-TITLE RIDER: Garden of Heroes $40M in Title VIII — unrelated to HELP jurisdiction, classic legislative rider
nodes.description: SEC. 86001 appropriates '$40,000,000 for the procurement of statues as described in Executive Order 13934 (85 Fed. Reg. 41165; relating to building and rebuilding monuments to American heroes), Executive Order 13978 (86 Fed. Reg. 6809; relating to building the National Garden of American Heroes), and Executive Order 14189 (90 Fed. Reg. 8849; relating to celebrating America's birthday).' NEH has tenuous connection to HELP Committee education jurisdiction, but statuary procurement from executive orders is unrelated to higher education finance, student loans, or workforce development. Classic legislative rider pattern: politically contentious standalone legislation embedded in larger must-pass bill. Garden of Heroes initiative could not pass as standalone legislation; embedding in Title VIII guarantees enactment. Pattern repeated in Subtitle H (ORR, $300M). Both subtitles G and H (lines 16360-16435) serve as vehicles for Trump executive priorities. Policy substance of Subtitle G arguably belongs with NEH appropriations or Interior/cultural agencies, not HELP. Subtitle H belongs with Homeland Security (node 14) or Judiciary (node 15) per committee jurisdiction.

nodes.title: SEC. 70423 — Permanent Extension of New Markets Tax Credit
nodes.description: Makes the New Markets Tax Credit (§45D) permanent. §45D(f)(1)(H): 'for each of calendar years 2020 through 2025' replaced with 'for each calendar year after 2019' — continuing $5 billion annual allocation indefinitely. §45D(f)(3): adds 5-year cap on unused allocation carryover — no amount may be carried to any calendar year after the fifth calendar year after the year in which the excess occurred; unused amounts from before 2026 treated as arising in calendar year 2025. Previously, allocations could be carried forward indefinitely. Benefits Community Development Entities (CDEs); investors receive 39% credit over 7 years; businesses in qualified low-income areas. Effective: calendar years beginning after December 31, 2025.

nodes.title: SEC. 70606 — Social Security Number Requirement for American Opportunity and Lifetime Learning Credits
nodes.description: Amends IRC § 25A(g)(1) and § 6213(g)(2)(J). (a) Rewrites § 25A(g)(1): '(1) IDENTIFICATION REQUIREMENT.— (A) SOCIAL SECURITY NUMBER REQUIREMENT.—No credit shall be allowed under subsection (a) to an individual unless the individual includes on the return of tax for the taxable year (i) such individual's social security number, and (ii) in the case of a credit with respect to the qualified tuition and related expenses of an individual other than the taxpayer or the taxpayer's spouse, the name and social security number of such individual. (B) INSTITUTION.—No American Opportunity Tax Credit shall be allowed under this section unless the taxpayer includes the employer identification number of any institution to which the taxpayer paid qualified tuition and related expenses taken into account under this section on the return of tax for the taxable year. (C) SOCIAL SECURITY NUMBER DEFINED.—For purposes of this paragraph, the term social security number shall have the meaning given such term in section 24(h)(7).' (b) MATHEMATICAL/CLERICAL ERROR: Amends § 6213(g)(2)(J) striking 'TIN' and inserting 'social security number or employer identification number' — allows IRS to summarily reject claims with wrong SSN or EIN without formal deficiency notice, stripping taxpayers of certain procedural challenge rights. Effective: taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025. Bars ITIN holders — undocumented immigrants or those with pending immigration status — from education credits. CBO ~$1-3 billion over 10 years.

nodes.title: SALT cap modifications (SEC. 70120) phase back from 0,000 to 0,000 after 2029 — affects state tax revenue and may impact state Medicaid matching requirements
nodes.description: The increase from 0,000 to 0,000 SALT cap starting 2025, with income-based clawback above ~33K, will boost demand for state/local tax deductions among upper-middle-income households, reducing state tax revenues. As the cap reverts post-2029, state revenue should recover, potentially easing Medicaid financing pressures.

nodes.title: Child Tax Credit SSN tightening (SEC. 70104) excludes children without SSNs issued to citizens or lawful permanent residents — creates consistent immigration eligibility restriction across CTC, tips deduction (SEC. 70201), overtime deduction (SEC. 70202), and Trump Accounts (SEC. 70204) via shared §24(h)(7) definition

nodes.description: Double lock on 1115 waiver flexibility: (1) SEC. 71118: beginning January 1, 2027, all new/renewed/amended 1115 waivers must have CMS Chief Actuary certification of budget neutrality under a baseline that includes costs for populations/services the state COULD have covered through normal state plan authority. This ends most coverage expansion waivers — states cannot credit hypothetical spending. Most major current waivers (CalAIM, NY 1115, coverage for immigrants) will fail this test at renewal. (2) SEC. 71119(xx)(10): 'Notwithstanding section 1115(a), the provisions of this subsection [work requirements] may not be waived.' Combined effect: states cannot use 1115 waivers to (a) expand coverage to populations not otherwise eligible, (b) provide non-traditional services cost-effectively, or (c) exempt any population from work requirements. The flexibility tool that most states rely on for Medicaid innovation is effectively eliminated for any purpose that would increase federal expenditures — which includes virtually all coverage expansions.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: Program accountability earnings test (Title VIII Subtitle E) vs. workforce development framework (WIOA/Perkins)
nodes.description: SEC. 84001 creates a federal earnings test: programs where graduates earn less than high school graduates for 2 of 3 years lose Title IV eligibility. The test uses Census Bureau state-level earnings data for comparison. The Workforce Pell Grant (SEC. 83002) in the same title uses a parallel but different earnings test: Workforce Pell programs must demonstrate tuition/fees do not exceed 'the difference between the median earnings of such students...and 150 percent of the poverty line.' These are two distinct accountability frameworks operating simultaneously in the same title. Interaction with external law: SEC. 83002 Workforce Pell cross-references 'section 122 of the Carl D. Perkins Career and Technical Education Act (20 U.S.C. 2342)' for high-skill/high-wage determination, and 'section 3 of the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act' for in-demand occupation definitions. But the Subtitle E earnings test (SEC. 84001) does NOT cross-reference WIOA or Perkins — it stands alone using Census data. This creates potential inconsistency: a program could be WIOA-certified as in-demand but still fail the Subtitle E earnings test because its graduates earn below the state median HS diploma holder. Community colleges and vocational programs that serve lower-wage labor markets (e.g., healthcare support roles in rural states) face compounding risk from both accountability regimes simultaneously.

nodes.title: SEC. 70425 — 0.5 Percent Floor on Deduction of Contributions Made by Individuals
nodes.description: Adds a 0.5% of contribution base (AGI) floor on individual charitable deductions. New §170(b)(1)(I): charitable contributions allowed only to extent aggregate contributions EXCEED 0.5% of taxpayer's contribution base for the taxable year. Application order: (i) subparagraph (D) contributions first; (ii) subparagraph (C); (iii) subparagraph (B); (iv) subparagraph (E); (v) subparagraph (A); (vi) subparagraph (G). Carryforward modified: §170(d)(1)(C): amounts disallowed by 0.5% floor are carried forward only from years where the applicable carryover rule's limit was also exceeded — prevents double denial. §170(b)(1)(G)(i) rewritten: 60% of contribution base ceiling for cash contributions to public charities retained. Also modifies §170(b)(1)(B) coordination with other contribution types. Revenue raiser — affects donors who give small absolute amounts. Effective: tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.

nodes.title: Title X Legal Orientation Program Defunded via § 100013(k)
nodes.description: Section 100013(k) contains verbatim language: 'No fees collected pursuant to this section may be expended by the Executive Office for Immigration Review for the Legal Orientation Program, or for any successor program.' The Legal Orientation Program (LOP) is DOJ's primary program providing detained immigrants with basic information about immigration court procedures — not legal advice, but orientation. This does not formally abolish LOP but removes its primary potential funding stream from the new fee revenues. Combined with the absence of LOP as an eligible use in §§ 100051-100054, LOP faces effective defunding. LOP has operated since 2003 and serves approximately 50,000+ detained immigrants annually.

nodes.title: Title X: Immediate EAD Termination on BIA Denial — Coercion Against Judicial Review
nodes.description: Section 100011(b)(3) provides: 'Each initial employment authorization, or renewal or extension of such authorization, shall terminate— ... (3) immediately following the denial by the Board of Immigration Appeals of an appeal of a denial of an asylum application.' Under INA § 242 (8 U.S.C. 1252), aliens have a statutory right to petition the federal circuit court for review of a final order of removal. BIA denial triggers this right. However, § 100011(b)(3) terminates EAD IMMEDIATELY on BIA denial — before the alien can even file the petition for review with the circuit court. Under prior regulations (8 C.F.R.), EAD termination was tied to administrative finality and usually allowed a wind-down period. Under § 100011: no wind-down, no grace period, no tolling for pending circuit court review. An asylum seeker who loses at BIA and wants to appeal to the circuit court loses work authorization immediately, creating powerful economic pressure to abandon statutory judicial review. This provision disproportionately affects asylum seekers who have colorable legal claims.

SNAP and Medicaid work requirements create parallel disenrollment mechanics
STRUCTURAL: Immigration Fee Revenue Extraction (-3B annually) vs. System Capacity Impossibility (3M backlog, 800-judge cap)
