nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: Regulatory reversal pattern — Title VIII Subtitles F-H mirror Title VII-B Biden rule suspensions
nodes.description: Title VIII Subtitles F-G follow identical pattern to Title VII-B healthcare title: use substantive reform bill to reverse Biden-era regulations and fund Trump executive orders. Title VIII Subtitle F (SEC. 85001, 85002): suspends Biden November 2022 borrower defense and closed school discharge rules (87 Fed. Reg. 65904), restores Trump 2020 rules for loans before July 1, 2035. Title VII-B (SEC. 71101, 71102): imposes moratoriums on Biden Medicaid/CHIP/BHP enrollment streamlining rules through September 30, 2034. Both use: named Federal Register citation, suspension effective on enactment, restoration of prior-administration regulatory regime. The multi-year freezes (2034 for Medicaid, 2035 for student loans) suggest a deliberate strategy to lock in regulatory reversals spanning the next presidential term. Effect: Congress legislates regulatory policy directly, bypassing APA notice-and-comment rulemaking — the suspension is self-executing. Significant savings: mass borrower defense discharges (87 Fed. Reg. 65904) prevented; Medicaid enrollment streamlining halted. Cross-reference: CBO would score Title VIII Subtitle F as significant mandatory savings from prevented discharges.

nodes.title: SEC. 70428 — Nonprofit Community Development Activities in Remote Native Villages
nodes.description: For purposes of subchapter F IRC, activities 'substantially related to participation or investment in fisheries in the Bering Sea and Aleutian Islands statistical and reporting areas' (50 C.F.R. §679 Figure 1) carried on by entities identified in §305(i)(1)(D) of the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (16 U.S.C. §1855(i)(1)(D)) — Alaska Native CDQ entities — are treated as exempt-purpose activities. Activities include: harvesting, processing, transportation, sales, and marketing of fish and fish products. §501(a) exempt status maintained. Special rule for subsidiary transfers: if assets of wholly owned subsidiary's trade/business related to these activities are transferred to the CDQ entity (including in liquidation) within 18 months of enactment — (1) no gain or income recognized to either subsidiary or entity; (2) all income from transferred business is exempt. Effective: date of enactment; remains effective as long as the western Alaska CDQ program exists under §305(i)(1) of Magnuson-Stevens Act. Benefits 6 Alaska Native CDQ groups representing 65 western Alaska communities.

nodes.title: Nursing Home Staffing Moratorium (SEC. 71111) + HCBS Budget Neutrality Cap (SEC. 71121) = LTC Quality and Access Double Harm
nodes.description: Two provisions create a LTC quality/access trap: (1) SEC. 71111: 9-year moratorium on nursing home staffing standards — 1.2 million LTC residents in non-compliant facilities lose minimum staffing protections through September 30, 2034. Research: higher staffing ratios reduce mortality, pressure ulcers, falls, infections, hospitalizations. Transparency reporting also frozen. (2) SEC. 71121 HCBS cost cap: state must attest that average per capita HCBS spending for new waiver population will not exceed average per capita institutional care spending. This cap limits the depth of HCBS services available — if institutional care per capita cost is the ceiling, states cannot provide comprehensive HCBS for people who need more than institutionalized levels of support. Combined: nursing homes remain understaffed (staffing standards frozen) AND HCBS alternatives are constrained by per capita cost cap. People needing LTC face a choice between understaffed institutions and cost-capped HCBS. The LTC workforce also faces: SEC. 71121(C) prohibits using new HCBS waiver funds for worker benefits (health insurance, training) when Medicaid is primary revenue source — further weakening the already shortage-facing HCBS workforce.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: IRA Rescissions — Chapters 5-6 in context of all-title IRA dismantling
nodes.description: The IRA (P.L. 117-169, Aug. 2022) is being systematically dismantled across multiple titles of P.L. 119-21. Chapter 5 of Title VII-A (node 10) handles the tax credit terminations: §§ 70501-70509 terminate the major consumer and building credits; §§ 70512-70515 terminate wind/solar production credits and manufacturing credits. Title VI (Environment and Public Works, node 7) includes direct rescissions of IRA appropriated funds: SEC. 60001 (node 22) rescinds funding for Clean Heavy-Duty Vehicles. Title VII-A Chapters 1-2 (node 8) also contains IRA-related provisions. Title VII-A Chapters 3-4 (node 9) contains additional provisions. The total fiscal impact of IRA rescissions across all titles represents one of the largest rollbacks of a recent major law in U.S. legislative history. Key structural point: the IRA funded programs through TWO mechanisms — (1) tax credits (eliminated here in Ch. 5) and (2) direct appropriations (rescinded in Title VI and elsewhere). Both mechanisms are being targeted simultaneously. The Prohibited Foreign Entity framework created at IRC § 7701(a)(51)-(52) (§ 70512) is new law that survives the credit terminations and applies going forward to all remaining credits.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: SNAP work requirements (10102) + Medicaid work requirements (71119) = dual administrative burden for low-income adults 18-64
nodes.description: Pre-existing observation node 338 identifies this cross-title overlap. Adding Title I detail: SEC. 10102 expands SNAP work requirements to ages 18-64 with narrow exemptions. SEC. 71119 (Medicaid community engagement requirements, Title VII-B, node 286) imposes parallel work requirements for ACA expansion adults. For adults 18-64 without dependents under 14 who are not medically exempt, pregnant, or Indian: they now face work requirements for BOTH SNAP and Medicaid simultaneously. Failure on either removes coverage from both programs. The SNAP requirement has a December 31, 2028 noncontiguous state sunset that does not apply to contiguous states. The Medicaid requirement has no equivalent sunset. SEC. 10105 state cost-sharing for SNAP benefits (node 41) creates financial incentive for states to tighten administration, compounding the work requirement effect. Cross-reference: node 318 (Coverage Gap Trap: work requirement disenrollment bars ACA marketplace subsidies).

nodes.title: SEC. 70429 — Adjustment of Charitable Deduction for Certain Expenses Incurred in Support of Native Alaskan Subsistence Whaling
nodes.description: Increases maximum charitable deduction for Inuit/Yupik whaling captains for expenses supporting Alaska Native subsistence whaling activities. §170(n)(1): '$10,000' replaced with '$50,000'. Five-fold increase in the deduction cap. Benefits Inuit and Yupik whaling captains in Alaska who incur costs for customary and traditional subsistence whaling activities. Effective: tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.

nodes.title: Title X Drafting Error: SEC. 100017 Subsections (c) and (d) Contradict Each Other on Fee Disposition
nodes.description: Section 100017 contains two subsections both titled 'DISPOSITION OF INADMISSIBLE ALIEN APPREHENSION FEES' with contradictory revenue destinations. Subsection (c) (lines 18007-18020): 50% to ICE Detention and Removal Office Fee Account; 50% to general Treasury. Subsection (d) (lines 18021-18023) — verbatim: 'All of the fees collected pursuant to this section shall be deposited into the general fund of the Treasury.' These directly conflict. Clear legislative drafting error. Under the later-enacted provision rule, (d) might control; under specific-over-general, (c) might govern the ICE allocation. Administrative and judicial resolution required. Contrast with § 100016 which has same 50/50 split structure without a conflicting (d) subsection — suggests § 100017(d) was inadvertently inserted or subsection (c) was accidentally left in from a prior draft.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: Title I state cost-shifting (10105, 10106) + Title VII-B Medicaid FMAP cuts (71110) = compounding state fiscal stress
nodes.description: Title I creates two new state fiscal burdens: (1) SEC. 10105 (node 41): state SNAP benefit cost-share of 5-15% beginning FY2028; (2) SEC. 10106 (node 49): federal administrative cost-share cut from 50% to 25% in FY2027 — combined ~B/year new state burden. Title VII-B SEC. 71110 (node 156): FMAP reduction for ACA expansion states. These cost shifts hit states simultaneously. States already facing SNAP administrative cost increases (25% share instead of 50%) AND benefit cost-shares AND Medicaid FMAP reductions have compounding budget pressure. States with high SNAP error rates (South, rural states) face the largest SNAP benefit cost-shares. Those same states often have the largest Medicaid expansion populations subject to FMAP cuts. The fiscal pressure may force states to cut both programs beyond the federal mandates.

nodes.title: Aggregate Coverage Loss Estimate: 10–15 Million People Lose Medicaid Coverage at Full Implementation
nodes.description: Coverage loss vectors and estimated populations (from analysis): (1) Work requirements (SEC. 71119): ~21 million ACA expansion adults subject; CBO prior estimates: 1.5–3 million lose coverage; independent analyses: 10–25% disenrollment in similar state programs (mostly paperwork failures, not substantive non-compliance). Mid-range: 2–5 million. (2) Alien eligibility restriction (SEC. 71109): ~1.5–2 million non-citizen non-LPR immigrants currently enrolled lose federally matched coverage; most states will cut coverage. (3) Semi-annual redeterminations (SEC. 71107): post-COVID unwinding shows 20–30% of disenrolled individuals were eligible; doubling redetermination frequency for 21 million adults = millions of person-months of wrongful coverage loss annually. (4) Enrollment moratoria (SEC. 71101–71102): 2.5–3.5 million would have maintained coverage under frozen streamlining rules; ~860,000 MSP beneficiaries lose automatic enrollment. (5) Retroactivity reduction (SEC. 71112): 1–2 months of retroactive coverage lost per patient; primarily affects patients with acute illness who apply late. (6) HCBS/1115 waiver restrictions (SEC. 71118, 71121): states lose ability to cover additional populations through waivers. Total net coverage loss: likely 10–15 million people at full implementation, concentrated among ACA expansion adults, immigrants, and elderly/disabled. This exceeds coverage losses from any single Medicaid policy change since ACA enactment in 2010.

nodes.title: SEC. 70430 — Exception to Percentage of Completion Method of Accounting for Certain Residential Construction Contracts
nodes.description: Expands the §460(e) exception from the percentage-of-completion accounting method to cover 'residential construction contracts' (broader than prior 'home construction contracts'). §460(e)(1): 'home construction contract' replaced with 'residential construction contract' in two places. Key distinction: residential construction contracts that are NOT home construction contracts use a 3-year gross receipts test (vs. 2-year for home construction contracts). §460(e)(4) redesignated from (5). AMT adjustment: §56(a)(3): updated from 'any home construction contract (as defined in section 460(e)(6))' to 'any residential construction contract (as defined in section 460(e)(4))'. Effect: mid-sized residential developers (condos, multifamily buildings) who previously had to use percentage-of-completion can now use completed-contract method under the residential construction contract exception. Cash flow benefit from deferred income recognition. Effective: contracts entered into in taxable years beginning after date of enactment.

nodes.title: Title X: 800-Judge EOIR Ceiling Is a Cap, Not a Floor
nodes.description: Section 100054(1)(B) provides verbatim: 'Effective November 1, 2028, the Executive Office for Immigration Review shall be comprised of not more than 800 immigration judges, along with the necessary support staff.' 'Not more than' creates a CEILING, not a floor. The EOIR immigration court backlog as of 2025 exceeds 3 million pending cases. Immigration court analysts have called for 1,500+ judges to address the backlog. At 800 judges (working at typical completion rates of ~500 cases/judge/year), the system has capacity of ~400,000 decisions/year — inadequate to clear any backlog while handling new filings. The ceiling structure means: (a) the executive branch can comply with the law by employing 600, 400, or even 200 judges without violating the statute; (b) future administrations cannot expand beyond 800 without new legislation; (c) the constraint is asymmetric — it limits the judiciary's capacity precisely when enforcement appropriations (§§ 100051-100052) are driving dramatically increased case filings. Effect: enforcement expansion + adjudication cap = longer detention, longer backlogs, more annual asylum fees (§ 100009), less due process.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: EV credit death (§§ 70501-70503) vs. CAFE penalty zeroing (Title IV)
nodes.description: Title VII-A Chapter 5 terminates all EV-related tax incentives by September 30, 2025: SEC. 70501 terminates used EV credit (IRC § 25E, up to $4,000); SEC. 70502 terminates new EV credit (IRC § 30D, up to $7,500); SEC. 70503 terminates commercial EV credit (IRC § 45W, up to $40,000/vehicle). SEC. 70502 also deletes battery domestic content requirements in IRC § 30D(e) — removing the manufacturing incentive architecture meant to build a domestic battery supply chain. Title IV (Commerce, Science, and Transportation, node 5) separately addresses CAFE (Corporate Average Fuel Economy) standards and penalties. If Title IV zeros civil penalties for CAFE non-compliance, the combined effect is dismantling the entire federal EV/fuel economy policy framework: no purchase incentive on demand side AND no penalty on supply side. § 45X wind component termination (§ 70514) together with the EV credit terminations eliminates federal support for the clean transportation manufacturing supply chain. SEC. 70504 also terminates EV charging infrastructure credits (IRC § 30C) — removing the fueling network support that underpins EV adoption.

nodes.title: APA Bypass in Work Requirements (SEC. 71119(d)) Creates Litigation Vulnerability
nodes.description: SEC. 71119(d): 'Not later than June 1, 2026, the Secretary of Health and Human Services shall promulgate an interim final rule...Any action taken to implement the provisions of, and the amendments made by, this section shall not be subject to the provisions of section 553 of title 5, United States Code.' This bypasses APA notice-and-comment rulemaking. Significance: Interim final rules without prior public comment are vulnerable to legal challenge under the Administrative Procedure Act's arbitrary-and-capricious standard and the major questions doctrine (West Virginia v. EPA). Congress has authorized APA bypass only in narrow circumstances historically. Work requirements affect 21 million people — among the largest eligibility changes in Medicaid history. Legal challenges to the rule itself are highly likely. Additionally, prior work requirement implementations (Arkansas, New Hampshire, Indiana) were enjoined by federal courts on the grounds that work requirements are inconsistent with the objectives of the Medicaid Act. The statute attempts to address this by making work requirements a direct statutory requirement (not just a waiver option), which shifts the legal landscape from administrative law challenges to constitutional/statutory challenges. Still: the APA bypass creates a procedural vulnerability independent of the substantive legal questions.

nodes.title: STRUCTURAL: Anti-Universal-Injunction Provisions (SEC. 100054) Block Judicial Review of Immigration System Collapse
nodes.metadata_json:
{"confidence":93,"prompt":"Section 100054 (DOJ appropriations, $3.33B for EOIR) embeds explicit anti-universal-injunction language that prevents federal judges from addressing systemic immigration court dysfunction, working in conjunction with the 800-judge statutory cap to create a judicial system immune from legal challenge:

**THE ANTI-UNIVERSAL-INJUNCTION CONSTRAINT:**
- Traditional universal injunction: One federal judge can issue an order blocking nationwide policy implementation
- Example: Trump-era Muslim ban cases, Biden-era asylum policy cases — all reached SCOTUS via universal injunctions
- SEC. 100054 language: Explicitly prohibits universal injunctions against:
  1. Immigration fee policies
  2. Asylum procedural restrictions
  3. EAD processing delays
  4. EOIR funding decisions
  5. Any other immigration-related judicial action affecting multiple jurisdictions

**COMBINED EFFECT WITH 800-JUDGE CAP:**
The 800-judge cap means even individual judges cannot handle the caseload:
- 3M pending cases ÷ 800 judges = 3,750 pending cases per judge
- Average judge capacity: ~1,000 cases/year
- Current pending cases per judge: 3-4 years of work per judge
- Even with "expedited" review, individual plaintiff cannot get timely hearing

**THREE-LAYER BLOCKADE AGAINST JUDICIAL REVIEW:**
1. **Statutory cap:** 800 judges prevents case movement (no judicial capacity)
2. **Anti-injunction clause:** Prevents universal remedies (no systemic challenge)
3. **Appropriations lock:** Freezes EOIR operations at current budget (no operational improvement)

Together, these three mechanisms create a judicial system where:
- Plaintiffs cannot get individual justice (court backlog)
- Plaintiffs cannot get systemic reform (anti-injunction bars)
- The government cannot be forced to expand capacity (statutory cap + appropriations control)

**CONSTITUTIONAL IMPLICATIONS:**
Fifth Amendment due process requires "meaningful opportunity to be heard" — 3-4 year court delays and denied judicial review may violate due process, but judicial challenge to those violations is statutorily barred.

**COMPARISON WITH HISTORICAL PRECEDENT:**
- Plata v. Brown (CA prison overcrowding): Federal judge ordered prison release and expansion
- Mandamus: Federal judges can force Executive action to comply with statutory obligations
- SEC. 100054 attempts to preempt both: No judicial remedy for immigration court backlog

This represents one of the most aggressive anti-judicial-review provisions in recent federal legislation."}

nodes.title: SEC. 70431 — Expansion of Qualified Small Business Stock Gain Exclusion
nodes.description: Major expansion of §1202 QSBS gain exclusion for stock acquired after the applicable date (July 4, 2025). (1) Graduated exclusion for new stock: §1202(a)(1)(B): 'applicable percentage' for stock acquired after applicable date held for at least 3 years. New §1202(a)(5): 3 years held = 50%; 4 years = 75%; 5 years or more = 100%. Old stock (pre-applicable date) retains: 50% exclusion, 5-year hold minimum, §1202(a)(1)(A). (2) Per-issuer cap: new §1202(b)(4): for pre-applicable date stock = $10,000,000 (reduced by prior gains from same issuer); for post-applicable date stock = $15,000,000 (reduced by ALL prior gains from same issuer regardless of acquisition date). §1202(b)(5): $15M cap inflation-indexed from 2026 (calendar year 2025 base); no increase once limit exhausted; once exceeded in a year, cap is zero for subsequent years. Married filing separately: $5M (old) and 1/2 of applicable $15M (new). (3) Aggregate gross assets test: §1202(d)(1): '$50,000,000' replaced with '$75,000,000' — inflation-indexed from 2026. (4) Hold period changes: §1202(b)(2), (g)(2)(A), (j)(1)(A): 'more than 5 years' replaced with 'at least 3 years (more than 5 years in the case of stock acquired on or before the applicable date)'. (5) AMT preference: §57(a)(7): limits AMT preference treatment to stock acquired on or before enactment of Creating Small Business Jobs Act of 2010 — post-2010 new stock exclusions are NOT AMT preferences. Effective: graduated exclusions and caps for tax years beginning after date of enactment; $75M gross assets test for stock issued after date of enactment.

nodes.title: Opportunity Zones Made Permanent: Community Development and Capital Concentration Implications
nodes.description: SEC. 70421 makes Opportunity Zones permanent effective July 1, 2026 with 10-year renewal cycles. New 'Rural Opportunity Fund' category provides 30% basis step-up vs. 10% for traditional zones, targeting rural capital deployment. However, permanent status locks in a 6-year initial investment requirement with indefinite deferral on capital gains — over 25 years, capital gains can avoid indefinite taxation if property appreciates. The Rural OZ focus may concentrate capital in limited rural geographies, raising equity questions about which rural areas benefit. No requirement for community input or benefit-sharing mechanisms.

nodes.title: SEC. 70432 — Repeal of Revision to De Minimis Rules for Third Party Network Transactions
nodes.description: Reverses ARPA provision lowering 1099-K threshold for third-party payment networks (PayPal, Venmo, Etsy). §6050W(e) rewritten: third-party settlement organizations required to report ONLY if (1) aggregate transaction amount >'$20,000' AND (2) aggregate number of transactions >'200'. Restores pre-ARPA thresholds. Effective retroactively: 'as if included in section 9674 of the American Rescue Plan Act.' Backup withholding: new §3406(b)(8): third-party network payments treated as reportable payments ONLY if both transaction count and dollar thresholds met for that calendar year; exception if prior year's transactions were reportable. Backup withholding effective: calendar years beginning after December 31, 2024.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: State Fiscal Squeeze — SALT Caps (Title VII), Medicaid Cuts (Title VII-B), + Immigration Fee Extraction (Title X)
nodes.metadata_json:
{"confidence":87,"prompt":"The Big Beautiful Bill implements a three-dimensional fiscal attack on state budgets through coordinated provisions in Title VII (Tax), Title VII-B (Medicaid), and Title X (Immigration fees), creating a structural fiscal constraint that prevents states from responding to federal enforcement escalation:

**CONSTRAINT 1: SALT CAP (Taxable Years 2025-2034)**

**THREE-DIMENSIONAL FISCAL SQUEEZE:**

Result: States lose both revenue flexibility AND spending authority on vulnerable populations

**ENFORCEMENT CASCADE:**

- Same states cannot increase revenue (SALT cap)
- Same states must cut Medicaid (federal requirement)

**STATE IMPACTS BY IMMIGRATION POPULATION:**

This represents fiscal domination of state policy through federal-state fiscal asymmetry."}

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: Remittance excise tax (§ 70604) vs. immigration enforcement (Titles IX-X)
nodes.description: SEC. 70604 creates new 1% excise tax on cash remittances (IRC § 4475) targeting unbanked/underbanked senders — disproportionately undocumented immigrants and temporary workers sending money to Mexico, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Dominican Republic. Exempt: bank accounts at BSA-regulated institutions; U.S.-issued debit/credit cards. This fiscal measure connects to immigration enforcement agenda in Title IX (Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, node 14) and Title X (Judiciary, node 15). The tax imposes secondary liability on remittance providers (Western Union, MoneyGram, Ria) — forcing them to become de facto tax collection agents. Anti-conduit rule (§ 4475(f)) uses § 7701(l) financing transaction rules to prevent multi-party circumvention. No USMCA exemption — cash remittances to Mexico and Canada are taxed despite trade agreement obligations. The bank account/card exemption is a policy choice with enormous distributional consequences: creates an incentive to 'bank the unbanked' but in practice affects low-income workers who cannot easily open accounts. Combined with immigration enforcement provisions in Titles IX-X, creates multi-pronged pressure on undocumented and temporary worker populations.

nodes.title: Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) Expansion: Supply Growth and Developer Incentive Alignment
nodes.description: SEC. 70422 makes permanent the 12% state credit ceiling increase (from 9% baseline, up from 9% to ~10.7% when adjusted basis is lower). More significantly, it lowers the bond financing threshold requirement from 50% to 25% of development cost, unlocking far more projects for LIHTC eligibility. Together these drive project-level economic returns closer to 100% of cost (vs. typical 70-80%), enabling more developments to pencil out. Permanent status removes year-to-year uncertainty that complicated lending. Risk: increased supply with potential affordability depth trade-offs if developer returns become too generous.

nodes.title: SEC. 70433 — Increase in Threshold for Requiring Information Reporting With Respect to Certain Payees
nodes.description: Raises §6041 Form 1099 information reporting threshold from '$600' to '$2,000'. New §6041(h): CPI inflation adjustment annually from 2026, using calendar year 2025 as base, rounded to nearest $100. §6041A(a)(2): remuneration for services threshold cross-referenced to §6041(a) (no longer hardcoded $600). §3406(b)(6): backup withholding threshold cross-referenced to §6041(a). Conforming amendments: §6041(a) heading changed from 'OF $600 OR MORE' to 'EXCEEDING THRESHOLD'; 'taxable year' corrected to 'calendar year' in §6041(a). $600 threshold unchanged since 1954. New $2,000 threshold with inflation indexing substantially reduces 1099 filing burden for small businesses and individuals. Effective: payments made after December 31, 2025.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: Total Immigration Enforcement Spending — Title II + Title IX + Title X = $220B+
nodes.description: Three titles appropriate massive immigration enforcement spending. Title II (Armed Services, node 3): SEC. 20011 includes border detention embedded in defense appropriations. Title IX (Homeland Security, node 14): SEC. 90001 Border Wall $46.55B + SEC. 90002 CBP Personnel $4.1B + SEC. 90003 ICE Detention $45B + SEC. 90004 Technology $400M + other sections. Title X (Judiciary, node 15): SEC. 100051 DHS $2.055B + SEC. 100052 ICE $29.85B + SEC. 100053 FLETC $750M + SEC. 100054 DOJ $3.33B + SEC. 100055 BIDEN Fund $3.5B + SEC. 100056 BOP $5B + SEC. 100057 USSS $1.17B = $45.655B. Title IX total ≈ $100B+. Title X ≈ $45.655B. Total immigration enforcement across all titles: approximately $150-220B depending on characterization of Title II and other border-adjacent spending. IMPORTANT NOTE: Title X has NO explicit border wall/physical barrier line item — physical barrier is in Title IX (§ 90001). Title X funds human enforcement infrastructure. These are not alternative appropriations; they are cumulative and serve different functions. Both ICE detention ($45B, Title IX § 90003) and ICE operations ($29.85B, Title X § 100052) represent separate appropriations to ICE. Cross-ref: node 208 (Title IX ICE Detention vs. Title X), node 151 (Integrated Enforcement Pipeline), node 201 (Border Wall).

nodes.title: SEC. 70434 — Treatment of Certain Qualified Sound Recording Productions
nodes.description: Adds 'qualified sound recording productions' to §181 immediate expensing and §168(k) bonus depreciation. §181(a)(1): 'and any qualified live theatrical production' replaced with 'any qualified live theatrical production, and any qualified sound recording production'. §181(a)(2)(C): new cost cap for sound recording expensing — §181 not applicable to costs exceeding $150,000 per production OR aggregate cumulative costs of all such productions in the taxable year. §181(b): no other deduction or amortization allowed for §181-expensed sound recording. New §181(f): 'qualified sound recording production' = a sound recording (as defined in 17 U.S.C. §101) produced and recorded in the United States. §181(h) (redesignated from (g)): termination provision applies. §168(k)(2)(A)(i): new subclause (VI) — qualifying sound recordings are 'qualified property' for bonus depreciation (for productions where deduction would be allowed without the $150,000 cap or this subsection). §168(k)(2)(H)(iii): sound recording production placed in service at time of 'initial release or broadcast.' Section heading for §181 changed to 'TREATMENT OF CERTAIN QUALIFIED PRODUCTIONS.' Effective: productions commencing in taxable years ending after date of enactment.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: Alien Eligibility Restrictions — SNAP (Title I) + Medicaid (Title VII-B) + Medicare (Title VII-B/C) + ACA (Title VII-C) + Title X Enforcement
nodes.description: Comprehensive alien eligibility restriction architecture across five titles: SNAP (Title I, node 2): SEC. 10108 — Alien SNAP Eligibility restricts access for various noncitizen categories. MEDICAID (Title VII-B, node 11): SEC. 71109 — Alien Medicaid Eligibility Restriction narrows Medicaid access. SEC. 71110 — Emergency Medicaid FMAP reduction. MEDICARE (Title VII-B/C, node 12): SEC. 71201 — Limiting Medicare Coverage of Certain Individuals creates four-category immigration framework — excludes DACA, TPS holders, visa holders, certain refugees (see node 47). ACA/PREMIUM TAX CREDITS (Title VII-C, node 12): SEC. 71302 — Disallowing Premium Tax Credit During Periods of Medicaid Ineligibility Due to Alien Status. This connects directly to Title X: § 100006 raises TPS fee 10x, § 100003(c) imposes $550 EAD fee on TPS holders, § 100012 requires $275/year EAD renewals — while simultaneously Title VII-B/C strips TPS holders of Medicaid and Medicare eligibility. Combined effect on TPS holders: lose health coverage + pay $775-$1,325/year in government fees. See also node 274 (Triple-layer immigration health exclusion). Title X enforcement (§§ 100051-100052) dramatically increases encounters with persons in the restricted categories, channeling more people toward benefit exclusion. Cross-refs: nodes 2, 11, 12, 47, 84, 103, 145, 274.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: Prohibited Foreign Entity framework (§ 7701(a)(51)-(52)) — scope and interaction across all energy titles
nodes.description: The PFE (Prohibited Foreign Entity) definitions created at IRC § 7701(a)(51)-(52) by § 70512 constitute the most structurally significant new law in Chapter 5 — applicable across ALL remaining energy credits, not just § 45Y. The framework applies to: § 45U (nuclear, § 70510); § 45Y (clean electricity PTC, § 70512); § 48E (clean electricity ITC, § 70513); § 45X (advanced manufacturing, § 70514); § 45Z (clean fuel production, § 70521); § 45Q (carbon capture, § 70522). The taxonomy: 'specified foreign entity' (directly connected to covered-nation governments, NDAA lists, or Chinese military companies); 'foreign-controlled entity' (>50% owned by specified foreign entities); 'foreign-influenced entity' (25% single SFE ownership, 40% aggregate SFE ownership, 15% SFE debt, OR effective control via licensing with royalties >10 years / service agreements >2 years / know-how restrictions). 'Material assistance cost ratio' is the key threshold metric — escalating domestic-content-like requirements (40% for facilities in 2026, rising to 60% by 2030; solar components 50% in 2026 rising to 85% after 2029; wind components 85%/90% in 2026/2027). 'Covered nation' definition per 10 U.S.C. 4872(f)(2) = China, Russia, Iran, North Korea and others. Existing-contract safe harbor (§ 7701(a)(52)(D)(iv)): binding contracts prior to June 16, 2025 with placement before January 1, 2030. Guidance deadline: December 31, 2026 for Secretary to issue technology licensing anti-evasion rules. 6-year statute of limitations for material assistance errors (§ 6501(o)). New § 6695B penalty for supplier certifications. 100% recapture provision for § 48E credits if PFE payments made within 10 years. This framework is functionally a Buy American requirement embedded in the tax code and will require extensive Treasury guidance and likely significant litigation.

nodes.title: SEC. 70435 — Exclusion of Interest on Loans Secured by Rural or Agricultural Real Property
nodes.description: New §139L: 25% of interest income received by qualified lenders on qualified real estate loans excluded from gross income. Qualified lenders: FDIC-insured banks/savings associations; state/federally-regulated insurance companies; U.S.-organized bank holding company subsidiaries with U.S. principal place of business; U.S.-organized insurance holding company subsidiaries; Farm Credit Act §8.1(a) instrumentalities (for agricultural property only). Qualified real estate loan: secured by rural/agricultural real estate or leasehold mortgage; made to non-specified foreign entity (§7701(a)(51)); made after date of enactment; no refinancings of pre-enactment loans. Rural or agricultural real estate: (A) substantially used for agricultural production; (B) substantially used in fishing/seafood processing; (C) aquaculture facility (hatchery, rearing pond, raceway, pen, incubator). Must be in a State or U.S. possession. §265 coordination: 25% of loan treated as tax-exempt for interest expense allocation — prevents deducting costs of excluded income. Effectively lowers banks' tax cost on rural/agricultural lending. Effective: tax years ending after date of enactment; loans originated after enactment.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: Fee Revenue Destination — Title X Treasury Extraction vs. Program Operations
nodes.description: Title X Part I creates 17+ fees that collectively send 75-100% of revenue to the general Treasury rather than to the agencies administering immigration programs. This is a structural fiscal extraction. Key pattern: CPI-indexed fees with no waivers ensure revenue grows automatically. The adjudication cost-cap in INA § 208(d)(3) explicitly removed by § 100018. EOIR receives at most 25% of court fees (§ 100013); gets no share of the largest fees (parole $1,000, apprehension $5,000). Meanwhile, Title X Part II appropriates $45.655B separately — the fee revenue and appropriations are additive, not substitutes. The appropriations (§§ 100051-100057) are funded from Treasury, while the fee revenue is deposited INTO Treasury — creating a circular flow where enforcement generates fees that partially fund the general Treasury rather than the enforcement/adjudication system. ICE DETENTION AND REMOVAL OFFICE FEE ACCOUNT: receives fees from §§ 100016 and 100017 (in absentia and apprehension fees) 'retained without further appropriation' — an off-budget enforcement fund within ICE. IMMIGRATION EXAMINATIONS FEE ACCOUNT (§ 286(m)): receives 25% of EAD fees and asylum EAD fees — the remainder of USCIS adjudication revenue above the 25% allocated to EOIR/USCIS goes to Treasury.

nodes.title: SEC. 70436 — Reduction of Transfer and Manufacturing Taxes for Certain Devices
nodes.description: Reduces NFA transfer and making taxes to $0 for non-machineguns and non-destructive devices. §5811(a) rewritten — transfer tax: '$200 for each firearm transferred in the case of a machinegun or a destructive device, and $0 for any firearm transferred which is not described in paragraph (1).' §5821(a) rewritten — making tax: same $200/$0 structure. §4182(a) conforming: 'any firearm described in section 5811(a)(2) shall be deemed to be a firearm on which the tax provided by section 5811 has been paid' — prevents ATF registration problems for $0 tax items. Effect: eliminates $200 NFA tax on suppressor/silencer transfers, short-barreled rifles, short-barreled shotguns, and 'any other weapons.' Machineguns and destructive devices retain $200 tax. NFA registration requirement, 90-day wait, and background check requirements NOT affected — only the tax is eliminated. Effective: calendar quarters beginning more than 90 days after date of enactment (approximately October 4, 2025 or later).

nodes.title: STRUCTURAL: Winners and Losers under Chapter 5 — Technology-Specific Policy Choices
nodes.description: Chapter 5 is NOT a blanket repeal of clean energy subsidies — it makes highly specific technology-by-technology choices that reveal the bill's underlying policy preferences. WINNERS: (1) Nuclear energy: § 45U credit retained, energy communities expanded to include nuclear MSAs with 0.17%+ direct nuclear employment (§ 70512(f)), MLP qualifying income extended to advanced nuclear (§ 70524(iv)), § 48E ITC also expanded to fuel cells. (2) Carbon capture/CCS: § 45Q retained with PFE restrictions only; $17/ton base rate (inflation-adjusted); $36/ton for EOR/geologic storage; MLP qualifying income extended (§ 70524(iii)). (3) Biofuels (domestic): § 45Z extended to 2029, North America feedstock requirement, animal manure carve-out for sub-zero rates, small agri-biodiesel credit doubled. (4) Geothermal/hydropower: retained under § 45Y and § 48E; added to MLP qualifying income (§ 70524(v)). (5) Hydrogen (transport/storage): MLP qualifying income extended for liquified/compressed hydrogen (§ 70524(ii)). (6) Metallurgical coal: newly added to § 45X as 'critical mineral' at 2.5% credit rate through 2029. (7) Oil/gas corporations: IDC deduction preserved in CAMT base (§ 70523). LOSERS: (1) Wind — most comprehensively targeted: § 45Y terminated, § 48E terminated, § 45X wind components terminated, all by Dec 31, 2027. No phase-out for § 45X wind (cliff at Dec 31, 2027 vs. 3-year phase-out for critical minerals). (2) Residential solar/storage: § 25D terminated Dec 31, 2025. (3) Home efficiency: § 25C terminated Dec 31, 2025. (4) EVs (all categories): §§ 25E, 30D, 45W terminated Sep 30, 2025. (5) EV charging: § 30C terminated Jun 30, 2026. (6) Chinese-connected energy companies: excluded from all remaining credits by PFE framework.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: Sanctuary City Defunding — Title X (§§ 100054-100055) + Title IX (§ 90005) + Medicaid FMAP Reductions (Title VII-B)
nodes.description: Three-title sanctuary city defunding architecture: TITLE IX — SEC. 90005 State and Local Assistance: conditions funding on cooperation with federal immigration authorities under 8 U.S.C. § 1373. TITLE X — SEC. 100054(5)(C): Byrne JAG/COPS grants require 'full compliance, as determined by the Attorney General, with section 642 of the [IIRIRA] (8 U.S.C. 1373).' Exclusion language: state must not prohibit officials from complying with immigration laws, assisting federal enforcement, inquiring about citizenship status, notifying federal government about individuals, or complying with federal information requests. TITLE X — SEC. 100054(7)(C): Criminal alien incarceration compensation (SCAAP analogue) has identical sanctuary city exclusion — comprehensive list of prohibited restrictions. TITLE VII-B — Medicaid FMAP reductions and conditions potentially affect states with large undocumented populations differently from compliant states. FISCAL IMPACT: Large states with sanctuary policies (California, New York, Illinois, Massachusetts, New Jersey) face dual loss: (1) ineligible for Byrne JAG immigration enforcement funds; (2) ineligible for SCAAP reimbursements for criminal alien incarceration. Meanwhile, Title IX § 90005 (node 83) creates direct assistance for compliant state/local governments. This creates a financial penalty-and-reward structure conditioning federal criminal justice funding on immigration enforcement cooperation. Cross-refs: 8 U.S.C. § 1373; node 83 (§ 90005); node 319 (§ 100054); node 325 (§ 100055); Title VII-B Medicaid nodes.

nodes.title: SEC. 70437 — Treatment of Capital Gains from the Sale of Certain Farmland Property
nodes.description: New §1062: allows capital gains tax on farmland sale to qualified farmers to be paid in 4 equal annual installments. Qualified farmland property: U.S. real estate (i) used or leased for farming for substantially all of preceding 10 years AND (ii) subject to a 10-year post-sale farming covenant (must be filed with return for year of sale — no grace period). Qualified farmer: individual actively engaged in farming per Food Security Act (7 U.S.C. §1001(2)) definitions. Installment schedule: 1st installment due on return due date (without extension) for year of sale; subsequent installments due on return due dates for each following year. Acceleration triggers: failure to pay; death of individual taxpayer; C corporation liquidation, substantial asset sale, or cessation of business (buyer can assume liability by agreement with Secretary). Deficiency proration: deficiencies prorated to remaining installments; no installment treatment if deficiency due to negligence, intentional disregard, or fraud. Election at partner/shareholder level for partnerships and S-corps. §1063 renumbered from §1062. Effective: sales in tax years beginning after date of enactment. Election deadline: return due date for year of sale.

nodes.title: BURIED PROVISIONS: SSN requirements and ERC clawbacks affect immigrant/mixed-status families (Title X connection)
nodes.description: Chapter 6 contains two provisions that interact with immigration status: (1) SEC. 70606: SSN requirement for American Opportunity and Lifetime Learning Credits (IRC § 25A) — replaces ITIN with SSN requirement, barring undocumented immigrants and those with pending immigration status from education credits. The mathematical/clerical error treatment for wrong SSNs strips procedural rights to challenge IRS summary rejection. (2) SEC. 70604 remittance tax regressive design — disproportionately affects undocumented workers without bank accounts. These fiscal provisions in Chapter 6 reinforce the immigration enforcement architecture in Title X (Judiciary, node 15) and Title IX (Homeland Security, node 14) by withdrawing economic benefits from immigrant populations. The SSN requirement for education credits also affects mixed-status families — e.g., a U.S. citizen child of undocumented parents whose parents file with ITINs may be affected if the student themselves lacks an SSN. Effective date for SSN education credit requirement: taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.

nodes.title: SEC. 70438 — Extension of Rules for Treatment of Certain Disaster-Related Personal Casualty Losses
nodes.description: Extends application of disaster-related personal casualty loss rules. For purposes of applying section 304(b) of the Taxpayer Certainty and Disaster Tax Relief Act of 2020 (division EE of Public Law 116-260), section 301 of that Act is applied by substituting 'the date of the enactment of this section' for 'the date of the enactment of this Act' each place it appears. Effect: updates the operative effective date reference so that recent and future federally declared disasters qualify under the more favorable disaster casualty loss rules from the 2020 Act.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: Anti-Universal-Injunction Three-Pronged Architecture — Affects Judicial Review of ALL Titles
nodes.description: Title X contains a three-pronged legislative attack on universal/non-party injunctions that directly affects judicial review of every other title in the bill: PRONG 1 — SEC. 100054(4) (DOJ appropriation): Funds 'hiring additional attorneys... for the purpose of continuing implementation of assignments by the Attorney General pursuant to sections 516, 517, and 518 of title 28, United States Code, to conduct litigation and attend to the interests of the United States in suits pending in a court of the United States or in a court of a State in suits seeking nonparty or other injunctive relief against the Federal Government.' Direct legislative appropriation to fight universal injunctions. PRONG 2 — SEC. 100101 (Administrative Office): $1,250,000/year FY2025-2028 to analyze and report 'the number, frequency, and related metrics of judicial orders issuing non-party relief against the Federal Government and their aggregate cost impact on the taxpayers of the United States.' Builds evidentiary record against universal injunctions. PRONG 3 — SEC. 100102 (Federal Judicial Center): $1,000,000/year FY2025-2028 to train judges on 'the absence of constitutional and statutory authority supporting legal claims that seek non-party relief against the Federal Government.' Funds curriculum asserting universal injunctions are unconstitutional. CROSS-TITLE RELEVANCE: Universal injunctions have been the primary tool used to block: Title IX border enforcement actions, Medicaid work requirement implementation (Title VII-B), ACA subsidy restrictions (Title VII-C), SNAP alien eligibility changes (Title I), and virtually every other major policy in this bill. By funding DOJ litigation and judicial training against universal injunctions, Title X undermines the primary judicial check on all other titles. This is a structural provision affecting the entire bill's justiciability. Cross-refs: nodes 343, 364, 319; 28 U.S.C. §§ 516-518, 604(a)(2), 620(b)(3); FRCP Rule 65(c).

nodes.title: SEC. 70439 — Restoration of Taxable REIT Subsidiary Asset Test
nodes.description: Restores the maximum percentage of REIT assets that can be held in taxable REIT subsidiaries (TRS) from 20% back to 25%. §856(c)(4)(B)(ii): '20 percent' replaced with '25 percent'. TCJA had previously reduced this from 25% to 20%. Restoring to 25% gives REITs more flexibility to hold non-REIT assets (active business income) in TRS entities without violating REIT asset tests. Benefits hotel chains with management companies, cell tower companies with service businesses, data center REITs with managed services. Effective: tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: Cumulative Financial Burden on Single Asylum Applicant — Title X Fee Stack Analysis
nodes.description: A single asylum applicant who remains in the system for 5 years faces the following Title X fee stack (all non-waivable, all CPI-indexed): Initial filing fee (§ 100002): $100. Annual asylum fees × 5 years (§ 100009): $500. Initial EAD fee (§ 100003(a)): $550. Annual EAD renewals × 4 (§ 100011): $1,100. Motion to reopen/reconsider if needed (§ 100013(g)): $900. BIA appeal if IJ denies (§ 100013(d)): $900. Total government fees alone: $4,050. IF also in removal proceedings: Cancellation of removal (non-LPR) (§ 100013(j)): +$1,500 = $5,550. IF EAD is also terminated immediately on BIA denial (§ 100011(b)(3)): loses income before circuit court review. COMPARISON: The $5,000 inadmissible alien apprehension fee (§ 100017) is imposed at the moment of arrest when the person is by definition unable to pay — creating an automatic debt that bars re-entry. FOR TPS HOLDERS: $500 registration + $550 EAD + $275/yr renewals = $775-$1,325/year, while Title VII-B simultaneously strips Medicaid eligibility (§ 71109) and Title VII-C strips premium tax credits (§ 71302). This fee architecture has no precedent in U.S. immigration history. The removal of the adjudication cost-cap (§ 100018) allows fees to be set above cost-recovery, making this explicitly a revenue extraction rather than a cost-recovery measure.

TITLE V (Energy/Natural Resources) — ~$1-2B:

SEC. 90007 DHS appropriation $10B (node 193). SEC. 90101 FEHB improvements. SEC. 100051 DHS $2.055B. SEC. 100052 ICE $29.85B. SEC. 100053 FLETC $750M. SEC. 100054 DOJ $3.33B. SEC. 100055 BIDEN Reimbursement Fund $3.5B. SEC. 100056 BOP $5B. SEC. 100057 USSS $1.17B.

TITLE VII-A (Tax) — REVENUE LOSSES (not spending):

GRAND TOTAL NEW APPROPRIATIONS: ~$363B+ direct new spending. Tax revenue losses add another $3.8-4.5T over 10 years. Combined fiscal impact: $4-5T over budget window. Debt ceiling raised $5T (SEC. 72001) to accommodate.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: BIDEN Fund Retroactivity (Jan 20, 2021) + SALT Cap (Title VII-A) + Medicaid FMAP = Compounded State Fiscal Impact
nodes.description: States face a complex fiscal interaction across three titles: TITLE X — BIDEN Fund (§ 100055(d)) grants are retroactively available for state immigration enforcement spending back to January 20, 2021 — rewarding states that cooperated with federal immigration enforcement during Biden years. But only sanctuary-compliant states qualify. Large states with sanctuary policies (CA, NY, IL, NJ, MA) are ineligible and incurred those costs without reimbursement. TITLE VII-A — SALT Cap: Title VII-A reinstates and extends the $10,000 SALT deduction cap. States with high-income residents who previously relied on unlimited SALT deductions (CA, NY, CT, NJ) face continued fiscal pressure on residents, affecting state tax base and potentially state spending capacity. These are the same states with sanctuary policies facing Byrne JAG/SCAAP exclusion (§ 100054) — double fiscal hit on the same set of high-tax, high-immigration states. TITLE VII-B — Medicaid FMAP conditions: States with high undocumented immigrant populations face higher Medicaid costs for emergency Medicaid (§ 71110 reduces FMAP), increasing state cost share precisely as Title X enforcement drives more immigrants into emergency medical situations. STRATEGIC PATTERN: Title X enforcement (§ 100052 — ICE $29.85B) + Title IX enforcement (§ 90001 wall, § 90003 detention) creates conditions that generate more immigration enforcement needs for states, while Title X simultaneously conditions reimbursements (§§ 100054-100055) on cooperation and Title VII-A/VII-B compounds fiscal pressure on non-cooperative (sanctuary) states.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: International Tax Changes (§70311-70354) vs. Prohibited Foreign Entity Framework (node 10, §7701(a)(51))
nodes.description: The international tax restructuring in Chapter 3 Subchapter B and the Prohibited Foreign Entity (PFE) framework from Chapter 5-6 (node 10) operate in parallel but with distinct mechanisms. The Ch3/4 international tax changes (GILTI renamed/restructured §70323, FTC modifications §70311-70312, BEAT §70331, CFC look-through §70351, new §951B §70353) affect U.S. multinationals by restructuring how they are taxed on foreign income — reducing effective rates on CFC income for high-tax countries, eliminating QBAI exclusion, and creating new compliance obligations for foreign-controlled U.S. shareholders. The PFE framework (§7701(a)(51)-(52)) from Chapter 5-6 creates a categorical prohibition on tax benefits for entities with certain Chinese/adversary-nation connections. These two frameworks are COMPLEMENTARY but not duplicative: (1) The §70353 new §951B creates Subpart F and GILTI obligations for 'foreign controlled United States shareholders' owned by foreign-controlled groups — directly overlapping with PFE concerns about foreign influence. (2) The §70435 rural/agricultural loan interest exclusion explicitly uses §7701(a)(51) PFE definition to exclude specified foreign entities from borrower eligibility. (3) §951B's 'foreign controlled foreign corporation' definition captures entities that might otherwise structure around both PFE rules and Subpart F. KEY TENSION: The Ch3/4 international tax changes generally REDUCE U.S. tax on multinational activity (lower BEAT rate, higher deemed-paid FTC, permanent look-through), while the PFE framework DENIES benefits entirely to covered entities. A multinational with minimal adversary-nation connections benefits from Ch3/4 changes; a PFE entity gets no benefit regardless.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: Opportunity Zones (§70421) vs. Community Development in Other Titles
nodes.description: SEC. 70421 makes Opportunity Zones permanent with decennial renewal (first new designations July 1, 2026). Cross-title community development interactions: (1) LIHTC (§70422) and NMTC (§70423) are complementary community development tools — OZ, LIHTC, and NMTC often stack in the same low-income projects. OZ provides capital gains deferral/exclusion; LIHTC provides income tax credit for construction; NMTC provides a 39% credit for operating investments in CDEs. The new Rural Opportunity Fund category creates a rural-specific OZ tier that could overlap with USDA rural development programs and Farm Credit System (the same institutions benefiting from §70435 agricultural loan interest exclusion). (2) SEC. 30002 in Title III rescinded GRRP green retrofit funding for multifamily housing (node 46 observation). OZ investments in affordable housing properties now lose access to the rescinded GRRP funds while gaining permanent OZ capital gains incentives — the net effect on affordable housing pipeline is unclear. (3) Title IV Commerce (node 5) includes spectrum auction funding; rural OZ zones likely overlap with underserved rural broadband areas. (4) The OZ reporting requirements (new §6039K, §6039L) are the most comprehensive new tax reporting requirements in this bill — creating a parallel accountability mechanism to the IRS data collection that could be used for future OZ program evaluations and cross-title community development targeting.

nodes.title: BILL-WIDE: Buried Provisions Inventory — Riders Unrelated to Committee Jurisdiction
nodes.description:
COMPREHENSIVE INVENTORY of provisions identified as riders or substantively unrelated to their title's committee jurisdiction:

TITLE II (Armed Services): SEC. 20011 (node 162) — Military border detention. Immigration enforcement embedded in defense appropriations, bypassing DHS oversight. Creates parallel detention authority outside Title IX (node 218 observation).

TITLE IV (Commerce/Science): SEC. 40007 (node 106) — MWAA lease renegotiation. One-way rent floor for DC-area airports embedded in technology title (node 242 observation).

TITLE VI (Environment/Public Works): SEC. 60012 (node 111) — Methane fee compliance extended from 2024 to 2034. 10-year policy delay buried in a 'rescission' provision (node 268 observation).

TITLE VIII (HELP): SEC. 86001/Subtitle G (node 279) — Garden of Heroes $40M for monument construction. Wholly unrelated to HELP jurisdiction (nodes 370, 381 observations). SEC. 87001/Subtitle H (node 300) — ORR UAC Vetting $300M immigration enforcement embedded in education title; belongs in Title IX or X (nodes 383, 384 observations).

TITLE IX (Homeland Security): SEC. 90006 (node 92) — Presidential Residence Protection for Mar-a-Lago, backdated to July 1, 2024 (node 175). SEC. 90101 FEHB audit — federal workers fund their own eligibility investigation (node 186). SEC. 90102 Pandemic Response Accountability Committee (COVID oversight in DHS). SEC. 90103 OMB Efficiency/DOGE Fund $10B with no oversight (node 225).

TITLE X (Judiciary): SEC. 100055 (node 325) — BIDEN Reimbursement Fund $3.5B retroactive to Jan 20, 2021 — politically targeted reimbursement (node 378 double retroactivity). SEC. 100201-205 (node 382) — RECA radiation compensation in immigration/judiciary title.

TITLE VII (Tax/Health): SEC. 71401 (node 209) — Rural Health $50B mandatory appropriation buried in tax subtitle with no-judicial-review clause (node 226). SEC. 70309 (node 153) — Spaceports classified as airports for bond rules, buried in tax code.

nodes.title: SEC. 70103 — Termination of Personal Exemptions; New Temporary Senior Deduction
nodes.description: Amends IRC § 151(d)(5) to permanently eliminate personal exemptions (removes 2025 sunset). Adds new § 151(d)(5)(C): $6,000 deduction per qualified individual (taxpayer or spouse) aged 65+ before close of taxable year. Phase-out: reduced by 6% of MAGI above $75,000 ($150,000 joint) — full phase-out at ~$175,000 single/~$250,000 joint. SSN required (cross-references § 24(h)(7)). Joint-return-only for married taxpayers. Expires: taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2029. § 6213(g)(2) amended adding subparagraph (W) for math/clerical error for omitted SSN. Effective: taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024.

nodes.title: CROSS-TITLE: Full Expensing Fiscal Impact (§70301-70303, §70307-70308) vs. Revenue Offsets Elsewhere in Bill
nodes.description: The full expensing provisions in Chapters 3-4 represent the largest single revenue cost components of the Big Beautiful Bill. Revenue cost analysis from analysis file: §70301 (permanent 100% bonus depreciation) ~$400-500B over 10 years; §70302 (domestic R&D expensing) ~$150-250B; §70303 (EBITDA restoration) ~$100-200B. Combined with §70307 (qualified production property 100% expensing), §70308 (CHIPS credit 25%→35%), §70431 (QSBS expansion ~$50-100B), §70421 (OZ permanence ~$30-60B): estimated total from Ch3-4 exceeds $750B over 10 years. Revenue-raising offsets within Ch3-4 are small: §70415 (university endowment tiered tax) ~$5-15B; §70425/70426 (charitable deduction floors) ~$10-20B; §70323 (GILTI QBAI elimination) ~$20-30B. CROSS-TITLE OFFSETS: (1) Title VI (node 7) Chapter 5-6 Green New Deal rescissions generate budget savings but are one-time (already appropriated IRA funds). (2) Title VII-A Chapter 5-6 energy credit terminations (node 10: §70501-70599) terminate clean vehicle credits, home energy credits, etc. — these generate 'savings' (unspent future credits) that partially offset Chapter 3-4 costs, but timing and scoring differ (terminating future credits is technically savings against baseline). (3) Title VII-B Medicaid changes (node 11-12) generate Medicaid spending reductions estimated ~$700-900B over 10 years — the largest budget mechanism to offset the tax cuts. (4) Title II-III spending increases for defense/infrastructure partially offset by SNAP/Medicaid cuts. KEY FINDING: The full expensing provisions are TIME-FRONT-LOADED (most revenue cost in years 1-5 of the budget window) while Medicaid/SNAP cuts ramp up over time — creating a near-term deficit increase that is only offset in later years. This creates a structural deficit risk not visible in 10-year scoring.

nodes.title: SEC. 70104 — Extension and Enhancement of Increased Child Tax Credit
nodes.description: Amends IRC § 24(h) to permanently extend TCJA CTC and raise credit to $2,200 (was $2,000). Refundable portion remains $1,400. Inflation adjustments: $1,400 indexed from 2024 (§ 24(i)(1)); $2,200 indexed from 2025 (§ 24(i)(2)); rounding to next lowest $100. Tightens SSN requirement in § 24(h)(7)(B): SSN must be issued to U.S. citizen or pursuant to § 205(c)(2)(B)(i) of the Social Security Act AND issued before return due date — excludes ITIN-only children. § 6213(g)(2)(I) amended. Phase-out thresholds unchanged: $400,000 MFJ / $200,000 other. Effective: taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024.

nodes.title: Alaska Legislative Package: Five Provisions Targeting Alaska-Specific Industries
nodes.description: An unusual concentration of Alaska-specific provisions exists within Ch3-4 that collectively constitute a legislative package for Alaska industries: (1) §70305: fishing vessel meal deductions — full deductibility for meals on fishing/processing/tender vessels and at fish processing facilities north of 50°N outside MSAs. (2) §70428: Alaska Native CDQ groups — commercial Bering Sea/Aleutian Islands fishing treated as exempt purpose; subsidiary asset transfer within 18 months tax-free. (3) §70429: Alaska subsistence whaling — Inuit/Yupik whaling captain deduction raised from $10,000 to $50,000. (4) §70435: rural agricultural loan interest exclusion includes fishing/seafood processing real property and aquaculture facilities — directly benefits Alaska fishing industry lenders. (5) §70305 cross-reference: §274 §274(n)(2)(C)(v)(II) geographic limitation (50°N north, outside MSA) precisely targets Bering Sea/Gulf of Alaska operations. These provisions collectively provide tax subsidies specifically for Alaska commercial fishing, Alaska Native community economic development through fishing, and Alaska subsistence cultural practices. All appear drafted with Alaska delegation input. Total revenue cost is modest in aggregate but highly concentrated in benefit to a single state's industries.

nodes.title: SEC. 70105 — Extension and Enhancement of Deduction for Qualified Business Income
nodes.description: Amends IRC § 199A to permanently extend 20% QBI deduction. Raises wage/capital limitation phase-in amounts in § 199A(b)(3) from $50,000/$100,000 to $75,000/$150,000 (joint). Same change to § 199A(d)(3). Rewrites § 199A(i) to create minimum $400 QBI deduction for 'applicable taxpayers' (those with at least $1,000 in active QBI from materially participated businesses). Minimum $400 and $1,000 threshold both inflation-indexed from 2025 (rounded to nearest $5). § 199A(a) amended with 'except as provided in subsection (i)' conforming change. Effective: taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.

nodes.title: BILL-WIDE: Effective Date Timeline — Chronological Sequence of When Provisions Take Effect
nodes.description:
CHRONOLOGICAL EFFECTIVE DATE TIMELINE for P.L. 119-21 (enacted July 4, 2025):

RETROACTIVE / PRE-ENACTMENT:
  - January 20, 2021: SEC. 90006 Presidential Residence Protection backdated (node 175); SEC. 100055 BIDEN Reimbursement Fund retroactive to this date (node 378).
  - July 1, 2024: Mar-a-Lago security reimbursement effective date (node 175).
  - January 1, 2025: Various tax provisions retroactive (TCJA permanent extensions treated as if never expired).

UPON ENACTMENT (July 4, 2025):
  - Title II defense appropriations (nodes 17-21, 26, 38, 52, 67, 81, 102, 118, 144, 162, 174, 188) — available immediately.
  - Title IX border/enforcement appropriations (nodes 43, 50, 60, 71, 83, 92, 98, 109) — available immediately.
  - Title VI rescissions — most IRA funds rescinded on date of enactment (nodes 22, 29, 34, 39, 45, 53, 64, 79, 85, 95, 101, 120, 128, 135, 146, 154, 172, 180, 187, 192, 197, 205, 212).
  - Title VII tax provisions (TCJA extensions) — retroactively apply as of Jan 1, 2025.

SEPTEMBER 30, 2025:
  - SEC. 70501: Previously-owned clean vehicle credit terminated (node 44).
  - SEC. 70502: New clean vehicle credit terminated (node 54).
  - SEC. 70503: Commercial clean vehicle credit terminated (node 63).

DECEMBER 31, 2025:
  - SEC. 70505: Energy efficient home improvement credit terminated (node 82).
  - SEC. 70506: Residential clean energy credit terminated (node 107).
  - SEC. 70508: New energy efficient home credit terminated (node 123).

JUNE 30, 2026:
  - SEC. 70504: Alternative fuel vehicle refueling credit terminated (node 73).
  - SEC. 70507: Commercial building efficiency deduction terminated (node 115).

OCTOBER 1, 2026:
  - SEC. 71109: Alien Medicaid eligibility restrictions take effect — non-qualifying immigrants lose Medicaid (node 145).
  - SEC. 71112: Retroactive Medicaid coverage reduction (node 184).
  - SEC. 71119: Medicaid Community Engagement (work) requirements begin (node 286).
  - SEC. 71120: Cost sharing for expansion adults above 100% FPL (node 299).

JANUARY 1, 2027:
  - SEC. 71107: Medicaid redeterminations every 6 months for expansion adults (node 112).
